desc: A skydiver jumped from a stationary hot air balloon at an altitude of $$1000\;\mathrm{m}.$$ She fell freely for $$5.00\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Air drag can be neglected during this first part of the dive. Next, she opened her parachute and slowed to $$7.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in a negligible…
statement:
A skydiver jumped from a stationary hot air balloon at an altitude of $$1000\;\mathrm{m}.$$ She fell freely for $$5.00\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Air drag can be neglected during this first part of the dive.

Next, she opened her parachute and slowed to $$7.00\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in a negligible time. She then maintained this speed until she reached the ground. What was the total elapsed time from leaving the hot air balloon to landing on the ground?

(a) $$80.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ (b) $$105\;\mathrm{s}$$ (c) $$130 \;\mathrm{s}$$ (d) $$143\;\mathrm{s}$$ (e) $$210\;\mathrm{s}$$

statement:
A ball is thrown upward from ground height and passes a window on its way up.

$$0.3\;\mathrm{s}$$ pass between when the ball reaches the bottom of the window and when it reaches the top of the window. The distance from the bottom of the window to the top is $$1.2 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Find the height above the top of the window to which the ball rises.

(a) $$0.31\;\mathrm{m}$$ (b) $$0.80\;\mathrm{m}$$ (c) $$1.2\;\mathrm{m}$$ (d) $$5.6\;\mathrm{m}$$ (e) $$21.3\;\mathrm{m}$$

label: FMA01
name: You are standing on a river bank. The river is flowing at a rate of $$2.0\;\mathrm{…
desc: You are standing on a river bank. The river is flowing at a rate of $$2.0\;\mathrm{ m/s}.$$ You see a duck is floating in the river without swimming, and is being carried by the river downstream. You throw two pieces of bread at the duck. One piece lands upstream of the duck…
statement:
You are standing on a river bank. The river is flowing at a rate of $$2.0\;\mathrm{ m/s}.$$ You see a duck is floating in the river without swimming, and is being carried by the river downstream. You throw two pieces of bread at the duck. One piece lands upstream of the duck, and the other downstream equal distance. The duck can swim at $$1.0 \; \mathrm{m/s}.$$ The duck is hungry, and wants to reach the bread in the shortest amount of time. What should the duck do?

Assume that the bread moves along with the water underneath it immediately on hitting the water.

(a) Swim towards the upstream piece of bread (b) Swim towards the downstream piece of bread (c) Pick one and swim for it. It takes the same time to reach both. (d) The duck should not swim at all. It cannot reach either piece since it cannot swim as fast as the river is flowing. (e) The duck should not swim at all. It should wait for the upstream piece to come to it.

desc: Suppose you watch a video backwards and slowed down by a factor $$\lambda > 1,$$ so that if the video is one hour long when played normally, you watch it from end to beginning and it takes $$\lambda$$ hours to do so. The video shows some physical motion. If the motion in the…
statement:
Suppose you watch a video backwards and slowed down by a factor $$\lambda > 1,$$ so that if the video is one hour long when played normally, you watch it from end to beginning and it takes $$\lambda$$ hours to do so.

The video shows some physical motion. If the motion in the video has acceleration $$a$$ when played normally, what is the acceleration $$a'$$ you would measure when watching the video backwards and in slow motion?

(a) $$a' = -a$$ (b) $$a' = \lambda^{-2}a$$ (c) $$a' = -\lambda^{-1} a$$ (d) $$a' = \lambda^{2}a$$ (e) $$a' = \lambda a$$

statement:

(b) $$\dfrac{2s_1s_2}{s_1 + s_2}$$

(c) $$\sqrt{s_1^2+s_2^2}$$

(d) $$\dfrac{s_1 + s_2}{2}$$

(e) $$\sqrt{s_1s_2}$$

At what time(s) does the student have maximum downward velocity?

(a) At all times between $$2\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$4\;\mathrm{s}.$$ (b) At $$4\;\mathrm{s}$$ only. (c) At all times between $$4\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$22\;\mathrm{s}.$$ (d) At $$22\; \mathrm{s}$$ only. (e) At all times between $$22\; \mathrm{s}$$ and $$24\;\mathrm{s}.$$

desc: Each week there will be one optional problem based on the week's F=ma prep material, but in the style of the USAPhO exam. The USAPhO exam is the next exam after the F=ma exam, so these problems begin to prepare you for the USAPhO. (However, the USAPhO covers electromagnetism…
statement:
Each week there will be one optional problem based on the week's F=ma prep material, but in the style of the USAPhO exam. The USAPhO exam is the next exam after the F=ma exam, so these problems begin to prepare you for the USAPhO. (However, the USAPhO covers electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and other topics in addition to mechanics.)

Although these problems are not graded, you should write out your work for them completely in the same way you would if taking the actual USAPhO exam. See (https://artofproblemsolving.com/news/articles/how-to-write-a-solution) for advice on writing solutions.

You can discuss the problem on the message board.

View these problems as optional; if you finish all the week's multiple-choice questions and feel ready to practice writing solutions to problems in the style you'll see in the next stage, feel free to work on the week's USAPhO-style problem. If you prefer to spend more time on the multiple-choice questions and skip the USAPhO-style problem, that is also a good option.

label: FMA01
name: **a)** Suppose the sound waves emitted by a stationary ambulance siren are a length…
desc: **a)** Suppose the sound waves emitted by a stationary ambulance siren are a length $$\lambda.$$ This means the sound wave consists of a series of peaks (of air pressure), and the distance between adjacent peaks is $$\lambda,$$ as shown below. Sound from the ambulance siren…
statement:
**a)** Suppose the sound waves emitted by a stationary ambulance siren are a length $$\lambda.$$ This means the sound wave consists of a series of peaks (of air pressure), and the distance between adjacent peaks is $$\lambda,$$ as shown below.

Sound from the ambulance siren travels at speed $$v.$$ What is the time $$t$$ between when adjacent peaks of the sound wave reach your ear, in terms of $$\lambda$$ and $$v?$$

(The quantity $$f \equiv 1/t$$ is called the "frequency" of the sound, and corresponds to its musical pitch - i.e. if $$f$$ is a large number, then sound is a high pitch and if $$f$$ is a small number the sound is a low pitch.)

**b)** Suppose an ambulance drives at speed $$s$$ through still air. The sound waves given off by the ambulance still travel at speed $$v$$ through the air.

From the reference frame of the ambulance, at what speed do sound waves emitted by the ambulance travel out in front of the ambulance?

**c)** Consider two adjacent sound wave peaks emitted by an ambulance traveling toward you at speed $$s.$$ The first peak leaves the ambulance heading towards you, and a time $$t$$ later, a second sound wave peak leaves the ambulance heading towards you. What is the distance $$\lambda'$$ between these two peaks in terms of $$\lambda, s,$$ and $$v?$$

**d)** Suppose you are standing in front of the ambulance, which is rushing toward you. What frequency $$f'$$ of sound do you hear from the ambulance as a function of $$f, s,$$ and $$v?$$

This shift in frequency is called the Doppler shift.

**e)** Answer the previous question again, but for someone standing behind the ambulance.

**f)** A typical ambulance siren has $$f = 960\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$ The speed of sound in air is about $$v = 340\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ An ambulance in a residential area will typically travel about $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Given this information, by how much does the pitch of an ambulance siren appear to change when driving past you as you stand on the side of the road?

label: FMA01
name: Which Velocity Graph Fits the Equation? — While solving a kinematics problem, a student found the equation…
desc: While solving a kinematics problem, a student found the equation $$a = k - bv,$$ where $$a$$ is the acceleration of an object, $$v$$ is its velocity, and $$k$$ and $$b$$ are __positive__ constants. At $$t = 0$$ the velocity is $$v = 0.$$ Which of the velocity-versus-time graphs…
statement:
While solving a kinematics problem, a student found the equation $$a = k - bv,$$ where $$a$$ is the acceleration of an object, $$v$$ is its velocity, and $$k$$ and $$b$$ are __positive__ constants. At $$t = 0$$ the velocity is $$v = 0.$$ Which of the velocity-versus-time graphs below is consistent with the equation?

Finding the exact formula for $$v(t)$$ requires calculus, so use a different strategy: figure out __key features__ that the correct graph must have, then match them against the choices.

__(a)__ A common mistake is to notice that $$a = k - bv$$ is the equation of a straight line and immediately choose graph (E). What is wrong with that reasoning?

__(b)__ On a velocity-versus-time graph, the acceleration is the __slope__. Can the correct graph contain two points with the same velocity but different slopes? Use your answer to rule out some of the choices.

__(c)__ According to the equation, what happens to the acceleration as the velocity increases? Use this feature to rule out more choices and pick the answer.

__(d)__ The correct graph flattens out after a long time, approaching a horizontal __asymptote__. Find the velocity $$v_t$$ of that asymptote in terms of $$k$$ and $$b.$$ (This $$v_t$$ is the object's __terminal velocity__.)

__(e)__ Is there any way graph (E) could technically be correct after all? The F=ma exam has $$25$$ questions in $$75$$ minutes — what does your answer suggest about how to handle a question that seems flawed or ambiguous?

label: FMA01
name: A Ball Tossed Upward with Air Drag — A ball is tossed straight upward from the ground. It travels up, then…
desc: A ball is tossed straight upward from the ground. It travels up, then down, and finally hits the ground at the same place it was thrown from. The ball __does__ experience significant air drag during the flight. Taking upward as the positive direction, which of the graphs below…
statement:
A ball is tossed straight upward from the ground. It travels up, then down, and finally hits the ground at the same place it was thrown from. The ball __does__ experience significant air drag during the flight. Taking upward as the positive direction, which of the graphs below could show the velocity of the ball from the moment it is released to the moment just before it hits the ground? (Adapted from the 2018 F=ma exam, test A.)

Again, hunt for __key features__ rather than solving for the exact motion.

__(a)__ Graphs (C), (D), and (E) cross zero, while (A) and (B) never do. Should the correct graph have a zero? Why or why not?

__(b)__ Graph (E) has a __minimum__ — a moment of maximum downward speed — after which the ball's speed shrinks back toward zero while it is still falling. Explain why air drag cannot gradually slow a falling ball that way. What does the ball's velocity actually do after it has been falling for a long time? (The idea of __terminal velocity__ — the constant speed reached when air drag grows until it balances gravity — is useful here.)

__(c)__ Which graph is correct, and what is the physical meaning of its long-time behavior? What scenario does graph (C) describe?

label: FMA01
name: Cyclists Meeting on a Velodrome — Two cyclists travel at constant speeds around a $$400\;\mathrm{m}$$…
desc: Two cyclists travel at constant speeds around a $$400\;\mathrm{m}$$ velodrome (a closed track made for cycling) in __opposite__ directions. Cyclist $$A$$ travels at $$1.5$$ times the speed of cyclist $$B.$$ The cyclists meet every $$20.0\;\mathrm{s}.$$ What is the speed of…
statement:
Two cyclists travel at constant speeds around a $$400\;\mathrm{m}$$ velodrome (a closed track made for cycling) in __opposite__ directions. Cyclist $$A$$ travels at $$1.5$$ times the speed of cyclist $$B.$$ The cyclists meet every $$20.0\;\mathrm{s}.$$ What is the speed of cyclist $$A?$$ (Ontario Association of Physics Teachers contest, 1997.)

The diagram shows both cyclists from one meeting to the next: they separate at the start point and meet again $$20.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ later, with cyclist $$A$$ covering the distance $$d_A$$ and cyclist $$B$$ covering $$d_B.$$

__(a)__ A tempting first move is to plug the problem's numbers into the speed formula: $$v = \dfrac{d}{t} \stackrel{?}{=} \dfrac{400\;\mathrm{m}}{20\;\mathrm{s}} = 20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ What is wrong with calling that the answer?

__(b)__ Explain why $$d_A + d_B = 400\;\mathrm{m}.$$

__(c)__ The cyclists ride for the same time between meetings, so their distances are proportional to their speeds. Write a second equation relating $$d_A$$ and $$d_B,$$ and solve for $$d_A.$$

__(d)__ Find cyclist $$A$$'s speed. Then check that the number is physically reasonable, using the quick conversion $$1\;\mathrm{m/s} \approx 2\;\mathrm{mph}.$$

__(e)__ Generalize: if the track has length $$L,$$ the cyclists meet every time $$T,$$ and the ratio of their speeds is $$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \alpha,$$ find a formula for $$v_A.$$

label: FMA01
name: Barkimedes Runs Between Two Cyclists — Cyclists $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$30\;\mathrm{km}$$ apart. They cycle…
desc: Cyclists $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$30\;\mathrm{km}$$ apart. They cycle toward each other, $$A$$ at $$7\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and $$B$$ at $$8\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Barkimedes the super dog begins at cyclist $$A$$ and runs toward cyclist $$B$$ at $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ As soon as Barkimedes…
statement:
Cyclists $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$30\;\mathrm{km}$$ apart. They cycle toward each other, $$A$$ at $$7\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and $$B$$ at $$8\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Barkimedes the super dog begins at cyclist $$A$$ and runs toward cyclist $$B$$ at $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ As soon as Barkimedes reaches cyclist $$B,$$ he turns around and runs back toward $$A$$ at the same speed. When he reaches $$A,$$ he turns around again, and so on, continuing until the two cyclists meet. How far does Barkimedes run in total?

One possible plan is to compute each leg of Barkimedes's zig-zag journey and add them all up — the legs form an __infinite geometric series__, and the sum can be found. But on the F=ma exam, most questions are primarily conceptual: if you find yourself starting a long, complicated calculation, there is probably an easier way. Look for it here, using the definition of speed, $$v = \dfrac{d}{t}.$$

__(a)__ The total distance Barkimedes runs is $$d_{\rm Bark} = v_{\rm Bark}\, t_{\rm Bark},$$ where $$t_{\rm Bark}$$ is the total time he spends running — the time until the cyclists meet. How quickly is the gap between the cyclists shrinking, and how long does it take them to meet?

__(b)__ How far does Barkimedes run in total?

__(c)__ Re-derive the answer in a single step by comparing Barkimedes's speed to the rate at which the cyclists close the gap.

label: FMA01
name: Barkimedes' Average Speed over Two Laps — Barkimedes runs one lap around a track at $$15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How…
desc: Barkimedes runs one lap around a track at $$15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How fast must he run a second lap of the same track so that his __average speed__ over both laps is $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}?$$ Average speed means total distance divided by total time: $$v_{\rm avg} = \dfrac{d_{\rm…
statement:
Barkimedes runs one lap around a track at $$15\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ How fast must he run a second lap of the same track so that his __average speed__ over both laps is $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}?$$ Average speed means total distance divided by total time: $$v_{\rm avg} = \dfrac{d_{\rm tot}}{t_{\rm tot}}.$$

__(a)__ Many people immediately answer $$25\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ since $$20$$ is the average of $$15$$ and $$25.$$ Test this idea by pushing it to extremes. First: if Barkimedes ran the second lap in essentially __zero time__ (infinitely fast), what would his average speed over the two laps be? Second: if he ran the second lap at a crawl, say $$0.000000001\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ what would his average speed be close to? What do these extremes tell you about averaging the two lap speeds?

__(b)__ Without calculating, decide: is the correct answer faster or slower than $$25\;\mathrm{m/s}?$$ (Think about which lap Barkimedes spends more time on.)

__(c)__ The lap length is not given. Either invent a variable for it or simply choose a convenient value — the answer cannot depend on it. Now compute the required second-lap speed.

label: FMA01
name: The Strings of Falling Beads — You have five strings with small weights (beads) tied to them at various…
desc: You have five strings with small weights (beads) tied to them at various points, shown below. Each string hangs from the ceiling, with its lower end just reaching the floor; the horizontal gridlines are equally spaced. One at a time, each string is released from the top, so the…
statement:
You have five strings with small weights (beads) tied to them at various points, shown below. Each string hangs from the ceiling, with its lower end just reaching the floor; the horizontal gridlines are equally spaced. One at a time, each string is released from the top, so the whole string falls freely and the beads click against the floor one after another. Which string produces a __regular__ beating sound — equal time intervals between clicks?

Useful fact: an object that starts at rest and falls with constant acceleration $$a$$ travels a distance $$d = \dfrac12 a t^2$$ in time $$t.$$ Since the actual acceleration and gridline spacing are unknown, work with the __proportionality__ $$d \propto t^2.$$

__(a)__ The beads on string (B) are evenly spaced. As string (B) falls, what does the beating sound do — stay steady, speed up, or slow down?

__(b)__ Moving up the correct string, should the spacing between successive beads get longer, get shorter, or stay the same? Explain.

__(c)__ Invent a unit of time — call it the __tock__ — defined so that a bead starting one gridline above the floor lands after exactly one tock. For a regular beat, the next beads must land at $$2$$ tocks, $$3$$ tocks, and so on. Using $$d \propto t^2,$$ how many gridlines above the floor must the second and third beads start? Which string is correct?

__(d)__ String (E) has its gaps __between__ beads in the ratio $$1 : 4 : 9.$$ Why is that a tempting but wrong design?

label: FMA01
name: Coasting Car, Braking Car — Two cars, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ start with the same velocity $$v_0$$ at time zero…
desc: Two cars, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ start with the same velocity $$v_0$$ at time zero. Both travel in a straight line. Car $$A$$ travels at constant velocity. Car $$B$$ slows down with constant acceleration, reaching zero velocity at time $$T.$$ At that time, car $$A$$ has traveled a…
statement:
Two cars, $$A$$ and $$B,$$ start with the same velocity $$v_0$$ at time zero. Both travel in a straight line. Car $$A$$ travels at constant velocity. Car $$B$$ slows down with constant acceleration, reaching zero velocity at time $$T.$$ At that time, car $$A$$ has traveled a distance $$d_A$$ and car $$B$$ has traveled $$d_B.$$ What is $$\dfrac{d_A}{d_B}?$$ (From Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__.)

Solve it three ways — comparing methods builds flexibility for the exam.

__(a)__ Use the velocity-versus-time graph above. The distance traveled is the __area__ under a $$v$$ vs $$t$$ graph. Compare the two areas to find the ratio.

__(b)__ Use algebra. For constant acceleration, the displacement after time $$t$$ with initial velocity $$v_0$$ is $$d = v_0 t + \dfrac12 a t^2.$$ Write expressions for $$d_A$$ and $$d_B,$$ find the relationship between $$v_0,$$ $$a,$$ and $$T$$ from the fact that car $$B$$ stops at time $$T,$$ and finish the calculation.

__(c)__ Use average speeds. What is each car's average speed over the interval, and how does that immediately give the ratio?

label: FMA01
name: The Range of Possible Distances — You start from rest and accelerate to a given final speed $$v_f > 0$$ after…
desc: You start from rest and accelerate to a given final speed $$v_f > 0$$ after a time $$T.$$ Your acceleration need not be constant, but assume that it is always positive or zero. If $$d$$ is the total distance you travel, then the range of possible $$d$$ values is: (A) $$d =…
statement:
You start from rest and accelerate to a given final speed $$v_f > 0$$ after a time $$T.$$ Your acceleration need not be constant, but assume that it is always positive or zero. If $$d$$ is the total distance you travel, then the range of possible $$d$$ values is: (A) $$d = \dfrac{v_f T}{2}$$ exactly; (B) $$0 < d < \dfrac{v_f T}{2}$$; (C) $$\dfrac{v_f T}{2} < d < v_f T$$; (D) $$0 < d < v_f T$$; (E) $$0 < d < \infty.$$ (From Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__.)

Because the acceleration is not constant, the constant-acceleration formulas do not apply. Instead, reason with a velocity-versus-time graph, like the one below: the distance traveled is the __area__ under the graph, and the acceleration is its __slope__.

__(a)__ What two points must every allowed velocity-versus-time graph pass through?

__(b)__ Describe a graph through those two points, with acceleration everywhere zero or positive, that covers as __little__ distance as possible. What is the lower limit of $$d?$$

__(c)__ Describe a graph that covers as __much__ distance as possible. Can the velocity ever exceed $$v_f$$ during the motion? What is the upper limit of $$d?$$

__(d)__ Could $$d$$ be negative? Combine your results to choose the answer.

label: FMA01
name: The Barge and the Motor Boat — In physics it is often helpful to adopt a specific point of view — the point…
desc: In physics it is often helpful to adopt a specific point of view — the point of view of a running dog, or of flowing water. This is called __changing reference frames__. Velocities measured in a frame moving at speed $$u$$ differ from ground-frame velocities by $$u.$$ __(a)__…
statement:
In physics it is often helpful to adopt a specific point of view — the point of view of a running dog, or of flowing water. This is called __changing reference frames__. Velocities measured in a frame moving at speed $$u$$ differ from ground-frame velocities by $$u.$$

__(a)__ Warm-up: you throw a ball forward at $$30\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ You stay put, but Barkimedes chases the ball, running at $$18\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Ignoring any up-and-down motion, how fast is the ball moving in Barkimedes's reference frame?

Now the main problem. On a river coast there is a port. A barge floats down the river at the same speed as the water flows. At the same moment the barge passes the port, a motor boat departs from the port toward a village a distance $$s_1 = 15\;\mathrm{km}$$ downstream. The motor boat reaches the village after $$t = 45\;\mathrm{min},$$ turns around, and immediately heads back. At a distance $$s_2 = 9\;\mathrm{km}$$ from the village, the motor boat meets the barge. What is the speed of the river water, and what is the speed of the boat with respect to the water? (From Jaan Kalda's __Problems on Kinematics__.)

The boat is hard to track in the ground frame because it has two different speeds: going downstream it adds the water's speed to its own, and going upstream it subtracts. Choose a smarter frame.

__(b)__ Work in the reference frame of the __water__ — which is also the frame of the barge, since the barge drifts with the water. Explain why the boat has a single, constant speed in this frame, and why the return trip therefore also takes $$45\;\mathrm{min},$$ so the boat meets the barge $$90\;\mathrm{min}$$ after the start.

__(c)__ Back in the ground frame, use the meeting location to find the speed of the river water, in $$\mathrm{km/h}.$$

__(d)__ Find the speed of the motor boat with respect to the water, in $$\mathrm{km/h}.$$

name: A particle moves in the plane according to
desc: A particle moves in the plane according to \begin{aligned} x & = R\sin(\omega t) + \omega R t \\ y & = R \cos(\omega t) + R \end{aligned} Which of the following graphs shows the motion of the particle? You may assume $$R>0.$$ (A) (B) (C) (D) (E)

Assume that forces from the air can be ignored, gravity is uniform, and the ground is perfectly flat.

a) The bullets hit at the same time. b) The bullet fired from the gun hits the ground first. c) The bullet that was dropped hits the ground first. d) The order in which the bullets hit the ground depends on the gun speed. e) It depends on the masses of the bullets.

statement:

By what factor should the film be sped up or slowed down in order to look realistic, and what should the real speed of the toy car be as it approaches the cliff?

a) The video should be slowed by a factor of $$100$$ and the model car should go $$50\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ b) The video should be slowed by a factor of $$100$$ and the model car should go $$5\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ c) The video should be slowed by a factor of $$100$$ and the model car should go $$0.5\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ d) The video should be slowed by a factor of $$10$$ and the model car should go $$5\;\mathrm{mph}.$$ e) The video should be slowed by a factor of $$10$$ and the model car should go $$0.5\;\mathrm{mph}.$$

name: Last week, in our practice USAPhO-style question, we derived the Doppler shift formula…
desc: Last week, in our practice USAPhO-style question, we derived the Doppler shift formula with the assumption that you're standing either directly in front of or directly behind the source of the sound, which is moving directly toward or away from you. The week, we'll derive a more…
statement:
Last week, in our practice USAPhO-style question, we derived the Doppler shift formula with the assumption that you're standing either directly in front of or directly behind the source of the sound, which is moving directly toward or away from you.

The week, we'll derive a more general version of the Doppler shift formula.

**a)** Suppose your coordinates are $$(0,0).$$ An ambulance has the coordinates $$(x,y)$$ and is moving at speed $$v$$ in the positive $$x$$ direction. It emits the peak of one sound wave from the position $$(x,y).$$ The ambulance emits the peak of a sound wave every $$t$$ seconds. Find the position of the ambulance when it next emits a sound wave peak.

**b)** Find the time between the arrival of the two sound waves at your own position. Let the speed of sound be $$c.$$

**c)** The expression you found in (b) is difficult to work with. We can find a simpler expression that is still approximately correct. Suppose the two dots in the diagram below represent the position of the ambulance at times $$0$$ and $$t.$$ Argue that the extra distance sound must travel to reach you from the first position of the ambulance is very nearly equal to the red line's length.

You can assume that the angle that look like right angles are right angles. (Hint: how well does the solid black line approximate a piece of a circle? What circle?)

**d)** Find the length of the red line in part (c) as a function of $$v, t,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**e)** Find the approximate difference in arrival times between the two sound wave peaks at your position.

**f)** If the ambulance emits sound with frequency $$f,$$ what frequency sound do you hear as a function of $$v, c$$ and $$\theta?$$

label: FMA02
name: A Bug in a Cubical Room — (2008 F=ma exam) A bug is crawling along the walls inside a cubical room that has…
desc: (2008 F=ma exam) A bug is crawling along the walls inside a cubical room that has an edge length of $$3\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The bug starts from the back upper left corner of the cube and finishes at the front lower right corner, as shown. __(a)__ The question asks for the magnitude…
statement:
(2008 F=ma exam) A bug is crawling along the walls inside a cubical room that has an edge length of $$3\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The bug starts from the back upper left corner of the cube and finishes at the front lower right corner, as shown.

__(a)__ The question asks for the magnitude of the bug's __displacement__. Is that the same as the total distance the bug crawls? Explain the difference.

__(b)__ The __distance formula__ in three dimensions is the generalization of the Pythagorean theorem: $$(\Delta s)^2=(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2+(\Delta z)^2,$$ where $$\Delta s$$ is the magnitude of the displacement and $$\Delta x,$$ $$\Delta y,$$ $$\Delta z$$ are the changes in three perpendicular coordinates. Find the magnitude of the bug's displacement. (Don't forget the units!)

__(c)__ A quick check on unit bookkeeping. If $$\Delta x$$ stands for the length of one side of this room, which of these equations uses unit symbols correctly: $$\Delta x=3,$$ $$\Delta x=3\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$\Delta x\;\mathrm{m}=3,$$ or $$\Delta x\;\mathrm{m}=3\;\mathrm{m}?$$ Also: is $$3\;\mathrm{m}=300\;\mathrm{cm}$$ a correct equation, and what goes wrong if you strip the unit symbols off of it?

label: FMA02
name: A Plane in a Crosswind — The wind is blowing due north at $$30\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Relative to the air, a plane…
desc: The wind is blowing due north at $$30\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Relative to the air, a plane is flying at $$300\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ pointed $$10^\circ$$ north of east. At what angle north of east does the plane move relative to the ground? The plane's velocity relative to the ground is the…
statement:
The wind is blowing due north at $$30\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Relative to the air, a plane is flying at $$300\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ pointed $$10^\circ$$ north of east. At what angle north of east does the plane move relative to the ground?

The plane's velocity relative to the ground is the __vector sum__ $$\vec{v}_{\rm plane;g}=\vec{v}_{\rm plane;w}+\vec{v}_{\rm wind},$$ where $$\vec{v}_{\rm plane;w}$$ is the plane's velocity relative to the wind (the air) and $$\vec{v}_{\rm wind}$$ is the wind's velocity relative to the ground. Graphically, vectors add __tip-to-tail__: redraw $$\vec{v}_{\rm wind}$$ starting from the tip of $$\vec{v}_{\rm plane;w}$$; the sum runs from the common starting point to the final tip, as shown.

__(a)__ Find the north and east components of $$\vec{v}_{\rm plane;w}$$ (you'll want a calculator), and the north and east components of $$\vec{v}_{\rm wind}$$ (no calculator needed).

__(b)__ Add the components to find the north and east components of the plane's velocity relative to the ground.

__(c)__ Use your components to find the angle $$\theta_g$$ north of east at which the plane moves relative to the ground.

label: FMA02
name: Racing Around a Square Course — (2003 Ontario Association of Physics Teachers contest) A light aircraft was…
desc: (2003 Ontario Association of Physics Teachers contest) A light aircraft was trying to set a class speed record over a square closed course of side length $$150\;\mathrm{km}.$$ A steady wind of $$20.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ was blowing from the west. The pilot applied wind-correction…
statement:
(2003 Ontario Association of Physics Teachers contest) A light aircraft was trying to set a class speed record over a square closed course of side length $$150\;\mathrm{km}.$$ A steady wind of $$20.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ was blowing from the west. The pilot applied wind-correction angles such that the aircraft never left the prescribed course, flying at constant speed $$100\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ relative to the air. How long did the plane take to fly the course?

Solve this problem __symbolically__: let the wind speed be $$w,$$ the plane's speed relative to the air be $$v,$$ and the side length of the course be $$x,$$ and only plug in numbers at the very end. (A wind "from the west" blows toward the east.)

__(a)__ On the eastbound (downwind) leg the wind carries the plane along, and on the westbound (upwind) leg it opposes the plane. Find the plane's ground speed and the time taken on each of these two legs, in terms of $$v,$$ $$w,$$ and $$x.$$

__(b)__ On the two north–south legs the wind is a pure crosswind, so the pilot must angle the plane's nose partly into the wind to avoid being blown off the course. How large must the westward (into-wind) component of the plane's air velocity be? Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the along-course component of the plane's velocity, and the time for each of these legs.

__(c)__ Combine your results into a single formula for the total time $$t$$ around the course.

__(d)__ Before plugging in numbers, interrogate your formula. What does it give when $$w=0,$$ and why does that make sense? What happens as $$w\to v,$$ and what does that mean physically?

__(e)__ Now substitute $$v=100\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ $$w=20.0\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and $$x=150\;\mathrm{km}$$ — being careful about units — and find the time in seconds and in hours.

label: FMA02
name: The Monkey and the Banana Cannon — A monkey is hanging from a tree branch. A person on the ground aims a…
desc: A monkey is hanging from a tree branch. A person on the ground aims a banana cannon __directly at the monkey__ and fires a banana; at that exact moment, the monkey lets go of the branch and begins to fall. The cannon fires fast enough to shoot a banana all the way to the tree…
statement:
A monkey is hanging from a tree branch. A person on the ground aims a banana cannon __directly at the monkey__ and fires a banana; at that exact moment, the monkey lets go of the branch and begins to fall. The cannon fires fast enough to shoot a banana all the way to the tree. Ignore air resistance.

__(a)__ What happens? (A) The banana goes over the monkey's head. (B) The banana goes directly to the monkey. (C) The banana goes under the monkey. (D) If the cannon shoots the banana at a high speed, the banana goes over the monkey's head, and the opposite if it shoots the banana slower. (E) If the cannon shoots the banana at a high speed, the banana goes below the monkey, and the opposite if it shoots the banana slower.

__(b)__ Justify your answer by treating the horizontal and vertical directions __separately__. Suppose the banana leaves the cannon with speed $$v$$ at an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, and the horizontal distance from the cannon to the monkey is $$x.$$ First find the time $$t$$ for the banana to travel the horizontal distance to the tree. Then compare the vertical positions: the banana's height obeys $$y=y_0+v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^2,$$ where $$y_0$$ is its launch height and $$v_{0y}$$ its initial vertical velocity. How far below its no-gravity straight-line path is the banana at time $$t,$$ and how far has the monkey fallen?

__(c)__ Explain the result a second way, using a clever choice of __reference frame__: describe the banana's motion as seen by an observer who is in free fall, accelerating downward at $$g.$$

label: FMA02
name: The Best Angle for Range — At what angle should you launch a projectile to maximize its __range__ — the…
desc: At what angle should you launch a projectile to maximize its __range__ — the horizontal distance it covers before landing? The projectile is launched at the same fixed speed $$v_0$$ regardless of the angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, it begins and ends at the same height…
statement:
At what angle should you launch a projectile to maximize its __range__ — the horizontal distance it covers before landing? The projectile is launched at the same fixed speed $$v_0$$ regardless of the angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, it begins and ends at the same height, air resistance is ignored, and gravity is a uniform downward acceleration of magnitude $$g.$$

__(a)__ Think about the vertical direction first. The initial vertical velocity component is $$v_{0y}=v_0\sin\theta,$$ and gravity removes vertical velocity at the steady rate $$g.$$ Without solving any quadratic, find the time for the projectile to reach the top of its flight, and the total time $$t_{\rm return}$$ before it returns to its launch height.

__(b)__ Now the horizontal direction: the projectile moves horizontally at the constant speed $$v_0\cos\theta.$$ Find the range $$x_{\rm range}$$ in terms of $$v_0,$$ $$\theta,$$ and $$g,$$ and simplify it using the identity $$2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin(2\theta).$$

__(c)__ What launch angle maximizes the range, and what is the maximum range?

label: FMA02
name: Best Launch Angle from a Cliff — (2017 F=ma exam) A projectile is launched with speed $$v_0$$ off the edge of…
desc: (2017 F=ma exam) A projectile is launched with speed $$v_0$$ off the edge of a cliff of height $$h,$$ at an angle $$\theta$$ from the horizontal. Air friction is negligible. To maximize the horizontal range of the projectile, $$\theta$$ should satisfy: (A)…
statement:
(2017 F=ma exam) A projectile is launched with speed $$v_0$$ off the edge of a cliff of height $$h,$$ at an angle $$\theta$$ from the horizontal. Air friction is negligible. To maximize the horizontal range of the projectile, $$\theta$$ should satisfy: (A) $$45^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$$ (B) $$\theta=45^\circ$$ (C) $$0^\circ<\theta<45^\circ$$ (D) $$\theta=0^\circ$$ (E) $$\theta<45^\circ$$ or $$\theta>45^\circ$$ depending on the values of $$h$$ and $$v_0.$$

Useful background: for a projectile that lands at the __same height__ it was launched from, the range is $$x_{\rm range}=\dfrac{v_0^2\sin(2\theta)}{g},$$ which is maximized at exactly $$\theta=45^\circ.$$

__(a)__ Why can't we just answer $$45^\circ$$ here? What assumption behind that familiar result no longer holds?

__(b)__ The answer choices are wide ranges rather than exact formulas — a hint that a good qualitative argument beats an exact calculation (which turns out to be quite messy). Reason from an __extreme case__: imagine the cliff is so deep that the projectile takes three years to reach the bottom. Does aiming upward to add a few seconds of flight time meaningfully extend the range? What launch angle is best in this limit?

__(c)__ Now consider the opposite extreme: a cliff so shallow it is trivial compared with how high the projectile can fly. What angle is best in that limit?

__(d)__ Combine the two limits to choose the answer.

label: FMA02
name: Tangential and Perpendicular Acceleration — (2007 F=ma exam) A small point-like object is thrown horizontally…
desc: (2007 F=ma exam) A small point-like object is thrown horizontally off of a $$50.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ high building with an initial speed of $$10.0\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The object falls freely under the influence of gravity; ignore air resistance and take $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ At any…
statement:
(2007 F=ma exam) A small point-like object is thrown horizontally off of a $$50.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ high building with an initial speed of $$10.0\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The object falls freely under the influence of gravity; ignore air resistance and take $$g=10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ At any point along the trajectory, the acceleration due to gravity can be broken into a component __tangential__ to the trajectory and a component __perpendicular__ to the trajectory.

How many seconds after the object is thrown is the tangential component of its acceleration equal to the perpendicular component? (a) $$2.00\;\mathrm{s}$$ (b) $$1.50\;\mathrm{s}$$ (c) $$1.00\;\mathrm{s}$$ (d) $$0.50\;\mathrm{s}$$ (e) The building is not high enough for this to occur.

__(a)__ The tangential component $$\vec{g}_{\parallel}$$ lies along the velocity vector — it is the __projection__ of the gravitational acceleration onto the velocity, and $$\vec{g}_{\perp}$$ is what's left over. For these two components to be equal in magnitude, in what direction must the object be moving?

__(b)__ What does that direction of motion imply about the object's horizontal and vertical velocity components? Use that to find the time, and pick the answer choice.

__(c)__ Check that the object is still in the air at that moment by computing how far it has fallen.

label: FMA02
name: The Pea Shooter and the Edge — A certain pea shooter shoots a very large number of peas in two dimensions…
desc: A certain pea shooter shoots a very large number of peas in two dimensions around itself: viewed from above, the peas leave at equal angles of separation, all with the same speed $$s=10\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ relative to the pea shooter. The pea shooter is set drifting across a…
statement:
A certain pea shooter shoots a very large number of peas in two dimensions around itself: viewed from above, the peas leave at equal angles of separation, all with the same speed $$s=10\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ relative to the pea shooter. The pea shooter is set drifting across a frictionless horizontal surface, approaching one edge of the surface at $$v=5\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and it fires all of its peas while in motion. What fraction of the peas eventually fall off the edge the pea shooter is approaching? (The other edges are all very far away.) Work symbolically in terms of $$v$$ and $$s,$$ and plug in the numbers at the end.

__(a)__ Warm-up: if the pea shooter were __not__ moving, what fraction of the peas would fall off the edge? (Since the number of peas is very large, you can ignore the at-most-two peas fired exactly parallel to the edge.)

__(b)__ The surface's reference frame is awkward here, so switch to the __pea shooter's frame__: in it, the shooter sits still, the peas fly out at speed $$s$$ in all directions, and the edge moves toward the shooter at speed $$v.$$ A pea escapes only if it outruns the advancing edge. Consider a pea fired at angle $$\theta$$ from the direction pointing straight away from the edge; what is the component of its velocity directly away from the edge? Find the critical angle $$\theta_c$$ at which a pea just barely avoids falling.

__(c)__ Use $$\theta_c$$ to write the fraction of peas that fall off the edge as a function of $$v$$ and $$s.$$ Then test your formula in two special cases: $$v=0$$ (it should reproduce your answer to part (a)) and $$v=s.$$

__(d)__ Finally, put in $$v=5\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and $$s=10\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ to answer the question.

The handle of a floor mop makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the vertical direction as shown in the figure. Let $$\mu_k$$ be the coefficient of kinetic friction between mop and floor and $$\mu_s$$ the coefficient of static friction between mop and floor. Neglect the mass of the handle and mop. What is the minimum angle $$\theta_0$$ for it to be possible to slide the mop across the floor by applying force in the direction of the handle?

(a) $$\theta_0 = \mathrm{arccos}(\mu_s)$$ (b) $$\theta_0 = \mathrm{arctan}(\mu_s)$$ (c) $$\theta_0 = \mathrm{arccot}(\mu_s)$$ (d) $$\theta_0 = \mu_s/2$$ (e) $$\theta_0 = \mathrm{arcsin}(\mu_s)$$

label: FMA03
name: A horizontal force $$F$$ of $$12 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ pushes a block weighing $$5.0…
desc: A horizontal force $$F$$ of $$12 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ pushes a block weighing $$5.0 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ against a vertical wall as shown. The coefficient of static friction between the wall and the block is $$0.60$$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction is $$0.40.$$ Assume the block is…
statement:
A horizontal force $$F$$ of $$12 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ pushes a block weighing $$5.0 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ against a vertical wall as shown. The coefficient of static friction between the wall and the block is $$0.60$$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction is $$0.40.$$ Assume the block is not moving initially. What is the magnitude of the force exerted on the block by the wall?

This problem uses "pounds", with symbol $$\mathrm{lbs}\,,$$ to measure force. This is a common unit in the United States and is used occasionally in some other countries.

(a) $$5\;\mathrm{lb}$$ (b) $$7.2 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ (c) $$12 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ (d) $$13\;\mathrm{lb}$$ (e) $$17 \;\mathrm{lb}$$

label: FMA03
name: A block with mass $$m$$ is released from rest at the top of a frictionless ramp. The…
desc: A block with mass $$m$$ is released from rest at the top of a frictionless ramp. The block starts at a height $$h_1$$ above the base of the ramp, slides down the ramp, and then up a second ramp. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the second ramp is…
statement:
A block with mass $$m$$ is released from rest at the top of a frictionless ramp. The block starts at a height $$h_1$$ above the base of the ramp, slides down the ramp, and then up a second ramp. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the second ramp is $$\mu_k.$$ If both ramps make an angle of $$\theta$$ with the horizontal, to what height $$h_2$$ above the base of the second ramp will the block rise?

(a) $$h_2 = (h_1\sin\theta)/(\mu_k \cos\theta + \sin\theta)$$ (b) $$h_2 = (h_1\sin\theta)/(\mu_k + \sin\theta)$$ (c) $$h_2 = (h_1\sin\theta)/(\mu_k \cos^2\theta + \sin\theta)$$ (d) $$h_2 = (h_1\sin\theta)/(\mu_k \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)$$ (e) $$h_2 = (h_1\cos\theta)/(\mu_k \sin\theta + \cos\theta)$$

label: FMA03
name: A massless rope passes over a frictionless pulley. Particles of mass $$M$$ and $$M + m$$…
desc: A massless rope passes over a frictionless pulley. Particles of mass $$M$$ and $$M + m$$ are suspended from the two different ends of the rope. If $$m = 0,$$ the tension $$T$$ in the pulley rope is $$Mg.$$ If instead the value $$m$$ increases to infinity, the value of the…
statement:
A massless rope passes over a frictionless pulley. Particles of mass $$M$$ and $$M + m$$ are suspended from the two different ends of the rope. If $$m = 0,$$ the tension $$T$$ in the pulley rope is $$Mg.$$ If instead the value $$m$$ increases to infinity, the value of the tension

(a) stays constant (b) decreases, approaching a nonzero constant (c) decreases, approaching zero (d) increases, approaching a finite constant (e) increases to infinity

label: FMA03
name: A particle of mass $$2.00 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ moves under a force given by \[\vec{F} = -(8.00…
desc: A particle of mass $$2.00 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ moves under a force given by \[\vec{F} = -(8.00 \;\mathrm{N/m})(x\hat{\i} + y \hat{\j} )\] where $$\hat{\i}$$ and $$\hat{\j}$$ are unit vectors in the $$x$$ and $$y$$ directions. The particle is placed at the origin with an initial…
statement:
A particle of mass $$2.00 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ moves under a force given by \[\vec{F} = -(8.00 \;\mathrm{N/m})(x\hat{\i} + y \hat{\j} )\] where $$\hat{\i}$$ and $$\hat{\j}$$ are unit vectors in the $$x$$ and $$y$$ directions. The particle is placed at the origin with an initial velocity $$\vec{v} = (3.00 \;\mathrm{m/s})\hat{\i} + (4.00 \;\mathrm{m/s})\hat{\j}.$$

After how much time will the particle first return to the origin?

(a) $$0.785 \;\mathrm{s}$$ (b) $$1.26 \;\mathrm{s}$$ (c) $$1.57 \;\mathrm{s}$$ (d) $$2.00 \;\mathrm{s}$$ (e) $$3.14 \;\mathrm{s}$$

label: FMA03
name: Two objects, with masses $$m_1 = 1.65 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$m_2 = 3.22 \;\mathrm{kg},$$…
desc: Two objects, with masses $$m_1 = 1.65 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$m_2 = 3.22 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ attached by a massless rod parallel to the incline on which both slide, travel down the plane with $$m_1$$ trailing $$m_2.$$ The angle of the incline is $$\theta = 29.5^\circ.$$ The…
statement:
Two objects, with masses $$m_1 = 1.65 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$m_2 = 3.22 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ attached by a massless rod parallel to the incline on which both slide, travel down the plane with $$m_1$$ trailing $$m_2.$$ The angle of the incline is $$\theta = 29.5^\circ.$$ The coefficient of kinetic friction between $$m_1$$ and the incline is $$\mu_1= 0.226;$$ between $$m_2$$ and the incline the corresponding coefficient is $$\mu_2 = 0.127.$$

**a)** Compute the common acceleration of the two objects

**b)** Find the tension in the rod.

**c)** What are the answers to (a) and (b) if $$m_2$$ trails $$m_1?$$

label: FMA03
name: A Golf Ball Bounces off Concrete — You drop a golf ball of mass $$m$$ from a height $$h = 20\;\mathrm{m}$$ —…
desc: You drop a golf ball of mass $$m$$ from a height $$h = 20\;\mathrm{m}$$ — about the top of a five-story building — onto a concrete floor. The ball bounces back up to very nearly its original height. While the ball is in contact with the floor, the average force $$F$$ that the…
statement:
You drop a golf ball of mass $$m$$ from a height $$h = 20\;\mathrm{m}$$ — about the top of a five-story building — onto a concrete floor. The ball bounces back up to very nearly its original height. While the ball is in contact with the floor, the average force $$F$$ that the floor exerts on it is closest to which range?

(A) $$0 \le F < mg$$; (B) $$mg \le F < 2mg$$; (C) $$2mg \le F < 4mg$$; (D) $$4mg \le F < 5mg$$; (E) $$5mg \le F.$$

__(a)__ First, build some intuition. Someone gently places a golf ball on your head and balances it there, so the ball just sits, not accelerating. What force does the ball exert on your head? Would a stack of five golf balls balanced on your head be painful?

__(b)__ Now compare: would you want a golf ball that fell $$20\;\mathrm{m}$$ to land on your head? Use the comparison between the falling ball and the stack of five stationary balls to choose an answer — no calculation needed.

__(c)__ Explain the answer using Newton's second law, $$F_{\rm net} = ma,$$ together with $$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}.$$ Watching a golf ball bounce, you can barely perceive the time it spends touching the floor. Why does that force the average force to be much larger than $$mg?$$

__(d)__ Calling the contact time $$\Delta t$$ "small" only means something in comparison to some other time in the problem. The quantities available are $$m,$$ $$g,$$ and $$h.$$ Combine some of them into a quantity $$t_2$$ with dimensions of time, evaluate it numerically, and decide from your experience with bouncing golf balls whether $$\Delta t \ll t_2$$ is justified.

label: FMA03
name: Which String Breaks First? — A massless string with some elasticity hangs from the ceiling. A block of mass…
desc: A massless string with some elasticity hangs from the ceiling. A block of mass $$m$$ hangs at the bottom of the string, and a second, identical string hangs below the block. You grab the bottom of the lower string and pull straight down with a time-dependent force $$F,$$…
statement:
A massless string with some elasticity hangs from the ceiling. A block of mass $$m$$ hangs at the bottom of the string, and a second, identical string hangs below the block. You grab the bottom of the lower string and pull straight down with a time-dependent force $$F,$$ increasing $$F$$ until at least one of the strings breaks. Which string breaks?

(A) the top string always breaks first; (B) the bottom string always breaks first; (C) both strings break simultaneously; (D) the top string breaks first if you yank hard, but the bottom string breaks first if you increase your pulling force gradually; (E) the bottom string breaks first if you yank hard, but the top string breaks first if you increase your pulling force gradually.

__(a)__ First consider a very gradual pull — the force may eventually grow large, but it increases slowly, so the strings always have time to adjust and stay near equilibrium, and the block barely accelerates. Letting $$T_T$$ and $$T_B$$ be the tensions in the top and bottom strings, write the force-balance equation for the block. Which tension is larger, and so which string breaks first?

__(b)__ Now consider a sudden, sharp yank: $$F$$ jumps almost instantly from zero to beyond the strings' breaking strength. Explain why the bottom string's tension matches $$F$$ immediately, while the top string's tension lags behind. (Two details matter: the strings are massless, and they have some elasticity — an elastic string's tension grows only as it stretches.) Which string breaks first now?

__(c)__ Choose the answer.

label: FMA03
name: Third-Law Pairs: A Bench and an Astronaut — Newton's third law says that whenever object A exerts a force on…
desc: Newton's third law says that whenever object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A of equal magnitude and opposite direction: $$\left|F_{\text{A on B}}\right| = \left|F_{\text{B on A}}\right|.$$ The two forces of such a __third-law pair__ never act on the same…
statement:
Newton's third law says that whenever object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A of equal magnitude and opposite direction: $$\left|F_{\text{A on B}}\right| = \left|F_{\text{B on A}}\right|.$$ The two forces of such a __third-law pair__ never act on the same object — one acts on A and the other on B. This problem practices spotting the pairs.

__(a)__ You stand at rest on a bench. The bench exerts a normal force on you, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to your weight. Which force is related to this normal force by Newton's third law? (A) the gravitational force from the Earth on you; (B) the gravitational force from you on the Earth; (C) the normal force from you on the bench; (D) the normal force from the Earth on the bench; (E) none of the above.

__(b)__ While you stand at rest, the normal force from the bench on you and the gravitational force from the Earth on you happen to be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Describe a situation in which these two forces are __not__ equal in magnitude, and explain why two forces acting on the same object can never be a third-law pair.

__(c)__ A planet similar to Earth is at rest in space. An astronaut lands and stands stationary on its surface. The planet exerts a normal force on the astronaut (that's what keeps them from sinking toward its center), and the astronaut exerts a normal force on the planet (on soft dirt, their boots would leave footprints). Which normal force is greater in magnitude?

__(d)__ The astronaut exerts a normal force on the planet. Does this mean the planet starts accelerating? (A) Yes, but the planet is very massive, so the astronaut wouldn't notice the motion. (B) Yes, but the astronaut accelerates along with the planet, so they don't notice the motion. (C) No, because the normal force isn't a real force. (D) No, because the astronaut is also pulling on the planet gravitationally. (E) No, because there is also friction at the astronaut's feet. To decide, try an extreme case: imagine a giant astronaut whose mass is comparable to the planet's, as in the picture. Could the planet really zip off into space forever with an acceleration comparable to $$g?$$

__(e)__ The (normal-sized) astronaut stands at the planet's north pole and jumps straight up, then lands back at the pole. In what direction do they push the planet while jumping off? While landing? After the landing, is the planet left drifting with some small velocity in that direction? If not, identify the force that compensates while the astronaut is in the air.

label: FMA03
name: Three Boxes in a Row — Three boxes of masses $$m,$$ $$2m,$$ and $$3m$$ sit side by side, in that order, on a…
desc: Three boxes of masses $$m,$$ $$2m,$$ and $$3m$$ sit side by side, in that order, on a frictionless table. You push horizontally with a force $$F$$ on the lightest box, so all three boxes accelerate together, as shown. Let $$N_1$$ be the normal force between the left two boxes…
statement:
Three boxes of masses $$m,$$ $$2m,$$ and $$3m$$ sit side by side, in that order, on a frictionless table. You push horizontally with a force $$F$$ on the lightest box, so all three boxes accelerate together, as shown. Let $$N_1$$ be the normal force between the left two boxes ($$m$$ and $$2m$$), and let $$N_2$$ be the normal force between the right two boxes ($$2m$$ and $$3m$$). Then: (A) $$F = N_1 = N_2$$; (B) $$F + N_1 = N_2$$; (C) $$F > N_1 = N_2$$; (D) $$F < N_1 < N_2$$; (E) $$F > N_1 > N_2.$$ (Adapted from Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__.)

__(a)__ Treat the three boxes together as a single system. What is their common acceleration?

__(b)__ Now focus on the box of mass $$m$$ alone. Besides gravity and the normal force from the table (which cancel), which horizontal forces act on it? Use Newton's second law on this box to find $$N_1$$ in terms of $$F.$$

__(c)__ Find $$N_2.$$ (Hint: the rightmost box is the easiest one to analyze — only one horizontal force acts on it.)

__(d)__ Choose the answer.

__(e)__ Suppose the boxes were lined up in the reverse order — $$3m$$ pushed directly, then $$2m,$$ then $$m$$ — still pushed with force $$F.$$ Would the exact values of the normal forces change? Would the answer change? Argue without redoing the computation.

__(f)__ Now add some friction between the boxes and the floor, small enough that the boxes still accelerate to the right. Must $$F > N_1 > N_2$$ still hold? Argue without computing anything.

label: FMA03
name: A Box on a Frictionless Inclined Plane — A box of mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless inclined plane that makes…
desc: A box of mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless inclined plane that makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. The plane cannot move. (Inclined planes are very common on the F=ma exam — every single test since 2007 has featured at least one — so this problem builds the standard…
statement:
A box of mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless inclined plane that makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. The plane cannot move. (Inclined planes are very common on the F=ma exam — every single test since 2007 has featured at least one — so this problem builds the standard toolkit.) Find the box's acceleration and the normal force on it.

__(a)__ What forces act on the box, and in which direction does the normal force point? ("Normal" means perpendicular to the surface — but that still leaves two possible directions.)

__(b)__ In most problems we call the horizontal direction $$x$$ and the vertical direction $$y.$$ For inclined planes a tilted choice works better: let $$x$$ point down along the slope and $$y$$ point perpendicularly out of the slope. What makes these axes convenient here?

__(c)__ The component of gravity along the slope is either $$mg\sin\theta$$ or $$mg\cos\theta$$ — it is easy to forget which. Use the extreme case $$\theta \to 0$$ (a flat "incline") to decide, then find the box's acceleration.

__(d)__ Using the $$y$$ direction, find the magnitude of the normal force. What assumption about the box's motion does your argument rely on?

__(e)__ Now suppose the inclined plane itself sits on a frictionless table, free to slide. As the box slides down to the right, the plane scoots away to the left. The normal force is no longer $$mg\cos\theta.$$ Exactly which assumption from part (d) fails?

__(f)__ A related question about normal forces as __constraint__ forces: a mass $$m$$ sits on a horizontal table while a person pulls upward on it, gradually increasing the upward force. At the moment the mass is just about to leave the table, what is the normal force from the table on it?

label: FMA03
name: A Block at Rest on an Inclined Plane — A block of mass $$m$$ is at rest on a plane inclined at angle…
desc: A block of mass $$m$$ is at rest on a plane inclined at angle $$\theta.$$ The forces on it are the gravitational force $$mg,$$ the normal force $$N,$$ and the friction force $$F_f,$$ shown in the figure (not drawn to scale). The coefficient of static friction is $$\mu_s,$$ and…
statement:
A block of mass $$m$$ is at rest on a plane inclined at angle $$\theta.$$ The forces on it are the gravitational force $$mg,$$ the normal force $$N,$$ and the friction force $$F_f,$$ shown in the figure (not drawn to scale). The coefficient of static friction is $$\mu_s,$$ and the plane cannot move. Which of the following statements is always true, for __any__ angle $$\theta?$$ (A) $$mg \le N$$ and $$mg \le F_f$$; (B) $$mg \ge N$$ and $$mg \ge F_f$$; (C) $$F_f = N$$; (D) $$F_f + N = mg$$; (E) $$F_f \ge N$$ if $$\mu_s > 1.$$ (Adapted from Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__.)

__(a)__ Rather than launching into a general analysis, try extreme cases. Start with $$\theta = 0,$$ a flat "incline." What are $$N$$ and $$F_f$$ there? Which answer choices does this single case eliminate?

__(b)__ Next try $$\theta = \pi/2,$$ a vertical "incline": the block falls straight down with acceleration $$g$$ while staying right next to the surface. What are $$N$$ and $$F_f$$ now, and which remaining choice does this case eliminate?

__(c)__ Choose the answer.

__(d)__ Choice (E) is a trap for students who remember the equation $$F_f = \mu_s N.$$ What is wrong with that equation, and what is the correct relationship between $$F_f,$$ $$\mu_s,$$ and $$N$$ for static friction? And is a coefficient of friction greater than $$1$$ actually impossible?

label: FMA03
name: A Puck Kicked Up a Ramp — A puck is kicked up a ramp that makes an angle of $$30^\circ$$ with the horizontal…
desc: A puck is kicked up a ramp that makes an angle of $$30^\circ$$ with the horizontal. The graph below shows the puck's __speed__ versus time, drawn on a grid with no numbers on the axes. The speed first falls steeply to zero, dropping four grid squares over two squares of time…
statement:
A puck is kicked up a ramp that makes an angle of $$30^\circ$$ with the horizontal. The graph below shows the puck's __speed__ versus time, drawn on a grid with no numbers on the axes. The speed first falls steeply to zero, dropping four grid squares over two squares of time (the puck sliding up the ramp), and then rises again, gaining two grid squares over the next three squares of time (the puck sliding back down). What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the puck and the ramp? (A) $$0.07$$; (B) $$0.15$$; (C) $$0.22$$; (D) $$0.29$$; (E) $$0.37.$$

__(a)__ During which part of the graph is the puck moving up the ramp? Physically, why is the magnitude of its acceleration larger then than while it slides back down? (Think about which way kinetic friction points in each case, relative to gravity's pull along the slope.)

__(b)__ With no numbers on the axes you cannot read off either acceleration — but you can read off their __ratio__. What is $$\dfrac{a_{\rm up}}{a_{\rm down}}?$$

__(c)__ Draw free-body diagrams for the two phases and express $$a_{\rm up}$$ and $$a_{\rm down}$$ in terms of $$g,$$ $$\mu,$$ and $$\theta.$$ (Useful facts: on a fixed incline, gravity contributes $$mg\sin\theta$$ along the slope, the normal force is $$N = mg\cos\theta,$$ and kinetic friction has magnitude $$\mu N,$$ opposing the sliding.)

__(d)__ Combine parts (b) and (c) to find $$\mu,$$ using $$\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac12$$ and $$\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},$$ and choose the answer. (If the algebra fights back, you can instead plug each answer choice into your equation until one works.)

__(e)__ Test the formula $$\dfrac{a_{\rm up}}{a_{\rm down}} = \dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta}{\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta}$$ in two extreme cases: $$\mu \to 0$$ and $$\theta \to \pi/2.$$ Are the results intuitively correct?

__(f)__ The extreme case $$\theta \to 0$$ gives $$\dfrac{a_{\rm up}}{a_{\rm down}} \to -1,$$ which is absurd — the puck never accelerates up the ramp. Why is it acceptable for the formula to fail here? (Taking the static and kinetic coefficients equal, a puck that stops on the ramp slides back down only if $$\tan\theta > \mu.$$) And what does the formula predict as $$\tan\theta \to \mu$$ from above — is that prediction reasonable?

__(g)__ A friend's derivation produced $$\dfrac{a_{\rm up}}{a_{\rm down}} = \dfrac{\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu\sin\theta}$$ instead. Use an extreme case to show quickly that this formula must be wrong.

label: FMA03
name: One Horse or Two? — Two horses pull in opposite directions on a pair of pants, as in a tug-of-war. Then…
desc: Two horses pull in opposite directions on a pair of pants, as in a tug-of-war. Then someone tries the same stunt with only one horse: one side of the pants is tied by a rope to an immovable stump, and the horse pulls against it, as shown. Compared with the two-horse version…
statement:
Two horses pull in opposite directions on a pair of pants, as in a tug-of-war. Then someone tries the same stunt with only one horse: one side of the pants is tied by a rope to an immovable stump, and the horse pulls against it, as shown. Compared with the two-horse version, using only one horse would: (A) cut the tension in the pants by one-half; (B) not change the tension in the pants at all; (C) double the tension in the pants. (From Epstein, __Thinking Physics__.)

__(a)__ In the two-horse case, suppose the horse pulling to the right exerts a force of magnitude $$F$$ on the pants, and the pants stay in equilibrium. What force does the left horse exert?

__(b)__ In the one-horse case, the horse pulls to the right with the same force $$F.$$ What force does the stump exert on the pants? A common answer is zero, since the stump isn't "doing" anything — explain why that can't be right.

__(c)__ Choose the answer.

__(d)__ Consider a small piece of the rope between the horse and the pants, small enough that gravity on it is negligible. What forces act on this piece, and what are their magnitudes? What does this tell you about how the tension varies along a massless rope?

__(e)__ A classic puzzle in the same spirit: "A horse is hitched to a buggy by ropes. The horse tries to pull the buggy forward, but by Newton's third law the buggy always pulls backward on the horse exactly as hard. Therefore the horse can never move the buggy." The conclusion is obviously false — find the flaw. What force actually accelerates the horse-and-buggy system forward? (An extreme case to consider: how would the horse fare standing in the middle of a huge frictionless frozen lake?)

label: FMA03
name: A Hanging Block versus a Pulling Hand — A $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block sits on a frictionless table. A massless…
desc: A $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block sits on a frictionless table. A massless rope is attached to it and runs over a massless, frictionless pulley at the table's edge. In __Scenario 1__, a second $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block hangs from the other end of the rope. In __Scenario 2__, a hand…
statement:
A $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block sits on a frictionless table. A massless rope is attached to it and runs over a massless, frictionless pulley at the table's edge. In __Scenario 1__, a second $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block hangs from the other end of the rope. In __Scenario 2__, a hand instead pulls straight down on the rope with a constant force of $$\left(10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}\right) \times \left(6\;\mathrm{kg}\right) = 60\;\mathrm{N}$$ — exactly the weight of the hanging block it replaces. In which scenario does the block on the table have the greater acceleration? (A) Scenario 1; (B) Scenario 2; (C) the accelerations are equal. Use $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ (From Epstein, __Thinking Physics__.)

__(a)__ In Scenario 2, what is the tension in the piece of rope attached to the block on the table? Explain why the tension is the same everywhere along a massless rope, and find the block's acceleration.

__(b)__ In Scenario 1, is the rope's tension also $$60\;\mathrm{N}?$$ (Check: if it were, what would the hanging block do?) Is the tension more or less than $$60\;\mathrm{N}?$$

__(c)__ Find the acceleration of the blocks in Scenario 1 and the rope's tension, then choose the answer.

label: FMA04
name: A $$195\;\mathrm{lb}$$ man standing on a surface of negligible friction kicks forward a…
desc: A $$195\;\mathrm{lb}$$ man standing on a surface of negligible friction kicks forward a $$0.158 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ stone lying at his feet so that it acquires a velocity of $$12.7\;\mathrm{ft/s}$$. What velocity does the man acquire as a result? (a) $$-0.0103 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$ (b)…
statement:
A $$195\;\mathrm{lb}$$ man standing on a surface of negligible friction kicks forward a $$0.158 \;\mathrm{lb}$$ stone lying at his feet so that it acquires a velocity of $$12.7\;\mathrm{ft/s}$$. What velocity does the man acquire as a result?

(a) $$-0.0103 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$ (b) $$-0.1821 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$ (c) $$-0.3615 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$ (d) $$-1.5674 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$ (e) $$-2.4260 \;\mathrm{ft/s}$$

label: FMA04
name: A ball of radius $$R$$ and mass $$m$$ is put inside a thin shell of the same mass and…
desc: A ball of radius $$R$$ and mass $$m$$ is put inside a thin shell of the same mass and radius $$2R$$. The system is at rest on a horizontal frictionless surface initially. When the ball is released inside the shell, it sloshes around in the shell and eventually stops at the…
statement:
A ball of radius $$R$$ and mass $$m$$ is put inside a thin shell of the same mass and radius $$2R$$. The system is at rest on a horizontal frictionless surface initially. When the ball is released inside the shell, it sloshes around in the shell and eventually stops at the bottom of the shell. How far does the shell move from its initial contact point with the surface?

(a) $$R$$ (b) $$R/2$$ (c) $$R/4$$ (d) $$3R/8$$ (e) $$R/8$$

label: FMA04
name: A ball with mass $$m$$ is projected horizontally off the end of a table with an initial…
desc: A ball with mass $$m$$ is projected horizontally off the end of a table with an initial kinetic energy $$K$$. At a time $$t$$ after it leaves the end of the table it has kinetic energy $$3K$$. What is $$t$$? Neglect air resistance. (a) $$(3/g) \sqrt{K/m}$$ (b) $$(2/g)…
statement:
A ball with mass $$m$$ is projected horizontally off the end of a table with an initial kinetic energy $$K$$. At a time $$t$$ after it leaves the end of the table it has kinetic energy $$3K$$. What is $$t$$? Neglect air resistance.

(a) $$(3/g) \sqrt{K/m}$$ (b) $$(2/g) \sqrt{K/m}$$ (c) $$(1/g) \sqrt{8K/m}$$ (d) $$(K/g) \sqrt{6/m}$$ (e) $$(2K/g) \sqrt{1/m}$$

label: FMA04
name: A $$2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object falls from rest a distance of $$5.0$$ meters onto a…
desc: A $$2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object falls from rest a distance of $$5.0$$ meters onto a $$6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object that is supported by a vertical massless spring with spring constant $$k = 72 \;\mathrm{N/m}$$. The two objects stick together after the collision, which results in the…
statement:
A $$2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object falls from rest a distance of $$5.0$$ meters onto a $$6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object that is supported by a vertical massless spring with spring constant $$k = 72 \;\mathrm{N/m}$$. The two objects stick together after the collision, which results in the mass/spring system oscillating. What is the maximum magnitude of the displacement of the $$6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ object from its original location (its location before it is struck by the falling object)?

(a) $$0.27\;\mathrm{m}$$ (b) $$1.1\;\mathrm{m}$$ (c) $$2.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ (d) $$2.8\;\mathrm{m}$$ (e) $$3.1\;\mathrm{m}$$

label: FMA04
name: A block with mass $$m$$ starts from rest and slides down a plane inclined at an angle…
desc: A block with mass $$m$$ starts from rest and slides down a plane inclined at an angle $$\theta$$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $$\mu$$. Which equation correctly yields the block's speed $$v$$ after it has traveled a distance $$d$$ down along the plane, assuming that it…
statement:
A block with mass $$m$$ starts from rest and slides down a plane inclined at an angle $$\theta$$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $$\mu$$. Which equation correctly yields the block's speed $$v$$ after it has traveled a distance $$d$$ down along the plane, assuming that it does indeed start sliding down? (Here $$d$$ is a distance, so it is a positive quantity.)

(a) $$mgd \sin\theta + \mu mgd \cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}$$ (b) $$mgd \sin\theta - \mu mgd \cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}$$ (c) $$-mgd \sin\theta + \mu mgd \cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}$$ (d) $$mgd \cos\theta + \mu mgd \sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}$$ (e) $$mgd \cos\theta - \mu mgd \sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{2}$$

desc: A small block of mass $$m$$ is moving on a horizontal table surface at initial speed $$v_0$$. It then moves smoothly onto a sloped big block of mass $$M$$. The big block can also move on the table surface. The block slides up the slope a ways, then turns around and slides back…
statement:
A small block of mass $$m$$ is moving on a horizontal table surface at initial speed $$v_0$$. It then moves smoothly onto a sloped big block of mass $$M$$. The big block can also move on the table surface. The block slides up the slope a ways, then turns around and slides back down, and moves smoothly back onto the table.

Assume that everything moves without friction. Find the speed $$v$$ of the small block after it leaves the slope and returns to the table.

(a) $$v = v_0$$ (b) $$v = \frac{m}{m + M} v_0$$ (c) $$v = \frac{M}{m + M} v_0$$ (d) $$v = \frac{M - m}{m} v_0$$ (e) $$v = \frac{M - m}{m + M} v_0$$

After she jumps (or rather falls) off the platform, she is in freefall for a height $$\ell$$. After that, the spring becomes stretched. Assume that it acts like an ideal spring with a particular spring constant. (This applies only during the stretching motion, of course; the cord can't support compression like a normal spring.) It is observed that the lowest point the jumper reaches is a distance of $$2\ell$$ below the platform. What is the jumper's maximum speed?

(a) $$\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{g\ell}$$ (b) $$\sqrt{g\ell}$$ (c) $$\tfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{g\ell}$$ (d) $$2\sqrt{g\ell}$$ (e) $$\tfrac{5}{2}\sqrt{g\ell}$$

A stone of weight $$w$$ is launched vertically upward into the air from ground height. Its initial speed is $$v_0$$. Suppose that the air drag force $$f$$ dissipates an amount $$fy$$ of mechanical energy as the stone travels a distance $$y$$.

What is the maximum height reached by the stone?

(a) $$\frac{v_0^2}{2g(1 + f/w)}$$ (b) $$\frac{v_0^2}{2g(1 - f/w)}$$ (c) $$\frac{v_0^2}{g(1 + f/w)}$$ (d) $$\frac{v_0^2}{g(1 - f/w)}$$ (e) $$\frac{2v_0^2}{g(1 - f/w)}$$
