What is the speed of the stone upon impact with the ground?

(a) $$v_0 \left(\frac{w - 3f}{w + f}\right)^{1/2}$$ (b) $$v_0 \left(\frac{w - f}{w + f}\right)^{1/2}$$ (c) $$v_0 \left(\frac{w + 3f}{w + f}\right)^{1/2}$$ (d) $$v_0 \left(\frac{w}{w + f}\right)^{1/2}$$ (e) $$v_0 \left(\frac{w}{w - f}\right)^{1/2}$$

label: FMA04
name: In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will examine the basic physics behind the flight…
desc: In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will examine the basic physics behind the flight of a bird. Imagine an bird viewed from the frame where the bird is stationary and wind rushes past the bird at speed $$v.$$ (For convenience, we ignore the flapping of the birds wings and…
statement:
In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will examine the basic physics behind the flight of a bird. Imagine an bird viewed from the frame where the bird is stationary and wind rushes past the bird at speed $$v.$$ (For convenience, we ignore the flapping of the birds wings and think of them as fixed, with an ability to push air past them.)

The density of the air is $$\rho.$$ The bird has wings of length $$l$$ (direction of its wingspan) and depth $$d.$$ (The thickness of the bird's wings is not considered in this model.)

**a)** Suppose the wings are angled at some angle $$\theta$$ with respect to the incoming wind. The wings interact with all the air that is on a direct collision course with some part of the wing. Below, the incoming air is blue and the tilted wing is black. The length $$l$$ of the wing is into and out of your monitor.

How much air (in mass of air per unit time) do the wings interact with, as a function of $$v, \rho, l, d,$$ and $$\theta?$$

**b)** Suppose that as air flows past the wing, it is deflected downward by an angle $$\theta$$ while keeping constant speed. Find the weight $$W$$ of the bird in terms of $$v, \rho, l, d,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**c)** Suppose two birds have the same shape, but bird $$B$$ is twice the size of bird $$A$$ in every dimension. Assuming $$\theta$$ is the same for both birds, if bird $$A$$ flies at speed $$v,$$ what speed must bird $$B$$ fly?

**d)** The upward force from the air to the bird is called the **lift**. There is also a backwards force on the bird, called the **drag**. Generally, birds can be considered to have a fixed ratio of lift force magnitude to drag force magnitude. Call this ratio $$\alpha.$$ Find the power bird must provide as a function of $$v, \rho, l, d, \theta,$$ and $$\alpha.$$

**e)** Some data on the weight $$(W),$$ given in Newtons, and wing area $$(S),$$ given in square meters, and flying speed of various birds is provided in the chart below. Make a plot of the data on this chart showing how well the theory outlined in part (b) matches the real-world data. Your plot should be set up so that if the model is perfectly accurate, you will see a straight line on the plot.

__data source: Tennekes, Hendrik. The simple science of flight: from insects to jumbo jets. MIT press, 2009.__

label: FMA04
name: Sand Falling on a Moving Train — A train, originally of mass $$M,$$ is traveling without slipping on a…
desc: A train, originally of mass $$M,$$ is traveling without slipping on a straight horizontal track with constant speed $$v.$$ Sand starts to fall vertically into the train's open cars and sticks to the train at a steady rate $$r,$$ where $$r$$ has units of kilograms per second. The…
statement:
A train, originally of mass $$M,$$ is traveling without slipping on a straight horizontal track with constant speed $$v.$$ Sand starts to fall vertically into the train's open cars and sticks to the train at a steady rate $$r,$$ where $$r$$ has units of kilograms per second. The train's engine works to keep the speed exactly $$v$$ the whole time.

__(a)__ The mass of the train system (train plus collected sand) grows at the rate $$r$$ while its speed stays fixed at $$v.$$ At what rate does the kinetic energy of the train system increase?

__(b)__ Newton's second law in its most general form says that the net force on a system equals the rate of change of the system's momentum, $$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}.$$ The sand that lands on the train must be brought from zero horizontal speed up to speed $$v.$$ Use the rate-of-change-of-momentum form of Newton's second law to find the horizontal force the train exerts on the sand it is collecting.

__(c)__ The minimum power required from the engine to keep the train traveling at the constant speed $$v$$ is: (A) $$0$$ (B) $$Mgv$$ (C) $$\frac12 Mv^2$$ (D) $$\frac12 rv^2$$ (E) $$rv^2.$$ Use $$P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$ — power is force dotted with velocity — to choose the correct answer.

__(d)__ Your answers to (a) and (c) are not equal: the engine supplies energy at twice the rate the kinetic energy grows. Where does the other half of the power go? And why was it wrong to expect the power to equal the rate of change of kinetic energy, given the equation $$P = \dfrac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}?$$

label: FMA04
name: A Tennis Ball Bounces off a Wall — The figure below shows an approximate representation of the contact force…
desc: The figure below shows an approximate representation of the contact force versus time during the collision of a $$58\;\mathrm{g}$$ tennis ball with a wall. The ball hits the wall with velocity $$32\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ perpendicular to the wall, and it rebounds with the same speed…
statement:
The figure below shows an approximate representation of the contact force versus time during the collision of a $$58\;\mathrm{g}$$ tennis ball with a wall. The ball hits the wall with velocity $$32\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ perpendicular to the wall, and it rebounds with the same speed, also perpendicular to the wall. The force rises linearly from zero to $$F_{\mathrm{max}}$$ during the first $$2\;\mathrm{ms},$$ stays at $$F_{\mathrm{max}}$$ for the next $$2\;\mathrm{ms},$$ then falls linearly back to zero during the final $$2\;\mathrm{ms}.$$ (Problem from Halliday, Resnick, and Krane, __Physics__, 5th ed.)

Useful fact: just as the displacement of an object is the area under its velocity-versus-time graph, the change in an object's momentum is the area under the net-force-versus-time graph. (The relationships $$F\,\Delta t = \Delta p$$ and $$v\,\Delta t = \Delta x$$ have identical forms.) A force applied over a time interval is called an __impulse__.

__(a)__ Find the area under the force-versus-time graph, and hence the magnitude of the ball's momentum change during the collision, as a function of $$F_{\mathrm{max}}.$$ (Keep careful track of units: the answer should be a time multiplied by a force.)

__(b)__ Using the ball's mass and its velocities just before and just after the collision, compute the magnitude of the ball's momentum change numerically. (Careful: neither the initial nor the final velocity is zero.)

__(c)__ Combine (a) and (b) to find the value of $$F_{\mathrm{max}},$$ the maximum contact force during the collision.

__(d)__ The work-energy theorem relates force to energy through __distance__, $$\Delta E = F\,\Delta x.$$ Why is momentum, rather than the work-energy theorem, the natural tool for this problem?

label: FMA04
name: Two Rockets, Same Force, Same Distance (2007 F=ma) — Two rockets are in space in a negligible gravitational…
desc: Two rockets are in space in a negligible gravitational field. All observations are made by an observer in a reference frame in which both rockets are initially at rest. The masses of the rockets are $$m$$ and $$9m.$$ A constant force $$F$$ acts on the rocket of mass $$m$$ for a…
statement:
Two rockets are in space in a negligible gravitational field. All observations are made by an observer in a reference frame in which both rockets are initially at rest. The masses of the rockets are $$m$$ and $$9m.$$ A constant force $$F$$ acts on the rocket of mass $$m$$ for a distance $$d.$$ As a result, the rocket acquires a momentum $$p.$$ If the same constant force $$F$$ acts on the rocket of mass $$9m$$ for the same distance $$d,$$ how much momentum does the rocket of mass $$9m$$ acquire? (2007 F=ma) (A) $$p/9$$ (B) $$p/3$$ (C) $$p$$ (D) $$3p$$ (E) $$9p$$

__(a)__ Suppose the rocket of mass $$m$$ has kinetic energy $$T$$ after the push. Use the work-energy theorem — a constant force $$F$$ acting over a distance $$d$$ delivers kinetic energy $$\Delta T = Fd$$ — to find the kinetic energy of the rocket of mass $$9m$$ after its push.

__(b)__ Starting from $$T = \frac12 mv^2$$ and $$p = mv,$$ derive a formula for the kinetic energy of an object in terms of its momentum $$p$$ and mass $$m$$ alone. (This formula is worth memorizing for problems that give you momenta rather than velocities.)

__(c)__ Solve your formula from (b) for $$p$$ and answer the question.

__(d)__ Cross-check with kinematics: starting from rest with constant acceleration, an object satisfies $$F = ma$$ and $$d = \frac12 at^2.$$ Find the time $$t$$ each rocket needs to cover the distance $$d,$$ and use $$\Delta p = Ft$$ to confirm your answer to (c).

label: FMA04
name: Same Force, Same Time — Two carts sit at rest on a long frictionless track. One has mass $$m$$ and the other…
desc: Two carts sit at rest on a long frictionless track. One has mass $$m$$ and the other has mass $$4m.$$ The same constant horizontal force $$F$$ is applied to each cart for the same __time__ $$t_0$$ (note: the same time, not the same distance). __(a)__ Compare the momenta the two…
statement:
Two carts sit at rest on a long frictionless track. One has mass $$m$$ and the other has mass $$4m.$$ The same constant horizontal force $$F$$ is applied to each cart for the same __time__ $$t_0$$ (note: the same time, not the same distance).

__(a)__ Compare the momenta the two carts acquire. (Recall that the net force on a system equals the rate of change of its momentum, so a constant force $$F$$ acting for a time $$t_0$$ delivers momentum $$\Delta p = F t_0.$$)

__(b)__ Using the relation $$T = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$$ between kinetic energy, momentum, and mass, compare the kinetic energies the two carts acquire. Which cart ends up with more kinetic energy, and by what factor?

__(c)__ The work-energy theorem says each cart's final kinetic energy equals $$F$$ times the distance it travels while being pushed. Compute the distance each cart covers during the time $$t_0$$ (use $$a = F/m$$ and $$d = \frac12 a t_0^2$$) and show that the result is consistent with your answer to (b).

desc: This problem investigates **Compton scattering**, which is when a particle of light collides with a charged particle, usually an electron. During this process, the light particle gives some of its energy to the electron. This means the photon's energy goes down, which in turn…
statement:
This problem investigates **Compton scattering**, which is when a particle of light collides with a charged particle, usually an electron. During this process, the light particle gives some of its energy to the electron. This means the photon's energy goes down, which in turn means its wavelength gets longer. The explanation of Compton scattering (by Arthur Compton) in 1923 gave additional credence to the then-young idea that light consists of particles, which we know today as photons.

This is a type of 2D, elastic collision. In this collision, both momentum and energy are conserved. However, the formulas for momentum and energy are those used in special relativity and quantum mechanics, so not everything we've learned about collisions applies to Compton scattering.

A photon does not have mass, but it does have energy and momentum. Its energy is $$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}.$$ Here, $$h$$ is a constant known as **Planck's constant**, which is used ubiquitously in quantum mechanics. $$c$$ is the speed of light, and $$\lambda$$ is the wavelength of the photon.

The magnitude of the momentum of a photon is $$p = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$

An electron does have mass, which we will call $$m.$$ The equations of special relativity tell us that the momentum and energy of an electron moving with velocity $$\mathbf{v}$$ are

$$\mathbf{p} = \dfrac{m\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$$

and

$$E =\sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2 c^4}$$

We will consider a stationary electron and a photon which approaches from the left. The photon and electron collides, and the photon winds up traveling away up and to the right, at an angle $$\theta$$ with its previous trajectory. The photon's wavelength after the collision has increased to $$\lambda',$$ and the electron moves down and to the right.

__By JabberWok, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2078004__

**a)** Find an equation for energy conservation in the scattering process described above. You may need to introduce new variables for the speed and angle between the electron's final direction of motion and the original direction of motion of the photon.

**b)** Find an equation for momentum conservation in the original direction of travel of the photon.

**c)** Find an equation for momentum conservation in the direction perpendicular to the direction of travel of the photon.

**d)** Define $$\lambda_c = \dfrac{h}{mc}.$$ This is called the **Compton wavelength** of the electron. Also define $$\lambda_e$$ so that $$p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda_e}$$ for an electron. Rewrite the above formulas using these definitions. Eliminate $$h, c, v, m$$ and any variables other than the angles and the various $$\lambda's (\lambda, \lambda', \lambda_e, \lambda_c)$$ from your equations.

**e)** Eliminate the variable you introduced for the angle of motion of the electron. You may need to use the fact that $$\cos^2x + \sin^2 x = 1.$$ Solve the remaining equations to find $$\lambda' - \lambda,$$ the change in wavelength of the photon as a function of $$\lambda_c$$ and $$\theta.$$

label: FMA05
name: Children Colliding on a Frozen Lake — A child is sliding out of control with velocity $$v_c$$ across a frozen…
desc: A child is sliding out of control with velocity $$v_c$$ across a frozen lake. He runs head-on into a second child, initially at rest, whose mass is $$3$$ times the mass of the first child. The second child holds on, so that the two slide together after the collision. (The…
statement:
A child is sliding out of control with velocity $$v_c$$ across a frozen lake. He runs head-on into a second child, initially at rest, whose mass is $$3$$ times the mass of the first child. The second child holds on, so that the two slide together after the collision. (The surface is ice, so you may neglect friction.) This problem appeared on the 2011 F=ma exam.

A collision in which the objects stick together and move as one afterward is called a __perfectly inelastic collision__. Momentum, $$p=mv,$$ is conserved in every collision, and momentum conservation is all you need for most perfectly inelastic collision problems.

__(a)__ Find the velocity of the pair after the collision.

__(b)__ Explain how you could see the answer with almost no algebra, by thinking about how much mass is carrying the (unchanged) momentum after the collision.

label: FMA05
name: Blocks That Stick: How Much Kinetic Energy Disappears? — A $$12\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block moving east at…
desc: A $$12\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block moving east at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides head-on with a $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block moving west at $$2\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The two blocks move together after the collision — a __perfectly inelastic collision__. What is the __loss__ in kinetic energy in…
statement:
A $$12\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block moving east at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides head-on with a $$6\;\mathrm{kg}$$ block moving west at $$2\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The two blocks move together after the collision — a __perfectly inelastic collision__. What is the __loss__ in kinetic energy in this collision? This problem appeared on the 2012 F=ma exam.

Work with general variables before plugging in numbers: let the masses be $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ let $$v_1$$ and $$v_2$$ be the initial velocities (these carry signs — take east as positive, so a westward velocity is negative), and let $$v$$ be the common velocity of the blocks after they stick together.

__(a)__ Use conservation of momentum to find $$v$$ in terms of the masses and initial velocities. Your formula should be a __weighted average__ of the two initial velocities, with the masses as the weights.

__(b)__ The collision converts some kinetic energy into other forms (sound, deformation, and ultimately heat). Find a formula for the kinetic energy lost, $$\Delta T = T_i - T_f,$$ in terms of $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ $$v_1,$$ and $$v_2.$$

__(c)__ Before plugging in numbers, test your formula in special cases. Decide from physical intuition what $$\Delta T$$ should be in each case, then verify that the formula agrees: (i) $$m_1\to 0;$$ (ii) $$m_1=m_2$$ with $$v_1=-v_2;$$ (iii) $$v_1=v_2.$$ Finally, check that the formula is __symmetric__: swapping the labels $$1$$ and $$2$$ everywhere should leave it unchanged, since relabeling the blocks can't change the physics.

__(d)__ Now plug in the numbers and find the kinetic energy lost in this collision.

label: FMA05
name: A Sticky Collision in Two Dimensions — Two balls, each of mass $$m,$$ move toward each other with equal…
desc: Two balls, each of mass $$m,$$ move toward each other with equal speeds $$v$$ as shown: each ball's velocity makes an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, with the left ball moving up and to the right and the right ball moving up and to the left. The balls collide and stick…
statement:
Two balls, each of mass $$m,$$ move toward each other with equal speeds $$v$$ as shown: each ball's velocity makes an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, with the left ball moving up and to the right and the right ball moving up and to the left. The balls collide and stick together. How much energy is converted to heat? ("Energy converted to heat" is another name for the kinetic energy lost: in a real collision, the lost kinetic energy goes into sound and into deforming the balls, and all of that energy quickly dissipates into thermal energy.)

__(a)__ Both balls have the same vertical velocity component before the collision. Use conservation of momentum to find the vertical velocity of the stuck-together pair after the collision. (Test your answer against the cases $$\theta=0^\circ$$ and $$\theta=90^\circ.$$)

__(b)__ A powerful trick: __change reference frames__. Imagine an observer drifting straight upward at speed $$v\sin\theta.$$ To describe velocities in this observer's reference frame, add the same velocity shift (downward at $$v\sin\theta$$) to every object. What does the collision look like in this frame?

__(c)__ The kinetic energy lost in a collision is the same in every reference frame. (For instance, the lost energy could go into heating the balls, and the temperature they reach can't depend on who is watching.) Use the drifting observer's frame to find the energy converted to heat.

__(d)__ Check your answer by computing the kinetic energy lost in the original frame directly.

label: FMA05
name: The Stacked Ball Drop — In a famous demonstration, a small, light ball is stacked on top of a large, heavy…
desc: In a famous demonstration, a small, light ball is stacked on top of a large, heavy ball, and the stack is dropped from a height $$h$$: When the stack hits the ground and rebounds, the top ball shoots dramatically high into the air (if you try it yourself, don't look straight…
statement:
In a famous demonstration, a small, light ball is stacked on top of a large, heavy ball, and the stack is dropped from a height $$h$$:

When the stack hits the ground and rebounds, the top ball shoots dramatically high into the air (if you try it yourself, don't look straight down at the balls):

Model the demonstration with two balls as follows. The balls are dropped with a tiny separation, so the large ball reaches the ground slightly first, moving at some speed $$v$$ (the small ball is still moving down at $$v$$ at that moment). Assume every collision is __perfectly elastic__ — kinetic energy is conserved. Take the limit where the small ball is far lighter than the large ball, and the large ball is far lighter than the Earth. Ignore air resistance and the sizes of the balls. A useful fact about reference frames: switching frames adds the same velocity to every object (including the ground), and never changes the __relative velocity__ between two objects.

__(a)__ The large ball collides elastically with the ground. The ground (attached to the enormously heavy Earth) doesn't move, so it carries away no kinetic energy. What are the large ball's speed and direction just after this bounce?

__(b)__ Immediately after the bounce, the large ball moves up at $$v$$ while the small ball still moves down at $$v.$$ Switch to the reference frame of the large ball. What is the small ball's velocity in this frame?

__(c)__ In the large ball's frame, the collision is a very light ball bouncing elastically off a stationary, much heavier ball. Find the small ball's velocity just after this collision — first in the large ball's frame, and then transformed back to the ground frame.

__(d)__ A ball dropped alone from height $$h$$ and bouncing elastically off the ground returns to height $$h.$$ Using energy conservation, how high can the small ball in this two-ball stack rise?

label: FMA05
name: The Center of Mass Frame and One-Dimensional Elastic Collisions — An object of mass $$m_1$$ moves with…
desc: An object of mass $$m_1$$ moves with velocity $$v_1$$ along a line, and an object of mass $$m_2$$ moves with velocity $$v_2$$ along the same line. They undergo a __perfectly elastic collision__ — one in which kinetic energy is conserved. In principle, you can find the final…
statement:
An object of mass $$m_1$$ moves with velocity $$v_1$$ along a line, and an object of mass $$m_2$$ moves with velocity $$v_2$$ along the same line. They undergo a __perfectly elastic collision__ — one in which kinetic energy is conserved. In principle, you can find the final velocities $$u_1$$ and $$u_2$$ by solving the momentum equation $$m_1v_1+m_2v_2=m_1u_1+m_2u_2$$ together with the energy equation $$\dfrac12 m_1v_1^2+\dfrac12 m_2v_2^2=\dfrac12 m_1u_1^2+\dfrac12 m_2u_2^2,$$ but solving that quadratic system is a pain. This problem develops a much faster method using the __center of mass frame__: the reference frame moving with the center of mass, whose velocity is $$v_{CM}=\dfrac{m_1v_1+m_2v_2}{m_1+m_2}.$$ To switch into a moving frame, subtract the frame's velocity from every object's velocity; to switch back, add it to every object's velocity.

__(a)__ Show that the system's total momentum, measured in the center of mass frame, is zero.

__(b)__ In the center of mass frame, the objects approach with equal and opposite momenta. Show that "each object's velocity simply reverses direction, keeping its speed" conserves both momentum and kinetic energy in this frame. (This reversal is what actually happens in a 1D elastic collision — but only in a frame where the total momentum is zero, which is why we switch to the center of mass frame first.)

__(c)__ Use the method — switch to the center of mass frame, reverse the velocities, switch back — to solve this collision: a mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ collides elastically, head-on, with an identical stationary mass $$m.$$ What happens? You can see the outcome when one billiard ball strikes another dead-on:

__(d)__ Use the same method on this collision: a mass $$m$$ moving to the right at speed $$v$$ collides elastically, head-on, with a stationary mass $$2m.$$ Find both final velocities. (Sanity check first: should the lighter mass stop, keep going, or bounce backward? Imagine the target were $$1000m$$ instead of $$2m.$$)

__(e)__ For the collisions in parts (c) and (d), compute the __difference__ between the two objects' velocities just before and just after the collision. Then explain why, in __every__ 1D perfectly elastic collision, the relative velocity keeps the same magnitude and switches sign: $$\Delta v_{\mathrm{after}}=-\Delta v_{\mathrm{before}}.$$

label: FMA05
name: A Block and a Sliding Wedge: an Elastic Collision in Disguise — A small block of mass $$m$$ moves on a…
desc: A small block of mass $$m$$ moves on a horizontal table at initial speed $$v_0.$$ It slides smoothly onto the sloped face of a big block of mass $$M,$$ which is also free to slide on the table. Everything moves without friction. The small block rises some way up the slope, comes…
statement:
A small block of mass $$m$$ moves on a horizontal table at initial speed $$v_0.$$ It slides smoothly onto the sloped face of a big block of mass $$M,$$ which is also free to slide on the table. Everything moves without friction. The small block rises some way up the slope, comes back down, and leaves the slope. Find the speed $$v$$ of the small block after it leaves the slope. (This problem appeared on the F=ma exam.)

(A) $$v=v_0$$ (B) $$v=\frac{m}{m+M}v_0$$ (C) $$v=\frac{M}{m+M}v_0$$ (D) $$v=\frac{M-m}{m}v_0$$ (E) $$v=\left|\frac{M-m}{m+M}\right|v_0$$

__(a)__ The problem gives the masses and initial velocities of two objects, implies that mechanical energy is conserved (the block slides "smoothly," and everything is frictionless), and asks only for a final velocity. Explain why the answer must be exactly the same as for a 1D perfectly elastic collision between the two objects — and why the slope angle of the big block cannot appear in the answer.

__(b)__ In a 1D perfectly elastic collision, the relative velocity between the objects keeps its magnitude and switches sign: $$\Delta v_{\mathrm{after}}=-\Delta v_{\mathrm{before}}.$$ Use this rule together with conservation of momentum to find the small block's final velocity, and select the matching answer choice. (Choose your own sign conventions carefully: the problem asks for a speed, so take an absolute value at the end.)

__(c)__ Multiple-choice strategy: dimensional analysis won't help here (every choice has correct dimensions), but extreme and special cases will. Test the cases $$m\gg M,$$ $$m\to 0,$$ and $$m=M$$ against the five choices, and show that process of elimination singles out the same answer.

label: FMA05
name: The Billiards Right Angle — An object of mass $$m$$ moves to the right with velocity $$\vec v.$$ It collides…
desc: An object of mass $$m$$ moves to the right with velocity $$\vec v.$$ It collides __perfectly elastically__, but slightly off-center, with a stationary object of the same mass $$m,$$ so that after the collision both objects are moving — the incoming object deflects to one side…
statement:
An object of mass $$m$$ moves to the right with velocity $$\vec v.$$ It collides __perfectly elastically__, but slightly off-center, with a stationary object of the same mass $$m,$$ so that after the collision both objects are moving — the incoming object deflects to one side with velocity $$\vec v_1,$$ and the target moves off to the other side with velocity $$\vec v_2.$$ Find the angle between the final velocity vectors $$\vec v_1$$ and $$\vec v_2.$$ (This problem is from Morin, __Problems and Solutions in Introductory Mechanics__.)

__(a)__ Write conservation of momentum as a vector equation and cancel the (equal) masses to get $$\vec v=\vec v_1+\vec v_2.$$ What does this equation say, geometrically, about how the three velocity vectors fit together in a picture?

__(b)__ Write conservation of kinetic energy in terms of the speeds $$v,$$ $$v_1,$$ and $$v_2,$$ and simplify. Interpret the resulting equation as a statement about your picture from part (a), and find the angle between $$\vec v_1$$ and $$\vec v_2.$$

__(c)__ This result is well known to pool players: when the cue ball strikes a stationary ball off-center, the two balls separate along paths at this angle, as in the clip below. But when the cue ball strikes the target dead-on, it stops completely instead. How is the dead-on case consistent with your answer?

label: FMA05
name: An Elastic Collision with Equal Exit Speeds — A mass $$m$$ moving with speed $$v_0$$ collides __elastically__…
desc: A mass $$m$$ moving with speed $$v_0$$ collides __elastically__ with a stationary mass $$2m.$$ After the collision, the mass $$m$$ moves at an angle $$\theta_1$$ above the original direction of motion, and the mass $$2m$$ moves at an angle $$\theta_2$$ below it, as shown. The…
statement:
A mass $$m$$ moving with speed $$v_0$$ collides __elastically__ with a stationary mass $$2m.$$ After the collision, the mass $$m$$ moves at an angle $$\theta_1$$ above the original direction of motion, and the mass $$2m$$ moves at an angle $$\theta_2$$ below it, as shown. The final speeds of the two masses turn out to be equal; call the common speed $$v.$$ Find $$v,$$ and find the deflection angles $$\theta_1$$ and $$\theta_2.$$

__(a)__ The collision is elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved. Using the fact that both final speeds equal $$v,$$ find $$v$$ in terms of $$v_0.$$

__(b)__ Write conservation of momentum as a vector equation, simplify by canceling what you can, and then split it into components: one equation along the original direction of motion (the $$x$$ direction) and one perpendicular to it (the $$y$$ direction). Take both $$\theta_1$$ and $$\theta_2$$ to be positive angles as drawn.

__(c)__ Solve your equations for $$\theta_1$$ and $$\theta_2.$$ Algebra hints from class: substitute your value of $$v$$ from part (a); you will need $$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$$; before squaring the $$x$$ equation, first isolate one of the cosine terms on one side, so that squaring doesn't produce a messy cross term; then add your squared equations so the trig identity collapses them.

label: FMA05
name: A Particle Explodes into Three Pieces — A particle at rest explodes into three particles of equal mass $$m,$$…
desc: A particle at rest explodes into three particles of equal mass $$m,$$ in the absence of external forces. Two of the particles emerge at a right angle to each other, each with the same speed $$v.$$ What is the speed of the third particle? (This problem appeared on the 2012 F=ma…
statement:
A particle at rest explodes into three particles of equal mass $$m,$$ in the absence of external forces. Two of the particles emerge at a right angle to each other, each with the same speed $$v.$$ What is the speed of the third particle? (This problem appeared on the 2012 F=ma exam.)

A convenient setup: place the $$x$$-axis along the bisector of the first two particles' paths, so those two particles move at $$45^\circ$$ above and below the $$x$$-axis, as shown.

__(a)__ Momentum is conserved in this explosion, but conservation of mechanical energy is no help. Explain why each statement is true.

__(b)__ Explain how you know, before calculating, that the third particle must move along the negative $$x$$-axis. Then write a momentum conservation equation in the $$x$$ direction and solve for the third particle's speed $$v_3.$$

__(c)__ Confirm your answer geometrically: the three momentum vectors add to zero, so drawn tip-to-tail they form a closed triangle. What triangle is it, and what does it give for $$v_3?$$

__(d)__ Suppose the problem had not told you the angle between the first two particles. Show that the problem would then be unsolvable, by finding what $$v_3$$ approaches in the limit where the angle between the first two particles' paths shrinks toward $$0^\circ,$$ and in the limit where it approaches $$180^\circ.$$

label: FMA06
name: Albert Einstein, after formulating his general theory of relativity, used it to predict…
desc: Albert Einstein, after formulating his general theory of relativity, used it to predict that light traveling from a distant star and brushing past the surface of the sun should be deflected by $$\theta = 1.8''$$ by the sun's gravity. (That's 1.8 arcseconds. One arcsecond is one…
statement:
Albert Einstein, after formulating his general theory of relativity, used it to predict that light traveling from a distant star and brushing past the surface of the sun should be deflected by $$\theta = 1.8''$$ by the sun's gravity. (That's 1.8 arcseconds. One arcsecond is one 60th of an arcminute, which is one 60th of a degree.) Newtonian gravity predicted a deflection of $$0.9''.$$

Arthur Eddington and collaborators measured the deflection of starlight by the sun during the 1919 total solar eclipse. They found that light was deflected by $$ \theta = 2'' \pm 0.3 ''.$$ Eddington claimed this confirmed general relativity over Newtonian gravity. However, many scientists were not convinced by this test. Which of the following is a valid reason to object to the conclusion that the test supports general relativity over Newtonian physics?

(a) The error bars on Eddington's measurement are too large; scientific evidence should be more precise than to have a $$15\%$$ error. (b) Eddington may have underestimated the size of his error bars a moderate amount (a factor of 1.5 or less). (c) Eddington may have underestimated the size of his error bars by a large amount (a factor of 3 or more). (d) Multiple data points are needed; a single data point cannot be considered scientific evidence. (e) Einstein's theory was still too new to be considered established.

label: FMA06
name: You weigh 100 samples with a scale. The mean reading is $$126.1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and the…
desc: You weigh 100 samples with a scale. The mean reading is $$126.1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and the standard deviation of the readings is $$5.1 \;\mathrm{g}.$$ Although the scale you are using reports masses to the nearest tenth of a gram, you suspect that the scale is poorly-calibrated so…
statement:
You weigh 100 samples with a scale. The mean reading is $$126.1 \;\mathrm{g},$$ and the standard deviation of the readings is $$5.1 \;\mathrm{g}.$$

Although the scale you are using reports masses to the nearest tenth of a gram, you suspect that the scale is poorly-calibrated so that its readings are consistently incorrect - either all too large or all too small by the same percentage. You don't know the size of this effect, but suspect it to be on the order of $$0.5\%.$$ What is your uncertainty in the combined mass of the samples?

(a) $$\pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{g}$$ (b) $$\pm 0.51 \;\mathrm{g}$$ (c) $$\pm 0.63 \;\mathrm{g}$$ (d) $$\pm 5.1 \;\mathrm{g}$$ (e) $$\pm 60 \;\mathrm{g}$$

label: FMA06
name: Adult platypuses weigh $$2.1 \pm 0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ You wish to estimate the weight of…
desc: Adult platypuses weigh $$2.1 \pm 0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ You wish to estimate the weight of a pile of exactly 3000 adult platypuses, randomly and independently selected from the adult population. Compared to the weight of a single platypus, your estimate will have: (a) larger…
statement:
Adult platypuses weigh $$2.1 \pm 0.9 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ You wish to estimate the weight of a pile of exactly 3000 adult platypuses, randomly and independently selected from the adult population. Compared to the weight of a single platypus, your estimate will have:

(a) larger absolute uncertainty and larger relative uncertainty (b) larger absolute uncertainty and the same relative uncertainty (c) larger absolute uncertainty and smaller relative uncertainty (d) the same absolute uncertainty and the same relative uncertainty (e) the same absolute uncertainty and smaller relative uncertainty

label: FMA06
name: For small angles $$\theta,$$ the torque $$\tau$$ on a single pendulum of mass $$m$$ and…
desc: For small angles $$\theta,$$ the torque $$\tau$$ on a single pendulum of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is $$\tau = \ell mg\sin\theta\,.$$ Measuring $$\theta$$ in radians, an approximation is $$\tau \approx \ell mg \theta\,.$$ What is the approximate range of angles for which…
statement:
For small angles $$\theta,$$ the torque $$\tau$$ on a single pendulum of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is $$\tau = \ell mg\sin\theta\,.$$

Measuring $$\theta$$ in radians, an approximation is $$\tau \approx \ell mg \theta\,.$$

What is the approximate range of angles for which the error in this approximation for the torque value is smaller than $$1\%?$$

For this question, use the following information:

For small angles, $$\sin\theta \approx \theta,$$ where $$\theta$$ is measured in radians. (The answers are listed in degrees, so you may have to convert.)

A more-accurate equation, still using radians, is $$\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}\,.$$

(a) $$|\theta| < 0.24^\circ$$ (b) $$|\theta| < 0.57^\circ$$ (c) $$|\theta| < 1^\circ$$ (d) $$|\theta| < 14^\circ$$ (e) $$|\theta| < 22.4^\circ$$

label: FMA06
name: A car competes in a race. The car begins the race with initial speed $$v_0$$ and…
desc: A car competes in a race. The car begins the race with initial speed $$v_0$$ and maintains a constant acceleration $$a$$ throughout the race. You use $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ to calculate the time it takes the car to complete the race. Both $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ have relative uncertainties…
statement:
A car competes in a race. The car begins the race with initial speed $$v_0$$ and maintains a constant acceleration $$a$$ throughout the race. You use $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ to calculate the time it takes the car to complete the race. Both $$v_0$$ and $$a$$ have relative uncertainties of $$10\%,$$ and their uncertainties are independent.

Between the uncertainty in $$v_0$$ and the uncertainty in $$a,$$ which contributes greater uncertainty to your calculation of the time the car takes to complete the race?

(a) The uncertainty in $$v_0$$ for sufficiently short races and the uncertainty in $$a$$ for sufficiently long races. (b) The uncertainty in $$v_0$$ for sufficiently long races and the uncertainty in $$a$$ for sufficiently short races. (c) The uncertainty in $$v_0.$$ (d) The uncertainty in $$a.$$ (e) They contribute equal uncertainty.

label: FMA06
name: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
desc: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. In a certain batch of brass, the copper used had a density of $$8.96 \pm 0.19 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The zinc had a density of $$7.14 \pm 0.30 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The alloy was $$65.00 \pm 0.02 \%$$ copper by volume. These uncertainties are…
statement:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

In a certain batch of brass, the copper used had a density of $$8.96 \pm 0.19 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The zinc had a density of $$7.14 \pm 0.30 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}.$$ The alloy was $$65.00 \pm 0.02 \%$$ copper by volume. These uncertainties are all independent. What was the uncertainty in the density of the resulting brass?

You may assume that in smelting, both volume and mass of metal are conserved.

(a) $$0.09 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$ (b) $$0.13 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$ (c) $$0.16 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$ (d) $$0.21 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$ (e) $$0.25 \;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

label: FMA06
name: A student makes an estimate of the acceleration due to gravity, $$g,$$ by dropping a rock…
desc: A student makes an estimate of the acceleration due to gravity, $$g,$$ by dropping a rock from a known height $$h$$ and measuring the time $$t$$ it takes to hit the ground. Neglecting air resistance, which one of the following situations will lead to the smallest value of the…
statement:
A student makes an estimate of the acceleration due to gravity, $$g,$$ by dropping a rock from a known height $$h$$ and measuring the time $$t$$ it takes to hit the ground. Neglecting air resistance, which one of the following situations will lead to the smallest value of the relative uncertainty, $$\dfrac{\Delta g}{g},$$ in the estimate?

(a) There is no uncertainty in $$t$$ and $$h$$ has a $$10\%$$ uncertainty. (b) There is no uncertainty in $$h$$ and $$t$$ has a $$10\%$$ uncertainty. (c) Both $$t$$ and $$h$$ have a $$5\%$$ uncertainty. (d) (a) and (b) yield the same uncertainty, which is smaller than (c). (e) (a), (b), and (c) all yield the same uncertainty.

label: FMA06
name: A car begins from rest and moves with constant acceleration $$a.$$ This fact is used to…
desc: A car begins from rest and moves with constant acceleration $$a.$$ This fact is used to calculate the distance $$d$$ the car has traveled after a time $$t.$$ Which of the following is not true: (a) If $$t$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$a$$ is exact, the error in $$d$$…
statement:
A car begins from rest and moves with constant acceleration $$a.$$ This fact is used to calculate the distance $$d$$ the car has traveled after a time $$t.$$

Which of the following is not true:

(a) If $$t$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$a$$ is exact, the error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$ (b) If $$t$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$a$$ is exact, the relative error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$ (c) If $$a$$ is uncertain by a fixed amount and $$t$$ is exact, the relative error in $$d$$ is constant over time. (d) If both $$a$$ and $$t$$ are uncertain by 1%, the uncertainty in $$t$$ contributes more to the uncertainty in $$d$$ than the uncertainty in $$a$$ contributes. (e) If $$t$$ is uncertain by 1% and $$a$$ is exact, the error in $$d$$ grows with $$t.$$

label: FMA06
name: Faith wants to measure the depth $$d$$ of a well. She decides to drop a stone into the…
desc: Faith wants to measure the depth $$d$$ of a well. She decides to drop a stone into the well and measure the time $$t$$ until she hears the splash that the stone made at the bottom of the well. She models the fall of the stone accurately, but ignores the time it takes sound to…
statement:
Faith wants to measure the depth $$d$$ of a well. She decides to drop a stone into the well and measure the time $$t$$ until she hears the splash that the stone made at the bottom of the well. She models the fall of the stone accurately, but ignores the time it takes sound to travel back up the well.

Which of these is closest to the largest value of $$d$$ for which Faith will have less than a $$5\%$$ error in the depth measurement?

Take the speed of sound in air to be $$330 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

(a) $$3.5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (b) $$7 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (c) $$14 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (d) $$54 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (e) $$330 \;\mathrm{m}$$

label: FMA06
name: The King measures the length of his foot, determining it to within an error of…
desc: The King measures the length of his foot, determining it to within an error of $$\sigma_k.$$ Next, the Royal Measurer makes an independent measurement of The King's foot with an error of $$\sigma_m.$$ Both values are reported to the Royal Statistician, who explains that the…
statement:
The King measures the length of his foot, determining it to within an error of $$\sigma_k.$$

Next, the Royal Measurer makes an independent measurement of The King's foot with an error of $$\sigma_m.$$

Both values are reported to the Royal Statistician, who explains that the uncertainty in the size of The King's foot is now $$\sigma_k/2.$$

Assuming the Royal Statistician accurately minimized the error in the reported length of The King's foot, what is the ratio $$\dfrac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_k}?$$

(a) $$0.5$$ (b) $$0.58$$ (c) $$0.75$$ (d) $$1$$ (e) $$1.41$$

label: FMA06
name: **a)** Galileo attempted to measure the speed of light. At night time, he stood on a…
desc: **a)** Galileo attempted to measure the speed of light. At night time, he stood on a hilltop while his assistant stood on another hilltop several miles away. Each had a lamp that was shielded (so that no one could see the light), but could be unshielded (at which point people…
statement:
**a)** Galileo attempted to measure the speed of light. At night time, he stood on a hilltop while his assistant stood on another hilltop several miles away. Each had a lamp that was shielded (so that no one could see the light), but could be unshielded (at which point people could see the light it made). Galileo unshielded his lamp, and as soon as the assistant saw the light from Galileo's lamp, the assistant unshield his own lamp. Galileo recorded the time between unshielding his lamp and detecting light from his assistant's lamp. However, when using this method with distances up to five kilometers, Galileo could not detect any extra time delay.

If Galileo could measure times to within $$0.2\;\mathrm{s},$$ place a lower bound on the speed of light from Galileo's experiment.

**b)** The next improvement in measuring the speed of light was by Ole Rømer and others in 1676. Rømer observed Io, a moon of Jupiter. Due to its orbit, Io would disappear behind Jupiter from time to time, from the point of view of Earth. This is a very regular motion, but Rømer noticed that when Jupiter was far away from the Earth, Io emerged from eclipse later than when Jupiter was closer to Earth. Rømer was able to use observations of Io to estimate the time it takes light to travel from Earth to Jupiter. Then, using the known relative distances between the planets, he ultimately estimated that it takes light about 11 minutes to travel the Earth-Sun distance. His method was only accurate to 4 minutes.

Around the same time, the first estimates of the size of the solar system were made by measuring the parallax of Mars. These measurements estimated the Earth-Sun distance to be $$1.1 \times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m},$$ accurate to about $$30\%.$$ What was the best estimate of the speed of light at this time? To about what accuracy was the speed of light known?

**c)** Today, the speed of light is set, by definition, to be $$c = 2.99792458 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ This definition allows us to define the length one meter in terms of the duration one second. Because it is a definition, the error in $$c$$ is zero.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology claims that its best atomic clocks have an uncertainty of one second per 15 billion years. This is the best-known timekeeping in the world. What uncertainty does this imply over a length of $$4 \;\mathrm{km}?$$

**d)** The LIGO project has mirrors placed approximately $$4 \;\mathrm{km}$$ apart. In order to detect gravitational waves, the project attempts to measure displacements of mirrors on the order of $$10^{-19}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Briefly explain how this is conceivably achievable, despite the limit described in part (c).

label: FMA06
name: Reporting a Measurement: The Electron's Charge — You use a ruler whose finest markings are $$1\;\mathrm{mm}$$…
desc: You use a ruler whose finest markings are $$1\;\mathrm{mm}$$ apart to measure the thickness of your physics textbook, and you read off $$2.0\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ In physics, no measurement is perfect, so it is good practice to report every measurement together with its __error__ or…
statement:
You use a ruler whose finest markings are $$1\;\mathrm{mm}$$ apart to measure the thickness of your physics textbook, and you read off $$2.0\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ In physics, no measurement is perfect, so it is good practice to report every measurement together with its __error__ or __uncertainty__. (We use the two terms interchangeably, and neither one means "mistake".) An uncertain measurement is written with the $$\pm$$ symbol, as in $$x = 2.0 \pm 0.05\;\mathrm{cm},$$ meaning that if you made many independent measurements, they would all be roughly $$2.0\;\mathrm{cm}$$ but would typically vary from it by about $$0.05\;\mathrm{cm}.$$

__(a)__ Based on the spacing of the ruler's markings, estimate the uncertainty in your thickness measurement, and explain where your estimate comes from.

__(b)__ One convention of reporting is violated in the expression $$x = 2.0 \pm 0.05\;\mathrm{cm}$$: a measurement should be reported to the same digit as its error. Rewrite the measurement correctly.

__(c)__ A computer simulated one million people independently measuring the same book; a histogram of their measurements is shown below. (Its bell shape is called a __Gaussian distribution__, and some F=ma problems mention __Gaussian errors__, meaning errors drawn from a plot of this shape.) What does the uncertainty $$\Delta x = 0.05\;\mathrm{cm}$$ tell you about this histogram? Is every measurement guaranteed to fall between $$1.95\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and $$2.05\;\mathrm{cm}?$$

__(d)__ In 1913, Robert Millikan and Harvey Fletcher published the result of the first-ever measurement of the charge on an electron: $$(1.5924 \pm 0.0017) \times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{C}.$$ The modern-day accepted value is $$1.602176634 \times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{C}.$$ Is their result consistent with the modern value? Justify your answer, keeping in mind that the quoted uncertainty is a typical spread, not a hard bound.

__(e)__ The __relative error__ in a quantity $$x$$ is the error divided by the quantity itself, $$\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}.$$ (To distinguish it from relative error, the plain error $$\Delta x$$ is sometimes called the __absolute error__; if you just see "error", assume absolute error.) Find the relative error between Millikan and Fletcher's value and the modern value — that is, treat their actual discrepancy from the modern value as the error.

label: FMA06
name: The Speed of a Model Car (2019 F=ma A Exam) — The following problem appeared on the 2019 F=ma A exam. To test…
desc: The following problem appeared on the 2019 F=ma A exam. To test the speed of a model car, you time the car with a stopwatch as it travels a distance of $$100\;\mathrm{m}.$$ You record a time of $$5.0\;\mathrm{s},$$ and your measurement has an uncertainty of $$0.2\;\mathrm{s}.$$…
statement:
The following problem appeared on the 2019 F=ma A exam. To test the speed of a model car, you time the car with a stopwatch as it travels a distance of $$100\;\mathrm{m}.$$ You record a time of $$5.0\;\mathrm{s},$$ and your measurement has an uncertainty of $$0.2\;\mathrm{s}.$$ What is the uncertainty in your estimate of the car's speed? Assume that the car travels at constant speed and that the distance of $$100\;\mathrm{m}$$ is known very precisely.

(A) $$20 \pm 0.16\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (B) $$20 \pm 0.8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (C) $$20 \pm 1.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (D) $$20 \pm 1.25\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (E) $$20 \pm 4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$$

__(a)__ Ignoring uncertainty, what is your best estimate of the car's speed?

__(b)__ The statement $$t = 5.0 \pm 0.2\;\mathrm{s}$$ means the true time is usually between $$4.8\;\mathrm{s}$$ and $$5.2\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Find the range of speeds corresponding to that range of times, and use it to choose the best answer.

__(c)__ Compute the __relative error__ (error divided by value) in your speed estimate and the relative error in the time measurement. How do they compare?

__(d)__ Your result in (c) illustrates two general rules. First, the __scaling rule__: multiplying a measured quantity by an exact constant multiplies its absolute error by the same constant and leaves its relative error unchanged. Second, the __reciprocal rule__: the relative error in $$1/x$$ is approximately equal to the relative error in $$x,$$ as long as the relative error is small. Use these two rules to re-derive the uncertainty in the speed in one line, starting from $$v = x \cdot \dfrac{1}{t}.$$

label: FMA06
name: Timing an Oscillator — Suppose you are measuring the position $$x$$ of a mass oscillating on a spring, where…
desc: Suppose you are measuring the position $$x$$ of a mass oscillating on a spring, where $$x$$ is the displacement from equilibrium — so a graph of $$x$$ versus $$t$$ is a sine-like wave whose __peaks__ are the maximum $$x,$$ whose __troughs__ are the minimum $$x,$$ and which…
statement:
Suppose you are measuring the position $$x$$ of a mass oscillating on a spring, where $$x$$ is the displacement from equilibrium — so a graph of $$x$$ versus $$t$$ is a sine-like wave whose __peaks__ are the maximum $$x,$$ whose __troughs__ are the minimum $$x,$$ and which crosses $$x = 0$$ at the equilibrium position. You wish to make the measurement at a certain time $$t,$$ obtaining $$x(t).$$ Your device for measuring position is very accurate, so its reading contributes negligible uncertainty to your result. However, you are only able to activate the device to within an uncertainty in time $$\Delta t.$$ Then which of the following is true?

(A) There is no position uncertainty in your measurements of $$x(t).$$

(B) There is the same uncertainty $$\Delta x$$ for all your measurements.

(C) There is greater uncertainty $$\Delta x$$ when the oscillator is at a peak or trough than when it is at its equilibrium position.

(D) There is greater uncertainty $$\Delta x$$ when the oscillator is at its equilibrium position than when it is at a peak or trough.

(E) The uncertainty $$\Delta x$$ is the same at peaks, troughs, and the equilibrium position, but not the same everywhere.

The figure below shows the oscillator's position versus time, with shaded bands of width $$2\Delta t$$ (the possible activation times) drawn at a peak and at an equilibrium crossing, and dashed lines marking the corresponding ranges of measured positions.

__(a)__ Suppose one of your measurements comes out as $$x(1.2\;\mathrm{s}) = 3.3\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Explain why choice (A) is wrong — that is, why this measurement still has nonzero position uncertainty even though the position-measuring device is perfect.

__(b)__ Using the figure, decide which choice is correct, and explain the reasoning.

__(c)__ Generalize: if a quantity $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ and you know the error $$\Delta x,$$ what feature of the graph of $$y(x)$$ determines the error $$\Delta y?$$ Write the general rule as an equation.

label: FMA06
name: The Area of a Square Field — You measure the side length of a square field to be $$s = 75 \pm 1\;\mathrm{m}.$$
desc: You measure the side length of a square field to be $$s = 75 \pm 1\;\mathrm{m}.$$ __(a)__ How should you report your measurement of the area of the field? Find the range of possible areas by plugging in the top and bottom of the side-length range, and report the area in the form…
statement:
You measure the side length of a square field to be $$s = 75 \pm 1\;\mathrm{m}.$$

__(a)__ How should you report your measurement of the area of the field? Find the range of possible areas by plugging in the top and bottom of the side-length range, and report the area in the form (value) $$\pm$$ (error). Use scientific notation, rounding the value to the digit where the error lives.

__(b)__ The __relative error__ of a quantity $$x$$ with error $$\Delta x$$ is $$\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}.$$ How does the relative error in the area compare to the relative error in the side length?

__(c)__ Your result in (b) is an instance of a general rule: if $$u = x^n,$$ then $$\dfrac{\Delta u}{u} = |n|\,\dfrac{\Delta x}{x},$$ valid for any power $$n$$ (including negative and fractional powers) as long as the relative error is small compared to $$\dfrac{1}{n}.$$ Use this rule to answer two quick questions. First, if instead the __area__ of a square is measured with a relative error of $$3\%,$$ what is the relative error of the side length deduced from it? Second, what does the rule say about the relative error of $$\dfrac{1}{x}$$ compared to the relative error of $$x?$$

label: FMA06
name: Four Ways to Measure a String — When two measured quantities with __independent__ errors are added, their…
desc: When two measured quantities with __independent__ errors are added, their errors partially cancel: one error may come out positive while the other comes out negative. (Independent means that knowing one error tells you nothing about the other.) The cancellation isn't guaranteed…
statement:
When two measured quantities with __independent__ errors are added, their errors partially cancel: one error may come out positive while the other comes out negative. (Independent means that knowing one error tells you nothing about the other.) The cancellation isn't guaranteed, but on average it makes the error of the sum smaller than the sum of the errors. Independent errors __add in quadrature__: if $$m = m_1 + m_2$$ with independent errors, then $$\Delta m = \sqrt{(\Delta m_1)^2 + (\Delta m_2)^2}.$$ Geometrically, $$\Delta m$$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $$\Delta m_1$$ and $$\Delta m_2,$$ which by the triangle inequality is shorter than the two legs laid end to end:

By contrast, multiplying a single measurement by an exact constant just scales its error: $$\Delta(2x) = 2\,\Delta x.$$ The quadrature rule does not apply to $$x + x,$$ because a measurement's error is not independent of itself — if one copy of the error is positive, so is the other, and there is no chance for cancellation.

Four students measure the length of a $$1.50\;\mathrm{m}$$ string using different tools. Each student reports an uncertainty estimate representing an independent random error applicable to the measurement. Alice: a single measurement using a $$2.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ long tape measure, to within $$\pm 2\;\mathrm{mm}.$$ Bob: two measurements using a wooden meter stick, each to within $$\pm 2\;\mathrm{mm},$$ which he adds together. Christina: two measurements using a machinist's meter ruler, each to within $$\pm 1\;\mathrm{mm},$$ which she adds together. Dalton: a single measurement using a machinist's meter ruler to within $$\pm 1\;\mathrm{mm},$$ obtained after folding the string exactly in half; his final value is twice this measurement.

__(a)__ Find each student's total uncertainty.

__(b)__ Rank the four measurements from least to most error.

__(c)__ Now suppose $$100$$ students each independently measure the full string once, each with uncertainty $$\Delta x = 1\;\mathrm{mm},$$ and they average their results. Show that the error of the average of $$n$$ equally uncertain independent measurements is $$\Delta \bar{x} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\sqrt{n}},$$ and evaluate it for the $$100$$ students.

label: FMA06
name: Combining Alice's and Bob's Measurements (2018 F=ma A Exam, #25) — The following is problem 25 from the 2018…
desc: The following is problem 25 from the 2018 F=ma A exam. Alice and Bob are working on a lab report. Alice measures the period of a pendulum to be $$1.013 \pm 0.008\;\mathrm{s},$$ while Bob independently measures the period to be $$0.997 \pm 0.016\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Alice and Bob can…
statement:
The following is problem 25 from the 2018 F=ma A exam. Alice and Bob are working on a lab report. Alice measures the period of a pendulum to be $$1.013 \pm 0.008\;\mathrm{s},$$ while Bob independently measures the period to be $$0.997 \pm 0.016\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Alice and Bob can combine their measurements in several ways. Procedure 1: keep Alice's result and ignore Bob's. Procedure 2: average Alice's and Bob's results. Procedure 3: perform a weighted average of Alice's and Bob's results, with Alice's result weighted 4 times more than Bob's. Rank these three procedures in terms of their uncertainty.

You will need two error-propagation facts. Scaling: multiplying a measurement by an exact constant $$c$$ multiplies its error by $$|c|.$$ Quadrature: independent errors add in quadrature, $$\Delta(x_1 + x_2) = \sqrt{(\Delta x_1)^2 + (\Delta x_2)^2}.$$ A __weighted average__ of two measurements $$t_A$$ and $$t_B$$ is $$\bar{t}_w = \alpha t_A + (1-\alpha) t_B$$ for some weight $$0 \le \alpha \le 1$$; an ordinary average is the special case $$\alpha = \tfrac12.$$

__(a)__ What is the weight $$\alpha$$ in procedure 3?

__(b)__ Compute the uncertainty of each of the three procedures and rank them.

__(c)__ Find the weight $$\alpha$$ that minimizes the uncertainty of the weighted average of Alice's and Bob's measurements. (Hint: the squared uncertainty is a quadratic in $$\alpha,$$ and an upward-opening parabola $$y = ax^2 + bx + c$$ has its minimum at the vertex $$x = \dfrac{-b}{2a}.$$) How does the optimal weight compare with the weighting in procedure 3?

label: FMA06
name: An Ideal-Gas Thermometer — The ideal gas law states $$PV = N k_B T,$$ where $$P$$ is the pressure of a gas…
desc: The ideal gas law states $$PV = N k_B T,$$ where $$P$$ is the pressure of a gas, $$V$$ is its volume, $$N$$ is the number of molecules in the gas, $$k_B$$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $$T$$ is the temperature. Suppose that Boltzmann's constant is known exactly. A thermometer is…
statement:
The ideal gas law states $$PV = N k_B T,$$ where $$P$$ is the pressure of a gas, $$V$$ is its volume, $$N$$ is the number of molecules in the gas, $$k_B$$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $$T$$ is the temperature. Suppose that Boltzmann's constant is known exactly. A thermometer is constructed using an ideal gas. It is possible to measure the pressure of the gas to within $$0.1\%,$$ the volume to within $$0.5\%,$$ and the number of molecules to within $$0.2\%.$$ These errors are independent. To what percent accuracy is it possible to infer the temperature of the gas?

__(a)__ Warm-up: suppose your measurement of a quantity $$a$$ comes out $$1\%$$ too large, and your measurement of $$b$$ also comes out $$1\%$$ too large. By approximately what percent is your computed product $$ab$$ too large? What does this suggest about how errors combine when variables are multiplied?

__(b)__ Because the errors in the factors are independent, they partially cancel, and the relative errors actually add __in quadrature__: $$\left(\dfrac{\Delta(ab)}{ab}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta a}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\Delta b}{b}\right)^2.$$ Derive this from two facts you already have: the logarithm turns products into sums, $$\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b,$$ and the error in any function is $$\Delta y = (\text{slope of } y)\cdot\Delta x.$$ Given that the slope of $$\ln x$$ is $$\dfrac{1}{x},$$ first show that $$\Delta(\ln x) = \dfrac{\Delta x}{x}$$ — the relative error in $$x$$ — and then explain how applying the quadrature rule for sums to $$\ln(ab)$$ gives the product rule above.

__(c)__ Apply the product rule (it extends to any number of independent factors, and the relative error of $$\dfrac{1}{N}$$ equals the relative error of $$N$$) to find the percent accuracy to which the temperature can be inferred.

label: FMA06
name: Measuring g with a Pendulum (2018 F=ma A Exam) — The following problem is from the 2018 F=ma A exam. A group…
desc: The following problem is from the 2018 F=ma A exam. A group of students wish to measure the acceleration of gravity with a simple pendulum. They take one length measurement of the pendulum to be $$l = 1.00 \pm 0.05\;\mathrm{m}.$$ They then measure the period of a single swing to…
statement:
The following problem is from the 2018 F=ma A exam. A group of students wish to measure the acceleration of gravity with a simple pendulum. They take one length measurement of the pendulum to be $$l = 1.00 \pm 0.05\;\mathrm{m}.$$ They then measure the period of a single swing to be $$T = 2.00 \pm 0.10\;\mathrm{s}.$$ Assume that all uncertainties are Gaussian. The computed acceleration of gravity from this experiment, illustrating the range of possible values, should be recorded as:

(A) $$9.87 \pm 0.10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ (B) $$9.87 \pm 0.15\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ (C) $$9.9 \pm 0.25\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ (D) $$9.9 \pm 1.1\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ (E) $$9.9 \pm 1.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$

Useful facts: the angular frequency of a simple pendulum is $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{l}},$$ and angular frequency is related to the period by $$\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}.$$ For error propagation: scaling by an exact constant (like $$4\pi^2$$) leaves the relative error unchanged; when independent quantities are multiplied or divided, their relative errors add in quadrature; and if $$u = x^n,$$ then $$\dfrac{\Delta u}{u} = |n|\,\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}.$$

__(a)__ Combine the two pendulum formulas to express $$g$$ in terms of $$l$$ and $$T,$$ and compute the best estimate of $$g.$$

__(b)__ Propagate the uncertainties to find $$\Delta g,$$ and choose the correct answer.

label: FMA07
name: A plank rests on top of the axles of two identical wheels. Each wheel's outer radius is…
desc: A plank rests on top of the axles of two identical wheels. Each wheel's outer radius is $$0.25 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and each wheel's axle has radius $$0.05 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ If the wheels roll $$1.00 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from their original position, how much does the plank move from its…
statement:
A plank rests on top of the axles of two identical wheels. Each wheel's outer radius is $$0.25 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and each wheel's axle has radius $$0.05 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ If the wheels roll $$1.00 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from their original position, how much does the plank move from its original position?

Assume that there is no slipping anywhere, and that the plank does not tip.

(a) $$0.75 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (b) $$1.00 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (c) $$1.20 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (d) $$1.30 \;\mathrm{m}$$ (e) $$1.50 \;\mathrm{m}$$

desc: A uniform circular disk of radius $$R$$ begins with a mass $$M.$$ A hole is cut in the disk as shown in the diagram. In terms of the radius $$R$$ and the mass $$M$$ of the original disk, what is the moment of inertia of the resulting object about the same axis? The moment of…
statement:
A uniform circular disk of radius $$R$$ begins with a mass $$M.$$ A hole is cut in the disk as shown in the diagram. In terms of the radius $$R$$ and the mass $$M$$ of the original disk, what is the moment of inertia of the resulting object about the same axis? (a) $$(9/32) MR^2$$ (b) $$(3/8) MR^2$$ (c) $$(13/32) MR^2$$ (d) $$(15/32) MR^2$$ (e) $$(15/16) MR^2$$

label: FMA07
name: A person of mass $$M_2$$ stands on the edge of a disk of mass $$M_1$$ and radius $$R$$…
desc: A person of mass $$M_2$$ stands on the edge of a disk of mass $$M_1$$ and radius $$R$$. The disk can rotate freely about its center without friction, and there is enough friction between the disk and the person so that the person rotates with the disk. The disk and person are…
statement:
A person of mass $$M_2$$ stands on the edge of a disk of mass $$M_1$$ and radius $$R$$. The disk can rotate freely about its center without friction, and there is enough friction between the disk and the person so that the person rotates with the disk. The disk and person are initially stationary. If the person then throws a stone of mass $$m$$ in the direction tangent to the disk's edge with initial velocity $$v$$ relative to the center of the disk, what is the angular speed $$\omega$$ of the disk/person system about the center of the disk immediately after the stone is thrown?

(a) $$\frac{mv}{R(M_1 + 2M_2)}$$

(b) $$\frac{mv}{R(2M_1 + M_2)}$$

(c) $$\frac{2mv}{R(M_1 + M_2)}$$

(d) $$\frac{2mv}{R(2M_1 + M_2)}$$

(e) $$\frac{2mv}{R(M_1 + 2M_2)}$$

name: Two disks are mounted on thin, lightweight rods oriented through their centers and normal…
desc: Two disks are mounted on thin, lightweight rods oriented through their centers and normal to the disks. These axles are constrained to be vertical at all times, and the disks can pivot frictionlessly on the rods. The disks have identical thickness and are made of the same…
statement:
Two disks are mounted on thin, lightweight rods oriented through their centers and normal to the disks. These axles are constrained to be vertical at all times, and the disks can pivot frictionlessly on the rods. The disks have identical thickness and are made of the same material, but have differing radii $$r_1$$ and $$r_2$$. The disks are given angular velocities of magnitudes $$\omega_1$$ and $$\omega_2$$ respectively, and are brought into contact at their edges. After the disks interact via friction, it is found that both disks come exactly to a halt. Which of the following must hold? Ignore effects associated with the vertical rods.

(a) $$\omega_1^2 r_1 = \omega_2^2 r_2.$$

(b) $$\omega_1 r_1 = \omega_2 r_2.$$

(c) $$\omega_1 r_1^2 = \omega_2 r_2^2.$$

(d) $$\omega_1 r_1^3 = \omega_2 r_2^3.$$

(e) $$\omega_1 r_1^4 = \omega_2 r_2^4.$$

desc: The moment of inertia of a uniform equilateral triangle with mass $$m$$ and side length $$a$$ about an axis through one of its sides and parallel to that side is $$(1/8) ma^2$$. What is the moment of inertia of a uniform regular hexagon of mass $$m$$ and side length $$a$$ about…

The moment of inertia of a uniform equilateral triangle with mass $$m$$ and side length $$a$$ about an axis through one of its sides and parallel to that side is $$(1/8) ma^2$$. desc: A spherical shell of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is completely filled with a frictionless fluid, also of mass $$M.$$ It is released from rest, and then it rolls without slipping down an incline that makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. What will be the acceleration of…
statement:
A spherical shell of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is completely filled with a frictionless fluid, also of mass $$M.$$ It is released from rest, and then it rolls without slipping down an incline that makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. What will be the acceleration of the shell down the incline just after it is released?

The moment of inertia of a thin shell of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m$$ about the center of mass is $$I = \tfrac{2}{3} mr^2$$; the moment of inertia of a solid sphere of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m$$ about the center of mass is $$I = \tfrac{2}{5} mr^2.$$

(a) $$a = \tfrac{3}{8} g \sin\theta$$ (b) $$a = \tfrac{1}{2} g \sin\theta$$ (c) $$a = \tfrac{3}{5} g \sin\theta$$ (d) $$a = \tfrac{3}{4} g \sin\theta$$ (e) $$a = g \sin\theta$$

(b) $$\tfrac{2}{3} Mg$$

(c) $$Mg$$

(d) $$\tfrac{4}{3} Mg$$
