label: FMA07
name: A hanging rod with mass $$M = 3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and length $$\ell=0.8 \;\mathrm{m}$$ is…
desc: A hanging rod with mass $$M = 3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and length $$\ell=0.8 \;\mathrm{m}$$ is allowed to rotate freely around a hinge about one of its ends. A ball of mass $$m = 2.0 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ with horizontal velocity $$v_0 = 5.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides elastically with the…
statement:
A hanging rod with mass $$M = 3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and length $$\ell=0.8 \;\mathrm{m}$$ is allowed to rotate freely around a hinge about one of its ends. A ball of mass $$m = 2.0 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ with horizontal velocity $$v_0 = 5.0 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ collides elastically with the rod at the bottom so that the ball is deflected by an angle $$\theta$$, and such that the rod swings up to an angle of $$90^\circ$$. What is the value closest to the angle $$\theta$$ that the ball is deflected?

The moment of inertia of the rod about one of its ends is $$\tfrac{1}{3} M\ell^2$$.

(a) $$15^\circ$$ (b) $$23^\circ$$ (c) $$30^\circ$$ (d) $$45^\circ$$ (e) $$60^\circ$$

label: FMA07
name: A square block with mass $$m = 1\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and sidelength $$\ell = 1\;\mathrm{m}$$…
desc: A square block with mass $$m = 1\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and sidelength $$\ell = 1\;\mathrm{m}$$ sits at rest on a table, with its bottom right corner attached to the table with a pivot, as shown in the figure. A ball, also with mass $$m$$, moves horizontally to the right with speed…
statement:
A square block with mass $$m = 1\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and sidelength $$\ell = 1\;\mathrm{m}$$ sits at rest on a table, with its bottom right corner attached to the table with a pivot, as shown in the figure. A ball, also with mass $$m$$, moves horizontally to the right with speed $$v$$ and collides with the block and sticks to it at its upper left corner. The moment of inertia of the block around its __center__ is $$m\ell^2/6$$. What is the value that $$v$$ must be greater than in order for the block to tip over?

(a) $$4.07 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (b) $$5.18 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (c) $$5.76 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (d) $$7.20 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ (e) $$8.14 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$

label: FMA07
name: An empty tin can has radius can be modeled as a hollow cylinder. Wound around its…
desc: An empty tin can has radius can be modeled as a hollow cylinder. Wound around its circumference is a massless string which is attached to a winch. The can is placed on a slope at angle $$\theta$$ to the horizontal so that the string runs up the slope as in the figure. The can…
statement:
An empty tin can has radius can be modeled as a hollow cylinder. Wound around its circumference is a massless string which is attached to a winch. The can is placed on a slope at angle $$\theta$$ to the horizontal so that the string runs up the slope as in the figure. The can does not touch the slope directly.

We seek to design an experiment to determine both the slope of the incline and the mass of the can. The winch has radius $$r_w$$ and can be set to turn a fixed number of turns with a constant torque. Both the number of turns and torque can be adjusted. The torque applied by the winch is $$\tau = r_w F,$$ where $$F$$ is the tension in the string. In the experiment, the can is initially held stationary and is then released, with the winch set to wind $$n_t$$ turns of rope. The time taken, $$t,$$ is measured for a range of different torques, $$\tau.$$

In this problem, we will figure out how to analyze the data from the experiment to find the mass of the can and slope of the incline.

**a)** Find the acceleration $$a$$ of center of mass of the can in the direction up the slope in terms of $$F,$$ the tension in the rope, $$m, g,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**b)** By considering the torque and angular acceleration of the can, find an equation for the acceleration $$a_r$$ of the rope in the direction up the incline in terms of $$F, m, g,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**c)** Find combinations of the quantities $$\tau$$ and $$t,$$ which, when plotted against each other, should result in a straight line.

**d)** Suppose $$r_w = 84 \;\mathrm{cm}, n_t = 3.00,$$ and $$g = 9.80 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The table below shows the measured values of $$\tau$$ and $$t.$$ Drawing an appropriate graph, find $$m$$ and $$\theta.$$ \begin{tabular}{ c c c } $$\tau (\mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{m})$$ & $$t (\mathrm{s})$$ \\ \hline 1.00 & 6.73 \\ 2.00 & 2.60 \\ 3.00 & 1.91 \\ 4.00 & 1.59 \\ 5.00 & 1.38 \\ 6.00 & 1.24 \\ 7.00 & 1.14 \\ 8.00 & 1.05 \\ 9.00 & 0.99 \\ 10.00 & 0.93 \end{tabular}

label: FMA07
name: The Spinning Ring: Angular Speed and the Right-Hand Rule — A thin ring of radius $$R$$ spins about the axis…
desc: A thin ring of radius $$R$$ spins about the axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring — the axis sticks straight out of the plane in which the ring lies, like the handle of a spinning top. The ring makes one complete rotation in a time $$T,$$ called the __period__. You can…
statement:
A thin ring of radius $$R$$ spins about the axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring — the axis sticks straight out of the plane in which the ring lies, like the handle of a spinning top. The ring makes one complete rotation in a time $$T,$$ called the __period__.

You can view a 3D animation of the rotating ring (with a point on its edge and that point's velocity vector drawn in) at https://glowscript.org/#/user/mark.d.eichenlaub/folder/AoPS/program/rotatingring — right-click and move the mouse to change the viewing angle.

__(a)__ What is the speed $$v$$ of a point on the edge of the ring?

__(b)__ The __angular speed__ $$\omega$$ (lowercase Greek omega) of the ring is defined so that in a time $$t,$$ the angle through which the ring has rotated is $$\theta = \omega t,$$ with angles measured in radians (one full rotation is $$2\pi$$ radians). Find $$\omega$$ in terms of $$T.$$ Then combine your formulas for $$v$$ and $$\omega$$ into a single equation relating $$v,$$ $$\omega,$$ and $$R.$$

__(c)__ What are the __dimensions__ of $$\omega,$$ and how do they differ from the dimensions of an ordinary (linear) speed? Careful: the question asks for dimensions, not units — length is a dimension, while feet and meters are units. We write dimensions upright, $$\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{T}$$ for mass, length, and time. (Radians are dimensionless: the SI definition is $$1\;\mathrm{rad} = 1.$$)

__(d)__ Whenever an object's only motion is rotation about an axis, the speed of any point on it is $$v = \omega r,$$ where $$r$$ is that point's distance from the axis. Suppose a thin rod rotates about one of its ends, with beads attached at several points along its length, as in the animation below. Which bead has the largest $$\omega?$$ Which has the largest $$v?$$

__(e)__ The __angular velocity__ vector $$\vec{\omega}$$ of the ring is a single vector meant to describe the rotation of every point of the ring at once. Why can't it point anywhere in the plane of the ring? Which way does it point, and how does the __right-hand rule__ (illustrated below) pick between the two remaining possibilities?

__(f)__ The __angular acceleration__ $$\vec{\alpha}$$ (alpha) is the rate of change of the angular velocity, just as $$\vec{a}$$ is the rate of change of $$\vec{v}.$$ This gives a correspondence between linear and angular quantities: $$x \leftrightarrow \theta,$$ $$v \leftrightarrow \omega,$$ $$a \leftrightarrow \alpha.$$ Now suppose the ring instead starts at rest and spins up with __constant__ angular acceleration $$\alpha,$$ completing its first full rotation in a time $$T.$$ Using the linear formula $$x = \frac12 a t^2$$ (distance traveled from rest under constant acceleration) and the correspondence, find $$\alpha,$$ and check that your answer has the correct dimensions.

label: FMA07
name: Reading a Disk's Angular Velocity Graph — A flat disk rotates about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the…
desc: A flat disk rotates about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the disk and through its center. The graph below shows the disk's angular velocity: it begins at $$4\;\mathrm{rad/s}$$ at $$t = 0$$ and decreases linearly, crossing zero at $$t = 2.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ and reaching…
statement:
A flat disk rotates about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the disk and through its center. The graph below shows the disk's angular velocity: it begins at $$4\;\mathrm{rad/s}$$ at $$t = 0$$ and decreases linearly, crossing zero at $$t = 2.0\;\mathrm{s}$$ and reaching $$-2\;\mathrm{rad/s}$$ at $$t = 3.0\;\mathrm{s}.$$ (Negative angular velocity means the disk has reversed its direction of spin.)

Angular kinematics mirrors linear kinematics: just as the acceleration is the slope of a velocity-versus-time graph and the displacement is the signed area under it, the __angular acceleration__ $$\alpha$$ is the slope of the $$\omega$$ versus $$t$$ graph, and the __angular displacement__ $$\Delta\theta$$ (the net angle turned) is the signed area under it, with area below the axis counting as negative.

__(a)__ Determine the angular acceleration of the disk at $$t = 2.0\;\mathrm{s}.$$

__(b)__ Through what net angle does the disk turn during the $$3$$ seconds shown?

__(c)__ The angular acceleration is the slope of an $$\omega$$ versus $$t$$ graph. What sort of graph would have $$\omega$$ as its slope?

label: FMA07
name: The Special Points of a Rolling Wheel — A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls __without slipping__ to the right along…
desc: A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls __without slipping__ to the right along level ground, its center moving at constant speed $$v_{\rm cm}.$$ Rolling without slipping means there is no sliding between the surface of the wheel and the ground (and no hopping off the ground) — this is…
statement:
A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls __without slipping__ to the right along level ground, its center moving at constant speed $$v_{\rm cm}.$$ Rolling without slipping means there is no sliding between the surface of the wheel and the ground (and no hopping off the ground) — this is ordinary rolling, the kind a bicycle or car tire is supposed to do. Rolling can be thought of as the sum of two motions: the whole wheel __translates__ to the right at $$v_{\rm cm},$$ and the wheel also __rotates__ about its center with angular speed $$\omega,$$ so that relative to the center, every point on the rim moves at speed $$\omega R.$$ The animation below tracks the velocity of one point on the rim of a rolling wheel.

__(a)__ Does the wheel spin clockwise or counterclockwise? In the reference frame of the ground, what is the speed of the point of the wheel at the very bottom, where the wheel touches the ground? Explain directly from the definition of rolling without slipping. Then use the translation-plus-rotation picture to find what $$\omega$$ must be in terms of $$v_{\rm cm}$$ and $$R.$$

__(b)__ How fast is the point at the very top of the wheel moving, relative to the ground?

__(c)__ How fast is the point at the very back of the wheel — at the height of the axle — moving, relative to the ground?

__(d)__ Is there any point on the wheel other than the contact point with zero velocity relative to the ground?

__(e)__ The contact point has zero velocity, yet it does not stay at the ground — it rises and circles around the wheel. What it has, if not velocity, is nonzero __acceleration__. In the reference frame moving along with the wheel's center, every rim point simply travels in a circle of radius $$R$$ at angular speed $$\omega$$ (this is __uniform circular motion__), and acceleration is the same in any reference frame moving at constant velocity. Use dimensional analysis to find the only combination of $$\omega$$ and $$R$$ with the dimensions of acceleration, $$\mathrm{L \cdot T^{-2}}$$ (the dimensionless constant in front turns out to be $$1$$). Then rewrite this acceleration in terms of $$v_{\rm cm}$$ and $$R,$$ and in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$v_{\rm cm}.$$

label: FMA07
name: A Book Rolling Along a Row of Pencils — A book rests on a row of round pencils and is rolled along them…
desc: A book rests on a row of round pencils and is rolled along them. There is no slipping anywhere: not between the pencils and the floor they rest on, and not between the book and the pencils. As the book rolls over a pencil and leaves it behind, that pencil is picked up and placed…
statement:
A book rests on a row of round pencils and is rolled along them. There is no slipping anywhere: not between the pencils and the floor they rest on, and not between the book and the pencils. As the book rolls over a pencil and leaves it behind, that pencil is picked up and placed in front of the book so the book can keep moving. If the spacing between pencils under the book is $$d$$ and the speed of the book is $$v,$$ at what rate (in pencils per unit time) must pencils be moved to the front of the book?

(The picture is not to scale — real pencils are not nearly as thick as books. Some quantities are deliberately left out of the problem: the book's length doesn't matter as long as it exceeds $$2d,$$ so the book always rests on at least two pencils; and as parts (a) and (b) show, the book's thickness and the pencils' radii don't matter either.)

__(a)__ Each pencil rolls without slipping along the floor. For any cylinder rolling without slipping with its center moving at speed $$s,$$ the point at its bottom is momentarily at rest and the point at its top moves at $$2s$$ (the translation at $$s$$ and the rotation at $$s$$ add at the top). The tops of the pencils do not slip against the book, so they move with the book. How fast do the pencils' centers move, in terms of $$v?$$

__(b)__ How quickly does the back edge of the book gain on the pencils beneath it? Use this to find the rate at which pencils pop out from behind the book — the same rate at which they must be carried to the front.

__(c)__ One more point on the pencil: what is the speed of the point at the very back of a rolling pencil, at the height of its center?

label: FMA07
name: Mud Flying Off a Rolling Wheel — A wheel with radius $$r = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ is rolling without slipping…
desc: A wheel with radius $$r = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ is rolling without slipping along a level path at a constant speed of $$v = 5\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ A small piece of mud stuck to the wheel suddenly breaks loose just as it reaches the very top of the wheel. How far ahead of the axle is the…
statement:
A wheel with radius $$r = 0.5\;\mathrm{m}$$ is rolling without slipping along a level path at a constant speed of $$v = 5\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ A small piece of mud stuck to the wheel suddenly breaks loose just as it reaches the very top of the wheel. How far ahead of the axle is the piece of mud when it hits the path? Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Useful facts: for a wheel rolling without slipping with its center moving at speed $$v,$$ the point at the very top of the wheel moves __horizontally__ at $$2v$$; and an object whose vertical motion starts from rest falls a distance $$h = \frac12 g t^2$$ in time $$t.$$

__(a)__ Working in variables, how long is the mud in the air? (The top of the wheel is at height $$2r,$$ and the mud's velocity at the moment it breaks loose is purely horizontal.)

__(b)__ How far forward does the axle travel during that time, and how far forward does the mud travel?

__(c)__ How far ahead of the axle does the mud land? Answer in variables first, then plug in the numbers.

label: FMA07
name: Kinetic Energy of Spinning Shapes: Moment of Inertia — __(a)__ A thin ring of total mass $$m$$ and radius…
desc: __(a)__ A thin ring of total mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ rotates with angular speed $$\omega$$ about the axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring, through its center. Every point of the ring is a distance $$R$$ from the axis, so every point moves at the same speed $$v =…
statement:
__(a)__ A thin ring of total mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ rotates with angular speed $$\omega$$ about the axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring, through its center. Every point of the ring is a distance $$R$$ from the axis, so every point moves at the same speed $$v = \omega R.$$ Find the kinetic energy of the ring in terms of $$m, \omega,$$ and $$R.$$

__(b)__ Which has more kinetic energy: that ring, or a uniform solid disk of the __same__ mass $$m$$ and radius $$R$$ rotating about the same kind of axis with the same angular speed $$\omega?$$ (Neither object is rolling anywhere; they spin in place.) Answer without calculating, using just the basic idea of what kinetic energy is.

Dimensional analysis shows that the kinetic energy of __any__ rigid object of mass $$m$$ and outer radius $$R$$ spinning at angular speed $$\omega$$ must take the form $$T = c\,m\omega^2R^2$$ for some dimensionless constant $$c$$ that depends only on the object's shape and the chosen axis — that is as true for the shuriken below as for a ring or a disk. By convention we pull out a factor of $$\frac12$$ (inherited from $$\frac12 mv^2$$) and group the object-related pieces together: $$T = \frac12\left(c'\,mR^2\right)\omega^2 = \frac12 I\omega^2,$$ where $$I = c'\,mR^2$$ is called the __moment of inertia__ of the object about that axis.

__(c)__ The two rings below have the same mass $$m,$$ radius $$R,$$ and angular speed $$\omega,$$ but the left one rotates about the axis perpendicular to its plane while the right one rotates about one of its diameters. Which ring has more kinetic energy — and therefore the larger moment of inertia? (It turns out the diameter axis gives $$I = \frac12 mR^2.$$) What does the comparison tell you about whether $$I$$ is a property of the object alone?

__(d)__ The kinetic energy of any rigid object splits into two parts: the translational kinetic energy of its center of mass, $$\frac12 mv_{\rm cm}^2,$$ plus the rotational kinetic energy $$\frac12 I\omega^2$$ computed about the center of mass. A uniform solid sphere has $$I_{\rm sphere} = \frac25 mR^2$$ about its center. Find the total kinetic energy of a solid sphere of mass $$m$$ rolling without slipping at speed $$v$$ (for rolling without slipping, $$\omega = v/R$$).

label: FMA07
name: Spin-Up Race: Hoop, Disk, and Sphere — A uniform disk, a thin hoop, and a uniform solid sphere, all with the…
desc: A uniform disk, a thin hoop, and a uniform solid sphere, all with the same mass $$m$$ and the same outer radius $$R,$$ are each free to rotate about a fixed axis through their centers. (Assume the hoop is connected to its rotational axis by light spokes.) With the objects…
statement:
A uniform disk, a thin hoop, and a uniform solid sphere, all with the same mass $$m$$ and the same outer radius $$R,$$ are each free to rotate about a fixed axis through their centers. (Assume the hoop is connected to its rotational axis by light spokes.) With the objects starting from rest, identical forces of magnitude $$F$$ are simultaneously applied to the rims, staying tangent to the rim as each object turns, as shown. Rank the objects according to their kinetic energies after a given time $$t,$$ from least to greatest.

(a) disk, hoop, sphere (b) sphere, disk, hoop (c) hoop, sphere, disk (d) disk, sphere, hoop (e) hoop, disk, sphere

Background: the moment of inertia $$I$$ is the rotational analog of mass, and the rotational analog of a force is a __torque__ $$\tau$$ (the Greek letter tau). For a force applied tangentially at a distance $$R$$ from the axis, the torque is $$\tau = FR.$$ The rotational analog of Newton's second law $$F = ma$$ is $$\tau = I\alpha,$$ the analog of work $$W = F\,\Delta x$$ is $$W = \tau\,\Delta\theta,$$ and the analog of $$\Delta x = \frac12 at^2$$ (starting from rest) is $$\Delta\theta = \frac12\alpha t^2.$$ The moments of inertia about the central axes are: hoop $$mR^2,$$ disk $$\frac12 mR^2,$$ solid sphere $$\frac25 mR^2.$$

__(a)__ First think intuitively, without calculating. Each object feels the same force for the same time, so why should they end up with different kinetic energies? Which object do you expect to have the lowest angular acceleration, and why?

__(b)__ Now make it precise: combine the background equations to show that the work done on each object after time $$t$$ — which equals its kinetic energy, since it starts at rest — is $$W = \dfrac{\tau^2 t^2}{2I}.$$

__(c)__ Use the moments of inertia to rank the kinetic energies and pick the answer.

label: FMA07
name: The Collapsing Sun — When a star collapses, its radius suddenly decreases. For the sake of simplicity, model…
desc: When a star collapses, its radius suddenly decreases. For the sake of simplicity, model a star as a uniform sphere that rotates rigidly. The Sun currently rotates once every $$25$$ days. Suppose the Sun collapsed into a white dwarf whose radius was a factor of $$100$$ smaller…
statement:
When a star collapses, its radius suddenly decreases. For the sake of simplicity, model a star as a uniform sphere that rotates rigidly. The Sun currently rotates once every $$25$$ days. Suppose the Sun collapsed into a white dwarf whose radius was a factor of $$100$$ smaller than the Sun's current radius. How long would the white dwarf take to complete one rotation? You may assume that no matter leaves the Sun during its collapse and that there are no torques on it.

Background: the rotational analog of linear momentum $$p = mv$$ is the __angular momentum__ $$L = I\omega,$$ where the moment of inertia $$I$$ stands in for mass and the angular speed $$\omega$$ stands in for velocity. When no external torques act on a system, its angular momentum is conserved. For any fixed shape, $$I \propto mR^2,$$ with a shape-dependent constant of proportionality (for a uniform sphere, $$I = \frac25 mR^2$$).

__(a)__ The problem describes an isolated system, which is exactly the situation where conservation laws apply. But two familiar conservation laws are useless here: explain why conservation of __linear momentum__ and conservation of __mechanical energy__ (kinetic plus gravitational potential) don't help.

__(b)__ By what factor does the Sun's moment of inertia change during the collapse?

__(c)__ Use conservation of angular momentum to find the white dwarf's rotation period, in minutes.

label: FMA07
name: From Skidding to Rolling — A disk with mass $$M,$$ radius $$R,$$ and moment of inertia $$\frac12 MR^2$$ is…
desc: A disk with mass $$M,$$ radius $$R,$$ and moment of inertia $$\frac12 MR^2$$ is initially sliding __without rotating__ on a frictionless surface at constant velocity $$v_0$$ to the right. At time $$t = 0$$ it encounters a surface with coefficient of friction $$\mu$$ and begins…
statement:
A disk with mass $$M,$$ radius $$R,$$ and moment of inertia $$\frac12 MR^2$$ is initially sliding __without rotating__ on a frictionless surface at constant velocity $$v_0$$ to the right. At time $$t = 0$$ it encounters a surface with coefficient of friction $$\mu$$ and begins rotating while slipping. After traveling a distance $$L,$$ the disk begins rolling without slipping. Find $$L.$$

Background: while the disk slips, kinetic friction acts backward on its bottom surface with magnitude $$f = \mu Mg$$ (the normal force balances gravity on the level surface). This friction force does two things at once: it decelerates the disk's center, and it exerts a torque $$\tau = fR$$ about the center that spins the disk up. The rotational analog of Newton's second law is $$\tau = I\alpha,$$ where $$\alpha$$ is the angular acceleration. Rolling without slipping begins at the moment the contact point becomes stationary relative to the ground — that is, when $$v = R\omega.$$

__(a)__ Before calculating anything, sketch qualitative graphs of $$v$$ (the speed of the center) and $$R\omega$$ versus time on the same axes, from $$t = 0$$ until well after the disk starts rolling without slipping.

__(b)__ Find the angular acceleration $$\alpha$$ while the disk is slipping, in terms of $$\mu, g,$$ and $$R.$$ Your answer should not contain $$M$$ — give a physical reason why it can't.

__(c)__ Find the magnitude $$a$$ of the deceleration of the disk's center while it is slipping. Why does the rolling relation $$a = \alpha R$$ __not__ apply during this stage?

__(d)__ Find the time at which the disk begins to roll without slipping.

__(e)__ Find the distance $$L$$ the disk travels before it rolls without slipping.

label: FMA07
name: A Sticky Off-Center Collision — Two point masses, each of mass $$m,$$ are attached to the ends of a massless…
desc: Two point masses, each of mass $$m,$$ are attached to the ends of a massless rod of length $$\ell.$$ The assembly slides along a frictionless horizontal table with velocity $$v$$ perpendicular to the rod. A third mass $$m$$ sits stationary on the table, directly in the path of…
statement:
Two point masses, each of mass $$m,$$ are attached to the ends of a massless rod of length $$\ell.$$ The assembly slides along a frictionless horizontal table with velocity $$v$$ perpendicular to the rod. A third mass $$m$$ sits stationary on the table, directly in the path of the mass at the right-hand end of the rod. That end mass collides with the stationary mass and sticks to it (a perfectly __inelastic__ collision). What is the change in kinetic energy of the system as a result of the collision?

Background facts. (1) For a rigid system of point masses, the moment of inertia about an axis is $$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2,$$ where $$r_i$$ is the distance of mass $$i$$ from the axis. (On the F=ma exam you will either be told the moment of inertia of a continuous object or be able to find it without calculus.) (2) The kinetic energy of a rigid system splits as $$T = \frac12 M_{\rm tot}v_{\rm cm}^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2,$$ where the rotational part must be computed about the __center of mass__. (3) A point particle of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$u$$ has angular momentum $$L = mur$$ about an axis, where the __moment arm__ $$r$$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line along which the particle's velocity points; count one sense of circulation about the axis as positive and the other as negative. (4) A rigid body rotating at angular speed $$\omega$$ has $$L = I\omega.$$ With no external forces or torques, both linear momentum and angular momentum are conserved.

__(a)__ Find the kinetic energy of the system before the collision, and the speed of the system's center of mass (which, by conservation of momentum, is the same before and after the collision).

__(b)__ Locate the center of mass of the three-mass system, and compute the moment of inertia $$I$$ of the stuck-together system about an axis through it.

__(c)__ Switch to the reference frame moving with the center of mass, labeling the masses as in the figure: $$A$$ is the left end of the rod, $$B$$ the right end, and $$C$$ the initially stationary mass. Find each mass's velocity in this frame just before the collision, then each mass's angular momentum about the center of mass, and add them up.

__(d)__ Use $$L = I\omega$$ to find the rotation rate just after the collision, compute the total kinetic energy after the collision, and find the change in kinetic energy.

label: FMA08
name: Two stars rotate in circular orbits around their mutual center of mass in a binary star…
desc: Two stars rotate in circular orbits around their mutual center of mass in a binary star system. If the masses of the stars are $$m_a$$ and $$m_b,$$ where $$m_a > m_b,$$ and the distance between the stars is $$d,$$ what is the period $$T$$ of the rotation? (a)…
statement:
Two stars rotate in circular orbits around their mutual center of mass in a binary star system. If the masses of the stars are $$m_a$$ and $$m_b,$$ where $$m_a > m_b,$$ and the distance between the stars is $$d,$$ what is the period $$T$$ of the rotation?

(a) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{Gm_a}}$$

(b) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{Gm_b}}$$

(c) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{G(m_a+m_b)}}$$

(d) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3(m_a + m_b)}{Gm_am_b}}$$

(e) $$4\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{G(m_a+m_b)}}$$

label: FMA08
name: A planet of negligible mass moves around the Sun (mass $$M$$) along an ellipse so that…
desc: A planet of negligible mass moves around the Sun (mass $$M$$) along an ellipse so that its minimum distance to the Sun is $$r_1$$, and its maximum distance to the sun is $$r_2$$. Find the period of its revolution. (a) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r_1^3}{GM}}$$ (b)…
statement:
A planet of negligible mass moves around the Sun (mass $$M$$) along an ellipse so that its minimum distance to the Sun is $$r_1$$, and its maximum distance to the sun is $$r_2$$. Find the period of its revolution.

(a) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r_1^3}{GM}}$$

(b) $$2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r_2^3}{GM}}$$

(c) $$\sqrt{\frac{(r_1+r_2)^3}{2GM}}$$

(d) $$\pi\sqrt{\frac{(r_1+r_2)^3}{4GM}}$$

(e) $$\pi\sqrt{\frac{(r_1+r_2)^3}{2GM}}$$

label: FMA08
name: A planet is moving around a sun in a circular orbit with period $$T$$. Suddenly, the…
desc: A planet is moving around a sun in a circular orbit with period $$T$$. Suddenly, the planet stops moving relative to the sun. Find the time it takes for the planet to hit the sun. Assume that the radius of the sun is much smaller than the distance between the planet and the sun…
statement:
A planet is moving around a sun in a circular orbit with period $$T$$. Suddenly, the planet stops moving relative to the sun. Find the time it takes for the planet to hit the sun. Assume that the radius of the sun is much smaller than the distance between the planet and the sun initially.

(a) $$T$$

(b) $$\frac{T}{2}$$

(c) $$\frac{T}{2\sqrt{2}}$$

(d) $$\frac{T}{4\sqrt{2}}$$

(e) $$2T$$

label: FMA08
name: A spherical planet has radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Then a spherical cavity of radius…
desc: A spherical planet has radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Then a spherical cavity of radius $$r$$ is dug out. The cavity is centered at a distance $$d > r$$ from the center of the planet. Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force on a mass $$m$$ at the center of the planet…
statement:
A spherical planet has radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Then a spherical cavity of radius $$r$$ is dug out. The cavity is centered at a distance $$d > r$$ from the center of the planet.

Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force on a mass $$m$$ at the center of the planet.

(a) $$\frac{GMr^3m}{R^3d^2}$$

(b) $$\frac{GMr^2m}{R^3d}$$

(c) $$\frac{GMrm}{R^2d}$$

(d) $$\frac{GMr^3m}{R^2d^3}$$

(e) $$\frac{GMr^2m}{R^2d^2}$$

(You may ignore the __stability__ of the orbit; if an orbit in the approximate location could exist, count it.)

(a) $$\text{I}$$ (b) $$\text{II}$$ (c) $$\text{I}, \text{II}, \text{IV}$$ (d) $$\text{I}, \text{II}, \text{III}$$ (e) $$\text{I}, \text{II}, \text{III}, \text{IV}$$

label: FMA08
name: In this week's USAPhO-Style problem, we will study some basic physics related to the…
desc: In this week's USAPhO-Style problem, we will study some basic physics related to the rings of Saturn. **a)** Imagine the rings of Saturn to a single disk with a hole cut out in the middle (Saturn itself is in the hole). Define the following variables: \begin{aligned} G &=…
statement:
In this week's USAPhO-Style problem, we will study some basic physics related to the rings of Saturn.

**a)** Imagine the rings of Saturn to a single disk with a hole cut out in the middle (Saturn itself is in the hole). Define the following variables: \begin{aligned} G &= \text{Newton's gravitational constant} \\ M & = \text{mass of Saturn} \\ \rho & = \text{density of rings} \\ r & = \text{inner radius of the ring}\\ R &= \text{outer radius of the ring} \\ \omega &=\text{angular frequency of orbit of the ring}\\ t &= \text{thickness of the rings} \end{aligned}

Find $$\omega$$ such that the midline of the the ring (the strip at distance $$\dfrac{r+R}{2}$$ from its center) is in orbit around Saturn.

**b)** Assume the ring is in the orbit you found in part (a). Find the angular frequency of orbits at the inner edge of the ring and at the outer edge of the ring.

**c)** Suppose a small stone were placed on the inside edge of the ring, stationary relative to the ring. Ignore gravitational force from the ring itself. Would the stone fall towards Saturn or away from Saturn? Answer the same question for a stone at the outer edge of the ring.

**d)** Suppose the stone on the inside edge of the ring (from part (c)) is held to the inside edge of the ring by a short string. If the mass of the stone is $$m,$$ find the tension in the string.

**e)** The values of the variables in this problem may be assumed to be \begin{aligned} G &= 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{N \cdot m^2 \cdot kg^{-2}} \\ M &=5.68 \times 10^{26} \;\mathrm{kg} \\ \rho &= 4\times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg \cdot m^{-3}} \\ r &= 1.2 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{km} \\ R &= 4.0 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{km} \\ t &= 100 \;\mathrm{m} \end{aligned}

Additionally, if a rock experiences a tension force greater than about $$10^7 \;\mathrm{N \cdot m^{-2}},$$ it will tear apart.

Suppose we make the following model of the ring: [*] Take two rocks, each of mass $$m.$$ Tie a massless rope between them. [*] Place them in orbit around Saturn so that they have orbital angular frequency $$\omega,$$ as calculated in part (a). Spin the rope so that the same rock is always closest to Saturn. Adjust the length of the rope so that the inner rock is at distance $$r$$ from the planet and the outer rock is at a distance $$R$$ from the planet. [*] Make many copies of this rock-rope-rock system and place them alongside each other to form a ring all around Saturn. [*] The number of copies should be such that the total mass in the rocks is equal to the mass of the rings of Saturn. [*] The thickness of the ropes is set so that the total cross-sectional area of all the ropes is equal to $$2\pi r t.$$ [*] If the tension per unit cross-sectional area in a rope exceeds $$10^7 \;\mathrm{N \cdot m^{-2}},$$ the rope snaps.

Based on this model, is it possible for the rings of Saturn to be a single solid object, or would the rocks that make up the ring tear apart?

**f)** The model in part (e) is simplified to allow us to make calculations on it. Although a more-accurate model is possible, it would also be more complicated. Briefly discuss some of the inaccuracies in the model from part (e). Do you think the conclusion stands despite these inaccuracies?

label: FMA08
name: Velocity and Acceleration in Uniform Circular Motion — A particle moves around a circle at a constant angular…
desc: A particle moves around a circle at a constant angular frequency $$\omega$$ (radians per unit time), so if the circle has radius $$r,$$ the particle's speed is $$v = \omega r.$$ The animation below shows the particle along with its __position vector__ $$\vec{r},$$ drawn from the…
statement:
A particle moves around a circle at a constant angular frequency $$\omega$$ (radians per unit time), so if the circle has radius $$r,$$ the particle's speed is $$v = \omega r.$$ The animation below shows the particle along with its __position vector__ $$\vec{r},$$ drawn from the center of the circle. The goal of this problem is to find the particle's acceleration without calculus, by thinking about rotating vectors.

__(a)__ The particle never speeds up or slows down, and its angular velocity never changes. Explain why the particle nevertheless has a nonzero acceleration, and state which direction the velocity vector $$\vec{v}$$ points.

__(b)__ A vector can be drawn starting anywhere, so imagine drawing a copy of $$\vec{v}$$ that always starts at the center of the circle, as in the animation below. Describe what this copied vector does as time goes on, and explain why it is exactly the position vector rotated by $$90^\circ$$ in the direction of the particle's motion and scaled in length by the factor $$\omega.$$

__(c)__ Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, just as velocity is the rate of change of position. Use part (b) to find the acceleration vector $$\vec{a}$$ in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$\vec{r},$$ then rewrite its magnitude in terms of the speed $$v$$ and the radius $$r.$$ Which way does $$\vec{a}$$ point? (The notation $$\hat{r} = \vec{r}/r,$$ pronounced "$$r$$ hat," means a __unit vector__ — a vector of magnitude $$1$$ — in the direction of $$\vec{r}.$$)

__(d)__ In deep space, a ball on the end of a string is swung in a circle, making one revolution in time $$\tau.$$ The free-body diagram is shown below: the only force on the ball is the string tension $$T,$$ pointing toward the center. If the tension is doubled and the ball continues to move in a circle of the same radius, how long does a single revolution take?

label: FMA08
name: Where Gravity Cancels Between the Earth and the Moon — __Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation__ says that…
desc: __Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation__ says that two objects with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ separated by a distance $$r,$$ attract each other with a force of magnitude $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$ where $$G \approx 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$$ is the…
statement:
__Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation__ says that two objects with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ separated by a distance $$r,$$ attract each other with a force of magnitude $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$ where $$G \approx 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$$ is the gravitational constant. In vector form, $$\vec{F}_{12} = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{12},$$ where $$\hat{r}_{12}$$ is a unit vector pointing from object 1 to object 2 and $$\vec{F}_{12}$$ is the force object 1 exerts on object 2 — the minus sign makes the force attractive.

The Earth and the moon are separated from each other in space. The Earth is much more massive than the moon (about $$81$$ times the mass). Five points on the line through their centers are marked $$A$$ through $$E$$ below. At which marked point, if any, could an object feel zero net gravitational force from the Earth and the moon? (Ignore the sun, the galaxy, and everything else.) Answer without computing anything — reason from the directions and relative strengths of the two pulls.

label: FMA08
name: Gravity at a Small Height Above the Earth — Assume the Earth is a uniform sphere of radius $$R,$$ and let…
desc: Assume the Earth is a uniform sphere of radius $$R,$$ and let $$g_0$$ be the gravitational free-fall acceleration at its surface. What is the approximate free-fall acceleration $$g$$ at a height $$h \ll R$$ above the surface? (A) $$g = g_0$$ — there is no variation; (B) $$g…
statement:
Assume the Earth is a uniform sphere of radius $$R,$$ and let $$g_0$$ be the gravitational free-fall acceleration at its surface. What is the approximate free-fall acceleration $$g$$ at a height $$h \ll R$$ above the surface? (A) $$g = g_0$$ — there is no variation; (B) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$$; (C) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$$; (D) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$$; (E) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{3h}{R}\right).$$

You will need Newton's gravitational law, $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ where $$r$$ is the distance measured from the __center__ of the Earth, and the approximation $$\dfrac{1}{1+\epsilon} \approx 1 - \epsilon$$ for small $$\epsilon.$$

__(a)__ Without any algebra, which answer choices can you eliminate immediately, and why?

__(b)__ Write $$g_0$$ in terms of $$G,$$ the Earth's mass $$M,$$ and $$R.$$ Then write the exact expression for $$g$$ at height $$h.$$ (Keep the three lengths straight: $$R$$ is the Earth's radius, $$h$$ is the height above the surface, and the distance from the center is $$r = R + h.$$)

__(c)__ Factor your expression so it reads $$g = g_0\cdot(\text{something}),$$ decide which term is small enough to drop, apply the approximation, and choose the answer.

__(d)__ Suppose you didn't know the approximation formula but had a calculator. How could you check the answer numerically?

label: FMA08
name: Spy Satellites in Geosynchronous Orbit — __(a)__ A satellite of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of…
desc: __(a)__ A satellite of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a body of mass $$M.$$ Combine Newton's gravitational law, $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ with the circular-motion acceleration $$a = \omega^2 r$$ to find the orbit's angular frequency $$\omega$$ in…
statement:
__(a)__ A satellite of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a body of mass $$M.$$ Combine Newton's gravitational law, $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ with the circular-motion acceleration $$a = \omega^2 r$$ to find the orbit's angular frequency $$\omega$$ in terms of $$G,$$ $$M,$$ and $$r.$$ Then show that the orbital period $$T$$ satisfies $$T^2 \propto r^3.$$ (This is __Kepler's third law__.)

__(b)__ Spy satellites have been placed in the geosynchronous orbit above the Earth's equator. (__Geosynchronous__ means the satellite stays above the same spot of the Earth's surface at all times, so its period is about $$24$$ hours.) A satellite in a circular orbit just above the Earth's surface has a period of $$90$$ minutes. Use Kepler's third law to find the radius $$R'$$ of the geosynchronous orbit in terms of the Earth's radius $$R.$$

__(c)__ Using the figure below, find the greatest latitude $$L$$ from which the geosynchronous satellites are visible from the Earth's surface. The gray parts of the Earth in the figure are the regions from which the satellite cannot be seen. (Problem and figure from Halliday, Resnick, and Krane, __Physics__, 5th ed.)

label: FMA08
name: Timing a Hohmann Transfer — A __Hohmann transfer orbit__ moves a rocket between two circular orbits around…
desc: A __Hohmann transfer orbit__ moves a rocket between two circular orbits around the sun in several steps. (1) The rocket begins in a circular orbit of radius $$r_1.$$ (2) The rocket briefly fires its engines until its orbit is an ellipse whose farthest point is a distance $$r_3$$…
statement:
A __Hohmann transfer orbit__ moves a rocket between two circular orbits around the sun in several steps. (1) The rocket begins in a circular orbit of radius $$r_1.$$ (2) The rocket briefly fires its engines until its orbit is an ellipse whose farthest point is a distance $$r_3$$ from the sun. (3) The rocket coasts until it is a distance $$r_3$$ from the sun, then briefly fires its engines again until it enters a circular orbit of radius $$r_3.$$ The figure shows the initial orbit (1), the transfer ellipse (2), and the final orbit (3).

Some facts about orbits, all of which follow from Newton's laws: orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus (__Kepler's first law__). The __semi-major axis__ $$a$$ of an ellipse is half its long axis. __Kepler's third law__, $$T^2 \propto a^3,$$ holds for elliptical orbits with the semi-major axis $$a$$ in place of the circle's radius, so the period of an orbit depends only on the mass being orbited and on $$a$$ — orbits with the same semi-major axis have the same period regardless of shape. Finally, the total energy of an orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ so a larger semi-major axis means a higher energy.

__(a)__ At each of the two engine firings, does the rocket speed up or slow down?

__(b)__ Find the semi-major axis of the transfer ellipse in terms of $$r_1$$ and $$r_3.$$

__(c)__ If the period of the original circular orbit is $$T,$$ how long does step (2) — the trip along the transfer ellipse from distance $$r_1$$ to distance $$r_3$$ — take, in terms of $$T,$$ $$r_1,$$ and $$r_3?$$

label: FMA08
name: Kepler's Laws with Inverse-Cube Gravity — Kepler's laws state that: (I) the orbits of planets are elliptical…
desc: Kepler's laws state that: (I) the orbits of planets are elliptical with one focus at the sun; (II) a line connecting the sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times; and (III) the square of the period of a planet's orbit is proportional to the cube of its semi-major…
statement:
Kepler's laws state that: (I) the orbits of planets are elliptical with one focus at the sun; (II) a line connecting the sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times; and (III) the square of the period of a planet's orbit is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis. Which of these laws would remain true if the force of gravity were proportional to $$1/r^3$$ rather than $$1/r^2?$$ (From the F=ma exam.)

The animation below illustrates Kepler's second law: a planet moves faster when it is near the sun, in just such a way that the line from the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. (Animation by Gonfer, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

__(a)__ First, connect Kepler's second law to a conservation law. In a short time $$\Delta t,$$ a planet at distance $$r$$ from the sun, moving at speed $$v$$ with angle $$\theta$$ between its velocity and the line to the sun, sweeps out the thin shaded triangle below. Show that the swept area is $$A = \dfrac12\,v\Delta t\cdot r\sin\theta,$$ and that $$\dfrac{2m}{\Delta t}\cdot A$$ equals the magnitude of the planet's angular momentum $$L = |\vec{r}\times\vec{p}|.$$ Conclude that Kepler's second law is equivalent to conservation of angular momentum.

__(b)__ Using part (a), decide whether law II would survive the modified force. (A force that always points along the line toward the sun is called a __central force__.)

__(c)__ For a circular orbit under the modified force $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^3},$$ redo the usual period derivation (set the force equal to $$m\omega^2 r$$) and find the exponent $$\gamma$$ in $$T \propto r^{\gamma}.$$ Does law III survive?

__(d)__ For law I, you need a fact that is hard to prove: __Bertrand's theorem__ says that orbits are ellipses only for special force laws — for $$F \propto 1/r^2$$ the orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus, and for $$F \propto r$$ (Hooke's law) they are ellipses with the sun at the center; for other force laws, orbits do not have simple closed shapes at all. Does law I survive? State the final answer to the question.

label: FMA08
name: Gravitational Potential Energy and a Two-Particle Escape — __(a)__ The gravitational potential energy of a…
desc: __(a)__ The gravitational potential energy of a system of two particles with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ separated by a distance $$r$$ has the form $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^n}$$ for some number $$n.$$ Use __dimensional analysis__ to find $$n.$$ (Two useful facts: the…
statement:
__(a)__ The gravitational potential energy of a system of two particles with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ separated by a distance $$r$$ has the form $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^n}$$ for some number $$n.$$ Use __dimensional analysis__ to find $$n.$$ (Two useful facts: the gravitational force is $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$ and the work-energy theorem $$W = F\Delta x$$ shows that a force times a distance is an energy.)

__(b)__ Dimensional analysis cannot determine the sign or the overall numerical constant. Explain why the formula must carry a minus sign, $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r},$$ rather than being $$+\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}.$$ (Think about whether the potential energy should rise or fall as the particles move farther apart.)

__(c)__ Two point-like particles, each of mass $$m,$$ are originally separated by a distance $$d$$ and are moving in opposite directions along the line joining them, each with speed $$v.$$ What is the maximum value of $$v$$ so that the particles will eventually move back together under their mutual gravitational attraction? (Hint: forces are awkward here, because the force keeps changing as the separation changes — use conservation of energy. Note that $$d$$ is the distance __between__ the particles, so the system's potential energy is $$-\dfrac{Gm^2}{d},$$ not $$-\dfrac{Gm^2}{2d}.)$$

__(d)__ A gravitational system with total energy $$E < 0$$ is called __bound__: the bodies cannot escape each other. A system with $$E > 0$$ is called __free__: the bodies escape forever. If the two particles in part (c) are launched slightly faster than the maximum speed you found, are they bound or free? Also state which conic-section path a small body near a star follows in the cases $$E < 0,$$ $$E = 0,$$ and $$E > 0.$$

label: FMA08
name: The Energy of an Orbit, and Comparing Orbits — __(a)__ A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M$$ in…
desc: __(a)__ A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R.$$ Find the planet's kinetic energy, the system's gravitational potential energy (use $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}),$$ and the total energy, in terms of $$G,$$ $$M,$$ $$m,$$ and $$R.$$ (Hint…
statement:
__(a)__ A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R.$$ Find the planet's kinetic energy, the system's gravitational potential energy (use $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}),$$ and the total energy, in terms of $$G,$$ $$M,$$ $$m,$$ and $$R.$$ (Hint: the planet's acceleration is both $$\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ from circular motion and $$\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$$ from gravity; use that to eliminate $$v.)$$

__(b)__ Check that your answers satisfy $$KE = -\dfrac12 U.$$ This is a special case of the __virial theorem__: for any orbit, the kinetic energy averaged over a full orbit is $$-\dfrac12$$ times the averaged potential energy (for a circular orbit it holds at every instant). A second general fact: the total energy of any elliptical orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ where $$a$$ is the semi-major axis — your circular-orbit answer is the special case $$a = R.$$

Now use these tools on a classic comparison problem. The figure below (from Halliday, Resnick, and Krane, __Physics__, 5th ed.) shows several possible orbits of a satellite around the sun: two circular orbits — the larger circle $$A$$ and the smaller circle $$D$$ — and two elliptical orbits $$B$$ and $$C$$ whose farthest points lie on circle $$A.$$ Orbit $$C$$'s closest approach to the sun is at the radius of circle $$D,$$ while orbit $$B$$ passes much closer to the sun. For each part, give the answer and the reasoning.

__(c)__ Which orbit has the largest angular momentum? (Useful facts: the rate at which an orbit sweeps out area is $$\dfrac{A}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{L}{2m},$$ so comparing angular momenta is the same as comparing sweep rates; for a circular orbit the sweep rate is $$\dfrac12 vr$$; and combining Kepler's third law $$\omega \propto r^{-3/2}$$ with $$v = \omega r$$ gives $$v \propto r^{-1/2}$$ for circular orbits.)

__(d)__ Which orbit has the largest total energy?

__(e)__ On which orbit does the satellite reach the largest speed?

label: FMA08
name: Gravity Inside and Outside a Uniform Planet — The __shell theorem__, proved by Newton, has two parts. First…
desc: The __shell theorem__, proved by Newton, has two parts. First: the gravitational pull of any spherically symmetric body, felt from outside the body, is exactly the same as if all of its mass were concentrated at its center. (This is why we can use the Earth's radius as the…
statement:
The __shell theorem__, proved by Newton, has two parts. First: the gravitational pull of any spherically symmetric body, felt from outside the body, is exactly the same as if all of its mass were concentrated at its center. (This is why we can use the Earth's radius as the distance $$r$$ in $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$$ when standing on the surface, even though some of the Earth is just beneath our feet and some is a full diameter away — the averaging over the whole sphere works out perfectly. It holds even for spheres that are denser in the middle, like the Earth and the sun.) Second: a spherically symmetric __shell__ of mass exerts no net gravitational force at all on an object anywhere inside it.

A certain planet is a uniform sphere of radius $$R$$ and density $$\rho,$$ so its total mass is $$M = \dfrac43\pi R^3\rho.$$ Sketch a plot of the gravitational acceleration $$g$$ due to the planet as a function of the distance $$r$$ from the planet's center, from $$r = 0$$ out to several times $$R.$$ Proceed in stages:

__(a)__ Find $$g(r)$$ for points outside the planet, $$r > R.$$

__(b)__ For a point inside the planet at radius $$r < R,$$ divide the planet's mass into the part closer to the center than $$r$$ (the shaded sphere in the figure) and the part farther from the center (the surrounding shell). How much mass is in the inner part, in terms of $$M,$$ $$r,$$ and $$R,$$ and how much does each part contribute to the gravitational acceleration at radius $$r?$$

__(c)__ Find $$g(r)$$ for $$r < R,$$ then describe the complete plot: the shape of the curve on each side of $$r = R,$$ the value $$g_s$$ of the acceleration at the surface, and what happens at $$r = R.$$

statement:
A uniform rectangular block with mass $$M$$, length $$b$$, and height $$a$$ rests on an incline as shown. The incline and the block have a coefficient of static friction $$\mu_s$$. The incline is moved upwards from an angle of zero through an angle $$\theta$$. At some critical angle, the block will either tip over or slip down the plane. Determine the relationship between $$a$$, $$b$$, and $$\mu_s$$ such that the block will tip over (and not slip) at the critical angle.

(a) $$\mu_s > a/b$$ (b) $$\mu_s > 1 - a/b$$ (c) $$\mu_s > b/a$$ (d) $$\mu_s < a/b$$ (e) $$\mu_s < b/a - 1$$

statement:

However it is observed that pulling $$1 \;\mathrm{mm}$$ of rope out from the right hand side of the box always requires $$2 \;\mathrm{mm}$$ of rope to enter the left side of the box and vice versa. lesson: FMA09: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
label: FMA09
name: In many physics labs, we generate $$(x,y)$$ data. This means we have a long list…
desc: In many physics labs, we generate $$(x,y)$$ data. This means we have a long list $$(x_i,y_i),$$ where $$i$$ is an index that runs from $$1$$ to $$n,$$ the number of observations. For example, if $$n = 100:$$ \begin{aligned} (x_1,y_1) &= (2.2,3.6) \\ (x_2,y_2) &= (-3.4, -2.9) \\…
statement:
In many physics labs, we generate $$(x,y)$$ data. This means we have a long list $$(x_i,y_i),$$ where $$i$$ is an index that runs from $$1$$ to $$n,$$ the number of observations. For example, if $$n = 100:$$ \begin{aligned} (x_1,y_1) &= (2.2,3.6) \\ (x_2,y_2) &= (-3.4, -2.9) \\ (x_3,y_3) &= (1.8, 2.8) \\ & \vdotswithin{=} \\ (x_{100},y_{100}) &= (12.4, 15.1) \end{aligned}

Often, the data can be plotted as something close to a straight line. This is true even when the original relationship between variables is not linear because we can plot some transformation of the variable. For example, in a previous week's USAPhO-style problem, we plotted the square of the velocity of a bird's flight versus its weight to find a straight line.

We often draw a line through the data by eye, but it would be useful to have a more rigorous method. To do that, we need some way of defining the best line through a given set of data points. A common solution to this problem is **least squares linear regression**.

Usually, no line will go through all the data points. Instead, the line will have some error for each data point as shown below.

__By Sewaqu - Own work, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=11967659__

In least squares linear regression, we draw the line that has the smallest value for the sum of the square of the errors. Here is what this means.

For each data point $$(x_i, y_i)$$ and given a best fit line $$y = mx + b,$$ we define the error $$e_i$$ as $$e_i = y_i - (mx_i + b).$$

The sum of the squares of the errors is $$ S = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2.$$

In least squares linear regression, we find the line that minimizes $$S.$$ This means we choose $$m$$ and $$b$$ to make $$S$$ as small as possible. It would be convenient to find formulas for $$m$$ and $$b$$ that do this. The formulas should give $$m$$ and $$b$$ in terms of the values of the data points.

In this problem, we will derive such formulas for least squares linear regression using the physics of static equilibrium.

**a)** Considering that errors are signed, briefly explain why is it not sufficient to simply minimize the total error to find the best-fit line. That is, why is it not enough to find $$m$$ and $$b$$ to satisfy $$\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0?$$

**b)** Suppose that each error shown in the diagram above is replaced by an ideal spring which obey's Hooke's law. The line itself is replaced by a rigid rod. Gravity is ignored. The springs are constrained to be vertical. Write an equation for the potential energy of the system of springs.

**c)** Briefly explain the relationship between your result, the equilibrium position of the rod, and least-squares linear regression.

**d)** Find equations for force and torque that must be satisfied when the rod is at equilibrium. These equations will be sums over $$i.$$

**e)** Solve your equations to find equations for the slope and y-intercept of the least-square linear regression line. Your answer will be in terms of sums over $$i$$ of $$x_i, y_i,$$ and combinations of them. You may also want to use the average values of $$x$$ and $$y,$$ defined by \begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \\ \bar{y} &= \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i \end{aligned} in your answer calculations.

If you want, you may use the following definitions for the **variance** and **covariance** to simplify your answer: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{var}(x) & = \dfrac{1}{n} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right) - \bar{x}^2 \\ \mathrm{var}(y) & = \dfrac{1}{n} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2\right) - \bar{y}^2 \\ \mathrm{cov}(x,y) &= \dfrac{1}{n} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i\right) - \bar{x}\bar{y} \end{aligned}

lesson: FMA09: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
label: FMA09
name: A Rope Draped over a Frictionless Wedge — A uniform rope is draped over a frictionless triangular wedge. A…
desc: A uniform rope is draped over a frictionless triangular wedge. A length $$\ell_\alpha$$ of rope lies on the left face, which is inclined at angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal, and a length $$\ell_\beta$$ lies on the right face, inclined at angle $$\beta.$$ The rope passes over…
statement:
A uniform rope is draped over a frictionless triangular wedge. A length $$\ell_\alpha$$ of rope lies on the left face, which is inclined at angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal, and a length $$\ell_\beta$$ lies on the right face, inclined at angle $$\beta.$$ The rope passes over the sharp peak, and both ends hang above the base of the wedge. Find a condition on $$\ell_\alpha,$$ $$\ell_\beta,$$ $$\alpha,$$ and $$\beta$$ that guarantees the rope is in equilibrium.

Two facts you'll need. First, an object on a frictionless incline of angle $$\varphi$$ slides down with acceleration $$g\sin\varphi.$$ Second, since the rope is uniform, it has a mass per unit length $$\lambda = \dfrac{m}{\ell_\alpha+\ell_\beta},$$ where $$m$$ is the total mass; the left section, for example, has mass $$\lambda\,\ell_\alpha.$$

__(a)__ Imagine cutting the rope exactly at the peak, separating the left and right pieces. What would the acceleration of each piece be?

__(b)__ When the rope is __not__ cut, each piece is held in place by the tension at the peak, and the tension there has a single value, so it pulls on both pieces with the same magnitude. Use this to write an equation relating $$\ell_\alpha,$$ $$\ell_\beta,$$ $$\alpha,$$ and $$\beta.$$ That equation is the equilibrium condition.

__(c)__ The quantity $$\ell_\alpha\sin\alpha$$ has a simple geometric meaning. What is it, and what is the geometric interpretation of your condition from part (b)?

__(d)__ Statics problems can also be solved with energy: __a system with no external forces on it is in equilibrium when no small displacement can change its potential energy.__ Equilibrium at a potential energy __minimum__ is stable; at a __maximum__ it is unstable. Is the rope's equilibrium stable or unstable? Then suppose the rope's two ends are uneven by a small height $$\Delta y,$$ and slide the whole rope a tiny distance $$\mathrm{d}s$$ along its length toward the higher end. What happens to the potential energy, and how does this confirm your condition from part (c)?

__(e)__ Now suppose the same rope instead lies on a frictionless hill of arbitrary lumpy shape, draped over its highest point with the two ends hanging on either side. What is the condition for equilibrium, and why is the energy method dramatically easier than a force analysis here?

lesson: FMA09: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
label: FMA09
name: Feynman's Weights on a Board — A massless rigid rod rests on a pivot at its right end. A box of mass $$m_1$$…
desc: A massless rigid rod rests on a pivot at its right end. A box of mass $$m_1$$ sits on the rod a distance $$x_1$$ from the pivot, and a box of mass $$m_2$$ sits a distance $$x_2$$ from the pivot, with $$x_1 > x_2.$$ A string is tied to the rod a distance $$L$$ from the pivot (at…
statement:
A massless rigid rod rests on a pivot at its right end. A box of mass $$m_1$$ sits on the rod a distance $$x_1$$ from the pivot, and a box of mass $$m_2$$ sits a distance $$x_2$$ from the pivot, with $$x_1 > x_2.$$ A string is tied to the rod a distance $$L$$ from the pivot (at the left end, $$L > x_1$$); the string runs straight up, passes over an ideal pulley, and a block of mass $$M$$ hangs from its other end. What mass $$M$$ keeps the system in balance? (Adapted from "Conservation of Energy," The Feynman Lectures on Physics.)

An object in equilibrium has zero net force __and__ zero net torque: $$\sum_i \vec{F}_i = 0$$ and $$\sum_i \vec{\tau}_i = 0.$$ The torque of a force about a reference point is $$\tau = rF_\perp,$$ the __moment arm__ $$r$$ (distance from the reference point to the line of the force) times the component of force perpendicular to the arm. You may choose the reference point freely.

__(a)__ Using the pivot as the reference point and taking counterclockwise (the direction the boxes try to turn the rod) as positive, write the torque exerted by each of $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ and the string, with correct signs. Set the sum to zero and solve for $$M.$$

__(b)__ Check the answer using energy. A system with no external forces is in equilibrium when a small displacement does not change its potential energy. Let the rod tilt down by a small angle so that $$m_2$$ falls a small distance $$\mathrm{d}y_2.$$ Using similar triangles, find how far $$m_1$$ falls and how far $$M$$ rises, write the total change in potential energy, set it to zero, and show that you recover the answer from part (a).

__(c)__ Now remove the hanging block and instead pull down on the free end of the string with your hand, applying a constant force $$F.$$ What force keeps the system balanced? The energy principle in part (b) no longer applies as stated, since there is no longer a mass $$M$$ whose potential energy changes — how must the principle be restated when an external force acts on the system?

statement:
A jack is a device for lifting a car. It looks like this:

It goes under the car like this:

A handle attaches at the side and turns in a circle to turn the screw, which pulls the sides of the jack together and raises the car. When you turn the handle in one full circle, the jack rises by $$\Delta y = 0.5\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The handle has length $$h = 45\;\mathrm{cm},$$ and you push on its end with a force $$F$$ directed along the end's motion. What is the minimum force needed to raise a car of mass $$1500\;\mathrm{kg}?$$ Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and ignore friction in the jack.

__(a)__ Mapping out the forces inside the jack — the tension in the screw, the compression in the rods, the thread spacing — would be a mess. Instead, use energy conservation: the energy to lift the car has to come from somewhere. For one full turn of the handle, write the equation relating the work you do on the handle to the change in the car's potential energy.

__(b)__ Find a formula for $$F$$ in terms of the car's mass $$m,$$ $$g,$$ $$\Delta y,$$ and $$h,$$ then plug in the numbers. Is the result surprising?

__(c)__ Lifting the car isn't really statics, since the car moves. Explain how to rephrase the question as a true statics problem, and why the answer is the same force.

lesson: FMA09: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
label: FMA09
name: The Compound Pulley — A block of mass $$M$$ hangs from movable pulley $$C$$ in the system shown. A __long…
desc: A block of mass $$M$$ hangs from movable pulley $$C$$ in the system shown. A __long rope__ has one end tied to the ceiling; it runs down and around pulley $$C,$$ back up and over movable pulley $$B,$$ and its free end hangs down, where a downward force $$F$$ is applied. A…
statement:
A block of mass $$M$$ hangs from movable pulley $$C$$ in the system shown. A __long rope__ has one end tied to the ceiling; it runs down and around pulley $$C,$$ back up and over movable pulley $$B,$$ and its free end hangs down, where a downward force $$F$$ is applied. A __short rope__ is tied to the frame of pulley $$C,$$ runs up over pulley $$A$$ (which is fixed to the ceiling), and is tied to the frame of pulley $$B.$$ All pulleys and ropes are massless, the pulleys are frictionless, and the only forces on each pulley come from the ropes (and the hanger holding $$M$$). What force $$F$$ keeps the system in equilibrium? (System from Brown, __507 Mechanical Movements__.)

Key fact: in a massless rope running over frictionless pulleys, the tension has a single value along the whole rope. Call the tension in the long rope $$T_1$$ (so $$F = T_1$$) and the tension in the short rope $$T_2.$$ Also, each massless pulley must have zero net force on it.

__(a)__ Draw (or imagine) a free body diagram for pulley $$C,$$ counting every rope segment that pulls on it. Write the force-balance equation for pulley $$C$$ relating $$T_1,$$ $$T_2,$$ and $$Mg.$$

__(b)__ Do the same for pulley $$B$$ — careful: the long rope passes __over__ $$B,$$ so both of its segments pull downward on $$B.$$ Combine your two equations to find $$F.$$

__(c)__ Check with energy. Replace the force $$F$$ with a block of mass $$m$$ hanging from the free end, so $$F = mg.$$ Suppose the block $$M$$ falls by $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ (so pulley $$C$$ falls by $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$). How far does pulley $$B$$ move, and how far does $$m$$ rise? Use "a small displacement of the system leaves the potential energy unchanged at equilibrium" to find $$m,$$ and confirm your answer for $$F.$$

label: FMA09
name: The Spool of Thread — A spool of thread rests on a table. The thread is wound around the inner cylinder, of…
desc: A spool of thread rests on a table. The thread is wound around the inner cylinder, of radius $$r,$$ and the spool rolls on its outer rims, of radius $$R > r.$$ The spool rolls without slipping. The free end of the thread is pulled gently — gently enough that the spool never…
statement:
A spool of thread rests on a table. The thread is wound around the inner cylinder, of radius $$r,$$ and the spool rolls on its outer rims, of radius $$R > r.$$ The spool rolls without slipping. The free end of the thread is pulled gently — gently enough that the spool never slides.

__(a)__ First the thread is pulled __horizontally__, leaving the spool near the bottom of the inner cylinder. Which way does the spool roll — toward the pull (winding itself up) or away from it (unwinding)? You can see a demonstration in the animation below (from Veritasium's "Spool Right 2").

__(b)__ Next the thread is pulled straight __up__, leaving the inner cylinder at its side. Which way does the spool roll now?

__(c)__ Since the spool rolls one way for a horizontal pull and the other way for a vertical pull, there must be an in-between angle at which it doesn't move at all. Find the angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal at which the thread must be pulled so that the spool stays in equilibrium, in terms of $$r$$ and $$R.$$ Hints: torques may be computed about any axis you like, and a force whose line of action passes through the axis exerts zero torque about it. Four forces act on the spool: gravity, the normal force, friction from the table, and the pull of the thread. Choose the axis so that as many of these as possible drop out.

name: Balancing a Rock on a Meter Stick (2007 F=ma) — A $$2\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rock is suspended by a massless string…
desc: A $$2\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rock is suspended by a massless string from one end of a uniform $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ measuring stick. What is the mass of the measuring stick if it is balanced by a support force at the $$0.20\;\mathrm{m}$$ mark? (From the 2007 F=ma exam.) Useful rule for…
statement:
A $$2\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rock is suspended by a massless string from one end of a uniform $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ measuring stick. What is the mass of the measuring stick if it is balanced by a support force at the $$0.20\;\mathrm{m}$$ mark? (From the 2007 F=ma exam.)

Useful rule for torques on extended bodies: gravity can be treated as if it acts entirely at the object's __center of mass__. For a uniform stick, that's the midpoint.

__(a)__ Balance the torques about the support point to find the mass of the stick.

__(b)__ Here is a slick shortcut: part of the measuring stick is perfectly balanced all by itself and can be ignored. Which part? Use the shortcut to redo the problem, balancing the rock against only the remaining piece of stick, and check that you get the same answer.

lesson: FMA09: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
label: FMA09
name: The Cylinder with an Off-Center Hole (2012 F=ma) — A uniform cylinder of radius $$a$$ originally has a weight…
desc: A uniform cylinder of radius $$a$$ originally has a weight of $$80\;\mathrm{N}.$$ After an off-axis cylindrical hole was drilled through it, centered a distance $$2a/5$$ from the cylinder's axis, it weighs $$65\;\mathrm{N}.$$ The axes of the cylinder and the hole are parallel…
statement:
A uniform cylinder of radius $$a$$ originally has a weight of $$80\;\mathrm{N}.$$ After an off-axis cylindrical hole was drilled through it, centered a distance $$2a/5$$ from the cylinder's axis, it weighs $$65\;\mathrm{N}.$$ The axes of the cylinder and the hole are parallel, and their centers are at the same height. The cylinder rests on the ground (with friction, and it does not slip). A horizontal force $$T$$ is applied at the top of the cylinder. What magnitude of $$T$$ keeps the cylinder at rest? (From the 2012 F=ma exam.)

Useful facts: when a cylinder rolls without slipping through a small angle $$\Delta\theta,$$ its center moves a distance $$a\,\Delta\theta$$ and the __top__ of the cylinder moves twice as far, $$2a\,\Delta\theta$$ (the contact point is momentarily at rest). Also recall the energy principle: with an external force acting, the system is in equilibrium when a small displacement increases the potential energy by exactly the work done by the external force.

__(a)__ For "object with a hole" problems there is a standard trick: imagine the whole solid object is still there, and superimpose at the hole's location a second object of __negative mass__. What are the masses of the full cylinder and of the superimposed negative-mass cylinder here? (Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$)

__(b)__ Use the energy principle: imagine the cylinder rolling through a small angle $$\Delta\theta$$ toward the side the hole is on. The full cylinder's potential energy doesn't change as it rolls — only the negative-mass piece's does. Balance the change in potential energy against the work done by $$T$$ and solve for $$T.$$

__(c)__ Now try torques, taking the axis through the __center__ of the cylinder: balance the torque of the negative-mass piece's weight against the torque of $$T.$$ You will get a different answer than in part (b). What force did this calculation ignore?

__(d)__ Choose a smarter torque axis so the ignored force drops out, redo the torque balance, and confirm the energy answer.
