lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will build a simple model of the air in a tall…
desc: In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will build a simple model of the air in a tall room. The pressure in air is given by the ideal gas law, $$P = n k_B T$$ where $$P$$ is the pressure, $$n$$ the number density, or number of molecules per unit volume, $$k_B$$ is a constant…
statement:
In this week's USAPhO-style problem, we will build a simple model of the air in a tall room. The pressure in air is given by the ideal gas law, $$P = n k_B T$$ where $$P$$ is the pressure, $$n$$ the number density, or number of molecules per unit volume, $$k_B$$ is a constant called Boltzmann's constant, and $$T$$ the temperature (measured in Kelvin).

Suppose each air molecule has mass $$m.$$

We will model the atmosphere as a series of layers, each of uniform density and fixed thickness $$\Delta z.$$ We will imagine that the atmosphere has uniform temperature $$T.$$ (This is not true for the real atmosphere, so PhysicsWOOT engages in a more sophisticated model using thermodynamics.)

**a)** The bottom layer of the atmosphere can be taken to have pressure $$P_0.$$ Find the density of air in this layer as a function of $$P, m, k_B,$$ and $$T.$$

**b)** Find $$\Delta P,$$ the change in pressure from the bottom of the first layer to the bottom of the second layer.

**c)** Recall from the lesson on error analysis that $$\Delta \ln x = \dfrac{\Delta x}{x}.$$ Using this fact, find $$\Delta(\ln P)$$ as a function of $$m, g, k_B, T,$$ and $$\Delta z.$$

**d)** Find $$P$$ as a function of $$P_0, m, g, k_B,$$ and $$T.$$

**e)** Suppose an air molecule is selected at random. The theory of statistical mechanics suggests that the probability distribution for the height $$z$$ of the air molecule is $$\mathrm{prob}(z) \propto \exp(-E(z)/k_B T),$$ where $$E(z)$$ is the energy of a particle at height $$z.$$ (This is called the Boltzmann distribution, and applies very generally to any equilibrium state.) Does this probability distribution confirm or conflict with your answer from part (d)? How do you know?
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: The Hydraulic Press — A hydraulic press is a device for delivering very large forces. A conceptual sketch is…
desc: A hydraulic press is a device for delivering very large forces. A conceptual sketch is shown below: two vertical pistons of different sizes are connected by a chamber full of fluid. The radius of the left piston is $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and the radius of the right piston is…
statement:
A hydraulic press is a device for delivering very large forces. A conceptual sketch is shown below: two vertical pistons of different sizes are connected by a chamber full of fluid. The radius of the left piston is $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and the radius of the right piston is $$20\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The tops of the two pistons are at the same height. A truck of mass $$1500\;\mathrm{kg}$$ rests on the right piston. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

The press works because of the fluid's __pressure__. The basic equation relating pressure to force is $$P = \dfrac{F}{A},$$ or $$F = P\cdot A$$: the force applied by a fluid is its pressure times the area over which the force is applied.

__(a)__ A basic principle of fluid statics says: if there are no external forces on a stationary fluid, the pressure is the same everywhere in it. Justify this principle by considering a small cube of fluid somewhere in the middle of the chamber. (In this press, gravity does act on the fluid, so the pressure is actually slightly higher lower down — but since the tops of the two pistons are at the same height, we can safely ignore gravity's effect here.)

__(b)__ How much force $$F_L$$ must be applied downward on the left piston in order to support the truck? Before calculating, guess: does it take more or less than the truck's weight?

__(c)__ A small force lifting a heavy truck sounds too good to be true — what's the trade-off? If the left piston is pushed down a distance $$\Delta x_L,$$ how far $$\Delta x_R$$ does the truck rise? Answer using the work formula $$W = F\,\Delta x,$$ then show that your result is equivalent to a conservation law for the fluid. Conservation of what?

A more realistic hydraulic lift, shown below, adds at least one valve, so the small piston can be pumped back and forth many times without lowering the load — as you'll find in part (c), each pump raises the platform only a small amount.
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: The Hemispheres of Magdeburg — Otto von Guericke invented the vacuum pump in 1650. A few years later, he…
desc: Otto von Guericke invented the vacuum pump in 1650. A few years later, he staged a dramatic demonstration to show the device off. He placed two hollow copper hemispheres in contact, then used the vacuum pump to suck most of the air out from between them. Next, von Guericke had…
statement:
Otto von Guericke invented the vacuum pump in 1650. A few years later, he staged a dramatic demonstration to show the device off. He placed two hollow copper hemispheres in contact, then used the vacuum pump to suck most of the air out from between them. Next, von Guericke had two teams of eight horses each try to pull the hemispheres apart — and they couldn't.

Estimate the minimum radius of the hemispheres. Atmospheric pressure is approximately $$10^5\;\mathrm{Pa},$$ where the __pascal__ is the unit of pressure, $$1\;\mathrm{Pa} = 1\;\mathrm{N/m^2}.$$ Assume the mass of a horse is $$m = 500\;\mathrm{kg},$$ its coefficient of friction with the ground is $$\mu = 0.5,$$ and $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The force from a fluid at pressure $$P$$ on a flat surface of area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ First, the concept: why do the evacuated hemispheres stick together at all? And if air had been allowed to freely enter the gap, would they still stick?

__(b)__ Estimate the maximum force one team of eight horses can exert. (Careful: a horse's pulling force is not its weight $$mg.$$ What actually limits how hard a horse can pull?)

__(c)__ To balance that pull, the atmosphere must push the hemispheres together hard enough. A tempting move is to compute the force on one hemisphere as the pressure times the hemisphere's curved surface area, $$F \stackrel{?}{=} P_0 \cdot \dfrac12\, 4\pi r^2.$$ Explain why that is wrong. Then find the correct net horizontal force from the atmosphere on one hemisphere, using this trick: imagine the hemisphere with its open end covered by a flat sheet, sitting in a uniform atmosphere — what must the net force on it be?

__(d)__ Estimate the minimum radius of the hemispheres.
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: Pressure beneath the Surface of a Fluid — A vertical piston of cross-sectional area $$A$$ contains fluid of…
desc: A vertical piston of cross-sectional area $$A$$ contains fluid of density $$\rho.$$ The atmosphere above the fluid has pressure $$P_0.$$ We insert a thin massless plate into the piston a distance $$h$$ beneath the surface of the fluid, as shown. __(a)__ What is the mass of the…
statement:
A vertical piston of cross-sectional area $$A$$ contains fluid of density $$\rho.$$ The atmosphere above the fluid has pressure $$P_0.$$ We insert a thin massless plate into the piston a distance $$h$$ beneath the surface of the fluid, as shown.

__(a)__ What is the mass of the column of fluid above the plate, in terms of $$\rho,$$ $$A,$$ and $$h?$$

__(b)__ List all the downward forces on the column of fluid above the plate, and find the upward force $$F$$ we must exert on the plate in order to hold up that column of fluid (with zero acceleration). The force from a fluid at pressure $$P$$ acting on area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(c)__ Now focus on the plate itself: it is pushed down by the fluid's pressure $$P$$ at depth $$h$$ and held up by the force $$F$$ you found. Use this to derive the formula for the pressure at depth $$h$$ below the surface of a fluid, as a function of $$\rho,$$ $$g,$$ $$h,$$ and $$P_0.$$

(This derivation assumes the density $$\rho$$ is constant — an excellent assumption for liquids like water, which barely compress under everyday pressures, but a poor one for a tall column of air, whose density thins out with height. On the F=ma exam, assume fluids have constant density and that this formula applies unless the problem says otherwise.)
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: Ranking the Forces on Three Flask Bottoms — Flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C$$ each have a circular base with a…
desc: Flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C$$ each have a circular base with a radius of $$2\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Flask $$A$$ has straight vertical walls, flask $$B$$ widens toward the top, and flask $$C$$ narrows toward the top, as sketched below. An equal volume of water is poured into each…
statement:
Flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C$$ each have a circular base with a radius of $$2\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ Flask $$A$$ has straight vertical walls, flask $$B$$ widens toward the top, and flask $$C$$ narrows toward the top, as sketched below. An equal volume of water is poured into each flask, and none overflow. (From the 2017 F=ma exam.)

Useful facts: the pressure at depth $$h$$ below the surface of water of density $$\rho$$ is $$P = P_0 + \rho g h,$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure, and the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ Rank the forces $$F_A,$$ $$F_B,$$ and $$F_C$$ exerted by the water on the bases of flasks $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C,$$ from greatest to least.

__(b)__ Here is an argument that the ranking should be a three-way tie: "Each flask holds the same volume — and hence the same weight — of water. That weight must be supported by the upward force from the flask's bottom, so the upward forces are equal, and by Newton's third law the forces from water on the three bases are equal too." The conclusion contradicts part (a). What does this argument miss? (Hint: it has nothing to do with the atmosphere; the same resolution would work in vacuum.)

__(c)__ Now compare an hourglass-shaped flask to a straight-walled flask with the same base, each holding the same volume of water (just enough to fill the hourglass's lower bulb and waist region). The hourglass has walls that slope inward lower down and outward higher up. Which flask's bottom feels the greater force from the water? And why don't the downward wall forces from the lower (inward-sloping) walls simply cancel the upward wall forces from the upper (outward-sloping) walls?
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: Gauge Pressure in a Plugged Milk Jug — The handle of a gallon of milk is plugged by a manufacturing defect…
desc: The handle of a gallon of milk is plugged by a manufacturing defect. After removing the cap and pouring out some milk, the level of milk in the main part of the jug is lower than in the handle, as shown in the figure: the milk stands at height $$h$$ in the handle and at height…
statement:
The handle of a gallon of milk is plugged by a manufacturing defect. After removing the cap and pouring out some milk, the level of milk in the main part of the jug is lower than in the handle, as shown in the figure: the milk stands at height $$h$$ in the handle and at height $$H$$ in the main body, with $$h > H.$$ The main body is open to the atmosphere (pressure $$P_0$$); a pocket of trapped air sits at the top of the handle. The density of milk is $$\rho.$$ (From the 2017 F=ma exam.)

The __gauge pressure__ is the pressure minus atmospheric pressure: $$P_{\rm gauge} = P_{\rm abs} - P_0.$$ Recall that pressure in a fluid of constant density changes with height as $$\rho g \,\Delta y.$$

__(a)__ Which statement is true of the gauge pressure $$P$$ of the milk at the bottom of the jug? (a) $$P = \rho g h$$; (b) $$P = \rho g H$$; (c) $$\rho g H < P < \rho g h$$; (d) $$P > \rho g h$$; (e) $$P < \rho g H.$$ The key question: which height, $$h$$ or $$H,$$ is the relevant one, and why?

__(b)__ Find the pressure $$P_{\rm pocket}$$ of the trapped air pocket at the top of the handle, in terms of $$P_0,$$ $$\rho,$$ $$g,$$ $$h,$$ and $$H.$$ Is it higher or lower than atmospheric pressure?
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: The Bell That Lifts Itself — Water is poured through an orifice at the top into a hemispheric bell of radius…
desc: Water is poured through an orifice at the top into a hemispheric bell of radius $$R$$ lying on a table, tightly pressed against its surface. When the water level reaches the orifice — so the hemispherical space under the bell, of volume $$\dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac43 \pi R^3 =…
statement:
Water is poured through an orifice at the top into a hemispheric bell of radius $$R$$ lying on a table, tightly pressed against its surface. When the water level reaches the orifice — so the hemispherical space under the bell, of volume $$\dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac43 \pi R^3 = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi R^3,$$ is completely full — the bell lifts up and the water begins to flow out from underneath. Find the bell's mass $$M,$$ given that the density of water is $$\rho.$$ (From __Quantum__ magazine: Buzdin and Krotov, "Boy-oh-buoyancy," 1990.)

Useful facts: the (gauge) pressure at depth $$d$$ below the surface of water is $$\rho g d$$; the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$ You may ignore atmospheric pressure throughout, since the atmosphere pushes on everything evenly.

__(a)__ The bell lifts because the water's pressure pushes outward — and partly upward — on the bell's curved inner surface. Explain why computing that upward force directly is hard.

__(b)__ Find instead the downward pressure force from the water on the circle of table beneath the bell (radius $$R$$).

__(c)__ The force from part (b) is not the bell's weight — there's more work to do. Use Newton's third law and a force balance on the __water__ to find the net downward force the bell exerts on the water.

__(d)__ At the moment the bell is about to lift off, what supports the bell? Find the bell's mass $$M.$$
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: Deriving the Buoyant Force — A cube with side length $$s$$ sits fully immersed in water of density $$\rho,$$…
desc: A cube with side length $$s$$ sits fully immersed in water of density $$\rho,$$ with its top face horizontal a distance $$h$$ below the surface, as shown. Gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ In this problem we derive, step by step, the net force that the water's pressure exerts…
statement:
A cube with side length $$s$$ sits fully immersed in water of density $$\rho,$$ with its top face horizontal a distance $$h$$ below the surface, as shown. Gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ In this problem we derive, step by step, the net force that the water's pressure exerts on the cube. Recall that the pressure at depth $$d$$ below the surface is $$P = P_0 + \rho g d,$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure, and the force from pressure $$P$$ on a flat face of area $$A$$ is $$F = P\cdot A.$$

__(a)__ The water pushes inward on all six faces of the cube. Do these pressure forces sum to zero? If not, which way does the net force point, and why?

__(b)__ Compute the pressure force on the top face and on the bottom face of the cube, and find the magnitude of the net pressure force on the cube. (The forces on the four side faces cancel in pairs.)

__(c)__ Rewrite your answer in terms of the cube's volume $$V.$$ This net pressure force is called the __buoyant force__. State the general principle — __Archimedes' principle__ — that your formula illustrates.

__(d)__ A student analyzing a beach ball held under the ocean draws a free-body diagram showing the pressure forces pushing inward on all sides of the ball __and__ an upward buoyant force $$F_B.$$ What is wrong with that diagram?
tags: statics ii - fluids and material properties

lesson: FMA10: Statics II - Fluids and Material Properties
label: FMA10
name: The Pivoted Floating Rod — A uniform rod is partially in water with one end suspended from a pivot above the…
desc: A uniform rod is partially in water with one end suspended from a pivot above the surface, as shown in the figure. The density of the rod is $$\dfrac{5}{9}$$ that of water. At equilibrium, what portion of the rod is above water? (From the 2013 F=ma exam.) Treat the rod as very…
statement:
A uniform rod is partially in water with one end suspended from a pivot above the surface, as shown in the figure. The density of the rod is $$\dfrac{5}{9}$$ that of water. At equilibrium, what portion of the rod is above water? (From the 2013 F=ma exam.)

Treat the rod as very thin compared to its length $$\ell$$ (ignore the extra bits submerged because the rod is tilted). Let the rod have mass $$m$$ and uniform cross-sectional area $$A,$$ let a fraction $$\alpha$$ of its length be above the water, and let the rod make angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. Recall the buoyant force on an object has magnitude $$F_B = \rho_w g V_{\rm sub},$$ where $$\rho_w$$ is the water's density and $$V_{\rm sub}$$ the submerged volume, and that it points straight up.

__(a)__ This is a statics problem: the net force and the net torque on the rod must both be zero. Knowing the buoyant force's magnitude and direction isn't enough here — we also need to know __where__ it acts. The buoyant force can be modeled as acting at a single point called the __center of buoyancy__: the geometric center of the submerged part of the object (just as gravity acts at the center of mass). For our rod, how far from the pivot, measured along the rod, is the center of buoyancy? Is the center of buoyancy of an object always at the same place on the object?

__(b)__ Find the buoyant force on the rod in terms of $$m,$$ $$g,$$ and $$\alpha.$$ (First express the displaced mass using $$\rho_w,$$ $$A,$$ $$\ell,$$ and $$\alpha,$$ then eliminate $$\rho_w$$ using the given density ratio.)

__(c)__ Balance torques about the pivot to find $$\alpha.$$

__(d)__ If the rod were not pivoted but simply floated freely in the water, what fraction would be above the surface? Explain why the pivoted rod has more of its length above water than the free-floating rod.

name: How Much Does a Cable Stretch? — Any solid object deforms a little when forces act on it — every material…
desc: Any solid object deforms a little when forces act on it — every material behaves like a very stiff spring. In this problem we build up, by pure proportional reasoning, the law governing how much a cable stretches. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ A cable $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ long…
statement:
Any solid object deforms a little when forces act on it — every material behaves like a very stiff spring. In this problem we build up, by pure proportional reasoning, the law governing how much a cable stretches. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

A cable $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, of negligible weight, supports a hanging mass of $$100\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and stretches by $$0.5\;\mathrm{mm}.$$

__(a)__ How much would the same cable stretch if it supported $$200\;\mathrm{kg}$$ instead? (Materials under modest loads obey Hooke's law: stretch is proportional to the applied force.)

__(b)__ Keeping the $$200\;\mathrm{kg}$$ load, suppose the cable is replaced by one twice as long — $$2\;\mathrm{m}$$ — made of the same material with the same radius. What is the stretch now? (Hint: think of the $$2\;\mathrm{m}$$ cable as two $$1\;\mathrm{m}$$ cables joined end to end.)

__(c)__ Keeping everything from part (b), now double the radius of the cable. What is the stretch? (Hint: think of the thick cable as several of the original cables banded together side by side.)

__(d)__ Keeping everything from part (c), replace the material with one twice as stiff — i.e. one that produces twice the tension for a given stretch. What is the stretch?

__(e)__ Combine the patterns from (a)-(d): a cable of length $$l$$ and cross-sectional area $$A,$$ made of a material whose stiffness is described by a single constant $$Y$$ (the __Young's modulus__), supports a load $$F.$$ Write the formula for the stretch $$\Delta l$$ (by convention, no extra numerical factor — that convention is what defines $$Y$$). Then rearrange the formula into the form $$\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\,\dfrac{\Delta l}{l},$$ and give the names and interpretations of the quantities $$\dfrac{F}{A}$$ and $$\dfrac{\Delta l}{l}.$$

name: The Tightrope Walker's Cable — A massless cable of diameter $$2.54\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is tied horizontally…
desc: A massless cable of diameter $$2.54\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is tied horizontally between two trees $$18.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart. A tightrope walker with a mass of $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ stands at the center of the cable. The cable stretches and makes an angle of $$1.50^\circ$$ with the…
statement:
A massless cable of diameter $$2.54\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is tied horizontally between two trees $$18.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart. A tightrope walker with a mass of $$80\;\mathrm{kg}$$ stands at the center of the cable. The cable stretches and makes an angle of $$1.50^\circ$$ with the horizontal. What is the cable's Young's modulus? Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Definitions you'll need: the __stress__ in a cable of tension $$T$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ is $$\sigma = \dfrac{T}{A}$$; the __strain__ is the fractional increase in length, $$e = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l}$$; and the __Young's modulus__ is their ratio, $$Y = \dfrac{\sigma}{e}.$$ Work through the following plan:

__(a)__ The walker hangs from two cable segments, one on each side, each with tension $$T$$ and each at $$1.50^\circ$$ below the horizontal. Find $$T.$$

__(b)__ Find the stress in the cable.

__(c)__ Find the strain: by what fraction is each segment longer than its unstretched (horizontal) length? (Hint: compare each segment's stretched length to the $$9.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ horizontal distance it spans.)

__(d)__ Combine your results to find the Young's modulus.

desc: A thin, uniform rod of length $$L$$ and mass $$M$$ is suspended from a point a distance $$R$$ away from its center of mass. **a)** Suppose the pendulum is rotated by an angle $$\theta.$$ Draw a plot of torque on the pendulum about the point of suspension as a function of $$R.$$…
statement:
A thin, uniform rod of length $$L$$ and mass $$M$$ is suspended from a point a distance $$R$$ away from its center of mass.

**a)** Suppose the pendulum is rotated by an angle $$\theta.$$ Draw a plot of torque on the pendulum about the point of suspension as a function of $$R.$$

**b)** Similarly, draw a plot of the moment of inertia of the pendulum about the point of suspension as a function of $$R.$$ The moment of inertia of a rod about its center of $$\dfrac{1}{12} ML^2.$$

**c)** Based on the plots you drew in parts (a) and (b), will the rod's period be shortest for very small $$R, (R \ll L),$$ very long $$R (R = \dfrac{L}{2}),$$ or somewhere in the middle? Briefly explain your answer.

**d)** Find an equation for the period of the rod as a function of $$R.$$

**e)** The following data on the period of the rod was collected in an experiment: \begin{tabular}{cc} $$R$$ ($$\mathrm{m}$$) & $$T$$ ($$\mathrm{s}$$) \\ \hline 0.050 & 3.842 \\ 0.075 & 3.164 \\ 0.102 & 2.747 \\ 0.156 & 2.301 \\ 0.198 & 2.115 \\ 0.211 & 2.074 \\ 0.302 & 1.905 \\ 0.387 & 1.855 \\ 0.451 & 1.853 \\ 0.588 & 1.900 \end{tabular} We would like to use a graph of this data to determine both $$g,$$ the local gravitational acceleration, and $$L,$$ the length of the rod.

This will be difficult using a plot of $$T$$ vs $$R.$$ Instead, we will plot some combination of $$T$$ and $$R$$ on the $$y$$ axis and some function of $$R$$ on the $$x$$ axis.

Find an appropriate combination of $$T$$ and $$R$$ to plot on the $$y$$ axis and an appropriate function of $$R$$ to plot on the $$x$$ axis so that, according to the equation you found in part (d), the data should lie on a straight line. Do this by manipulating the equation from part (d) until it is of the form $$y = mx + b$$ where $$y$$ is a combination of $$T$$ and $$R,$$ $$x$$ is a function of $$R,$$ and $$m$$ and $$b$$ are functions of $$l, g,$$ and constants.

**f)** Add two extra columns to the data table, with with your combination of $$T$$ and $$R$$ that forms $$y$$ and one with your function of $$R$$ that forms $$x.$$

**g)** Draw a plot of the data. Draw a best-fit line through the data. From the slope and intercept of the line, estimate $$g$$ and $$L$$ for the rod.

Make sure that your plot has labels and units on the axes. Plot the scale of your axes so that the data takes up almost the entire piece of paper you use, but all the data fits on the plot.

label: FMA11
name: A Disk Twisting on a Wire — A disk with moment of inertia $$I$$ hangs horizontally from a vertical wire…
desc: A disk with moment of inertia $$I$$ hangs horizontally from a vertical wire attached to the center of the disk. If the disk is rotated through an angle $$\theta$$ in the horizontal plane (the solid radius in the figure moves to the dashed radius), the wire twists and exerts a…
statement:
A disk with moment of inertia $$I$$ hangs horizontally from a vertical wire attached to the center of the disk. If the disk is rotated through an angle $$\theta$$ in the horizontal plane (the solid radius in the figure moves to the dashed radius), the wire twists and exerts a __restoring torque__ on the disk. Assume this torque obeys a rotational version of Hooke's Law: it is proportional to the angular displacement and points opposite to it, $$\tau = -\kappa\theta,$$ where $$\kappa$$ is a constant property of the wire.

For a mass on a spring, the restoring force $$F = -kx$$ produces simple harmonic motion satisfying $$a = -\omega_f^2\,x,$$ where $$\omega_f = 2\pi f$$ is the __angular frequency__ of the oscillation. Exactly the same relationship holds between the angular analogs of these quantities: an angular oscillation satisfies $$\alpha = -\omega_f^2\,\theta,$$ where $$\alpha$$ is the angular acceleration.

__(a)__ A warning about notation: $$\omega_f$$ is the angular frequency of the oscillation, while $$\omega = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$$ is the angular speed of the rotating disk — two different things. Suppose the amplitude of the disk's oscillation were doubled, with the same disk and wire. Which of the two quantities would change, and which would stay the same? Explain.

__(b)__ Use the rotational form of Newton's second law, $$\tau_{\rm net} = I\alpha,$$ together with the two equations above, to find the angular frequency $$\omega_f$$ of the disk's oscillations in terms of $$\kappa$$ and $$I.$$

__(c)__ Write the period of the oscillations.

label: FMA11
name: The Period of a Simple Pendulum — A simple pendulum consists of a point mass $$m$$ attached to the end of a…
desc: A simple pendulum consists of a point mass $$m$$ attached to the end of a string of length $$l$$ whose other end is fixed at a pivot. The pendulum is displaced by a small angle and released. Find the period of the resulting oscillations. Treat the pendulum as a rotational…
statement:
A simple pendulum consists of a point mass $$m$$ attached to the end of a string of length $$l$$ whose other end is fixed at a pivot. The pendulum is displaced by a small angle and released. Find the period of the resulting oscillations.

Treat the pendulum as a rotational oscillator: if the restoring torque about the pivot has the Hooke's-Law form $$\tau = -\kappa\theta,$$ then the oscillation has angular frequency $$\omega_f = \sqrt{\kappa/I}$$ and period $$T = 2\pi/\omega_f,$$ where $$I$$ is the moment of inertia about the pivot. The figure shows a snapshot with the pendulum displaced by an angle $$\theta$$ from the vertical, along with the forces acting on the mass.

__(a)__ Two forces act on the mass: the string tension and gravity. Which of them exerts a torque about the pivot? Also explain why, for the pendulum to oscillate, the torque and the angular displacement $$\theta$$ must always have __opposite__ signs.

__(b)__ Show that the torque about the pivot is $$\tau = -mgl\sin\theta.$$

__(c)__ The torque in part (b) is proportional to $$\sin\theta,$$ not to $$\theta,$$ so it is not yet in the form $$\tau = -\kappa\theta.$$ The __small angle approximation__ fixes this: for small $$\theta$$ measured in __radians__, $$\sin\theta \approx \theta.$$ The graph below shows $$y = \theta$$ and $$y = \sin\theta$$; notice how the two are nearly identical near $$\theta = 0.$$ Use the approximation to put the torque in Hooke's-Law form and identify $$\kappa.$$

__(d)__ Find the moment of inertia of the pendulum about the pivot, and then find the angular frequency and the period of the oscillations.

label: FMA11
name: A Pivoted Rod and a Very Long Spring (2016 F=ma #14) — A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless…
desc: A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal surface. One end of the rod is attached to a pivot, about which it is free to rotate. An unstretched spring of length $$L \gg l$$ (much longer than the rod) lies on the surface perpendicular to the rod; one end of…
statement:
A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal surface. One end of the rod is attached to a pivot, about which it is free to rotate. An unstretched spring of length $$L \gg l$$ (much longer than the rod) lies on the surface perpendicular to the rod; one end of the spring is attached to the movable end of the rod, and the other end is attached to a fixed post. The spring constant is $$k.$$ When the rod is rotated slightly about the pivot, it oscillates at frequency $$f.$$

The spring attachment is then moved to the __midpoint__ of the rod, and the post is moved so that the spring remains unstretched and perpendicular to the rod, as in the right panel below. The system is again set into small oscillations. What is the new frequency of oscillation? (2016 F=ma exam, Problem 14.)

(A) $$f/2$$ (B) $$f/\sqrt{2}$$ (C) $$f$$ (D) $$\sqrt{2}f$$ (E) $$2f$$

Find the frequency of each setup separately, then compare. Throughout, use $$f = \dfrac{\omega_f}{2\pi}$$ with $$\omega_f = \sqrt{\kappa/I},$$ where $$\kappa$$ is the torsional constant in $$\tau = -\kappa\theta$$ and $$I$$ is the rod's moment of inertia about the pivot. You may leave $$I$$ as a symbol — it is the same in both setups, since the rod itself is unchanged.

__(a)__ Take a snapshot of the original setup with the rod displaced by a small angle $$\theta,$$ as in the figure below. Show that the components of the spring's length along and perpendicular to its original direction are $$L + l\sin\theta$$ and $$l(1-\cos\theta).$$ Then avoid the Pythagorean theorem by using this fact about right triangles: if the shorter leg is much smaller than the longer leg, the hypotenuse is essentially equal to the longer leg (for example, legs $$1$$ and $$1000$$ give a hypotenuse of $$1000.0005$$ — the increase is negligible). Conclude that the spring's elongation is approximately $$l\theta.$$

__(b)__ Because the spring is very long and the oscillations are small, the spring force stays very nearly perpendicular to the rod at all times, so you may treat it as exactly perpendicular. Find the torque on the rod, identify the torsional constant $$\kappa,$$ and write the frequency $$f$$ of the original setup in terms of $$k,$$ $$l,$$ and $$I.$$

__(c)__ Repeat the analysis for the midpoint setup: find the spring's elongation, the torque, the new torsional constant, and the new frequency. Which answer choice is correct?

label: FMA11
name: Moving the Post in Line with the Rod (2016 F=ma #15) — A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless…
desc: A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal surface, attached at one end to a pivot about which it is free to rotate. A spring with constant $$k$$ and unstretched length $$L \gg l$$ is attached to the free end of the rod. When the spring is perpendicular to…
statement:
A uniform rod of length $$l$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal surface, attached at one end to a pivot about which it is free to rotate. A spring with constant $$k$$ and unstretched length $$L \gg l$$ is attached to the free end of the rod. When the spring is perpendicular to the rod (anchored to a fixed post a distance $$L$$ away), small oscillations of the rod have frequency $$f$$; in that configuration the restoring torque is $$\tau = -kl^2\theta,$$ i.e. the torsional constant is $$\kappa = kl^2,$$ and $$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{kl^2}{I}}$$ where $$I$$ is the rod's moment of inertia about the pivot.

Now the post is instead placed __in line__ with the rod and the pivot, at the position where the spring is unstretched, and is then moved directly away from the pivot by an additional distance $$l,$$ stretching the spring by $$l.$$ The rod is set into small oscillations. What is the new frequency of oscillation? (2016 F=ma exam, Problem 15.)

(A) $$f/3$$ (B) $$f/\sqrt{3}$$ (C) $$f$$ (D) $$\sqrt{3}f$$ (E) $$3f$$

The figure shows a snapshot with the rod displaced by a small angle $$\theta.$$

__(a)__ Show that the components of the spring's length along and perpendicular to the pivot-post line are $$l(1-\cos\theta) + (L+l)$$ and $$l\sin\theta.$$ Then use the long-leg/short-leg fact (in a right triangle whose shorter leg is much smaller than its longer leg, the hypotenuse is essentially the longer leg) to approximate the spring's length.

__(b)__ The term $$l(1-\cos\theta)$$ is also negligible, but for a different reason. The graph below shows that near $$\theta = 0,$$ the function $$1 - \cos\theta$$ matches the quadratic $$\dfrac{\theta^2}{2}.$$ A term proportional to $$\theta^2$$ is called a __second-order term__: when $$\theta$$ is much less than $$1,$$ squaring it produces something far smaller still. Ignoring second-order (and higher) terms is called a __first-order approximation__. Use this to conclude that the spring's length is approximately $$L + l,$$ and find the magnitude and direction of the spring force.

__(c)__ Find the lever arm of the spring force about the pivot, the restoring torque, and the torsional constant $$\kappa.$$ What is the new frequency of oscillation? Which answer choice is correct?

__(d)__ Rigorize the long-leg/short-leg fact from part (a). For a right triangle with legs $$x \ll L,$$ multiply $$\sqrt{L^2 + x^2} - L$$ by the conjugate $$\dfrac{\sqrt{L^2+x^2}+L}{\sqrt{L^2+x^2}+L}$$ to show that $$\sqrt{L^2 + x^2} - L \approx \dfrac{x^2}{2L}.$$ Why does this justify dropping the short leg in a first-order approximation?

label: FMA11
name: What Increases a Pendulum's Period? (2011 F=ma #10) — Which of the following changes will result in an…
desc: Which of the following changes will result in an __increase__ in the period of a simple pendulum? (2011 F=ma exam, Problem 10.) (A) Decrease the length of the pendulum. (B) Increase the mass of the pendulum. (C) Increase the amplitude of the pendulum swing. (D) Operate the…
statement:
Which of the following changes will result in an __increase__ in the period of a simple pendulum? (2011 F=ma exam, Problem 10.)

(A) Decrease the length of the pendulum.

(B) Increase the mass of the pendulum.

(C) Increase the amplitude of the pendulum swing.

(D) Operate the pendulum in an elevator that is accelerating upward.

(E) Operate the pendulum in an elevator that is moving downward at constant speed.

Useful background: for __small__ oscillations, the period of a simple pendulum of length $$l$$ is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}.$$ This formula is derived from the restoring torque $$\tau = -mgl\sin\theta$$ by using the small angle approximation $$\sin\theta \approx \theta.$$

__(a)__ Use the period formula to evaluate choices (A) and (B).

__(b)__ Evaluate choices (D) and (E). For (D), recall that physics inside a reference frame accelerating upward with magnitude $$a$$ is the same as physics in a stronger gravitational field $$g + a$$ — this is why astronauts during a rocket launch are said to experience "$$6$$ G's," meaning their frame behaves as if $$g = 6g_{\rm earth}.$$ For (E), think about what is special about reference frames moving at constant velocity.

__(c)__ Now consider choice (C). The amplitude $$\theta_{\rm max}$$ does not appear in the period formula — but the formula was derived using an approximation. The strength of the restoring effect is indicated by the __slope__ of the graph of the torque magnitude $$mgl\sin\theta$$ versus $$\theta.$$ By comparing $$\sin\theta$$ to the straight line $$\theta$$ over the range $$[-\theta_{\rm max}, \theta_{\rm max}],$$ decide qualitatively whether a large amplitude makes the period longer or shorter, and select the answer to the problem.

statement: Individual, single-celled __Dictyostelium discoideum__ amoeba sometimes combine to form a small slug, typically about $$500 \;\mu\mathrm{m}$$ by $$60 \;\mu\mathrm{m}$$ by $$60 \;\mu\mathrm{m}.$$ Scientists estimated the number of amoeba per slug, assuming that the radius of a typical amoeba was $$5 \;\mu\mathrm{m},$$ but they later found that the radius of a typical amoeba is actually $$2.5 \;\mu\mathrm{m}.$$ How far off was the original estimate for the number of amoeba in a slug? (a) It was too small by a factor of $$8$$ (b) It was too small by a factor of $$2$$ (c) It was correct the first time. (d) It was too big by a factor of $$2$$ (e) It was too big by a factor of $$8$$

statement:

(b) $$\frac{kA^2}{m}$$

(c) $$\sqrt{\frac{kA}{m}}$$

(d) $$\sqrt{\frac{kA^2}{m}}$$

(e) $$\sqrt{mkA^2}$$

statement: A water droplet falling through the air can oscillate with some angular frequency that depends on its surface tension, density, and radius. The surface tension may be interpreted as the energy per unit area of surface of the drop. If a certain drop oscillates with angular frequency $$\omega,$$ what is the oscillation angular frequency of a drop with half of the first drop's radius? (a) $$\omega/2$$ (b) $$\omega$$ (c) $$\sqrt{2}\omega$$ (d) $$2\omega$$ (e) $$2\sqrt{2}\omega$$

desc: This problem extends the previous problem on oscillations of a liquid droplet. Liquid water drops hang on a faucet via surface tension. The droplets gradually accumulate size due to the slow flow of water through the faucet. When the droplet achieves sufficient size, it falls…
statement:
This problem extends the previous problem on oscillations of a liquid droplet.

Liquid water drops hang on a faucet via surface tension. The droplets gradually accumulate size due to the slow flow of water through the faucet. When the droplet achieves sufficient size, it falls off the faucet.

The surface tension of the drop depends on temperature. If changes in the temperature change the surface tension by $$1\%,$$ by about what percent does the radius of drops change?

(a) $$0.33 \%.$$ (b) $$0.5 \%.$$ (c) $$1 \%.$$ (d) $$2 \%.$$ (e) $$3 \%.$$

name: A point charge moving in a circle radiates energy. The power radiated can depend on the…
desc: A point charge moving in a circle radiates energy. The power radiated can depend on the charge, the acceleration, and the speed of light. The formula for the force between two charges is $$F = kq_1q_2/r^2,$$ where $$q_1$$ and $$q_2$$ are the charges with dimensions of $$C$$, and…
statement:
A point charge moving in a circle radiates energy. The power radiated can depend on the charge, the acceleration, and the speed of light. The formula for the force between two charges is $$F = kq_1q_2/r^2,$$ where $$q_1$$ and $$q_2$$ are the charges with dimensions of $$C$$, and $$r$$ is the distance between them. $$k$$ is a constant with dimensions $$L^3MT^{-2}C^{-2}.$$ Suppose that in a small particle accelerator, particles travel in (non-relativistic) circles of radius $$r_1$$ and speed $$v_1.$$ A new accelerator is built with the radius twice as large. If the power radiated per charge is the same for the second accelerator, what is the speed in the new accelerator?

(a) $$\frac{1}{2} v_1$$

(b) $$\frac{1}{\sqrt 2} v_1$$

(c) $$v_1$$

(d) $$\sqrt{2} v_1$$

(e) $$2 v_1$$

label: FMA12
name: In our final USAPhO-style problem, we'll examine surface tension, a phenomenon that…
desc: In our final USAPhO-style problem, we'll examine surface tension, a phenomenon that occurs at all interfaces between fluids. Molecules in the interior of a fluid form bonds with their neighboring molecules. This puts them into a lower-energy state, as bonded states are lower in…
statement:
In our final USAPhO-style problem, we'll examine surface tension, a phenomenon that occurs at all interfaces between fluids.

Molecules in the interior of a fluid form bonds with their neighboring molecules. This puts them into a lower-energy state, as bonded states are lower in energy than free (unbonded) states.

When a molecule moves to the surface of a fluid, it cannot bond with as many of its neighbors as it could when in the interior of the fluid. This means there is an energy cost to creating more surface to a fluid.

**a)** The dimensions of surface tension $$\sigma$$ are $$ [\sigma] = M T^{-2} .$$ Suppose we were to define dimensions not in terms of mass, length, and time($$M,L,T$$), but instead in terms of force, length, and time $$(F,L,T).$$ What would the dimensions of surface tension be in this system? What if we defined dimensions in terms of energy, length, and time $$(E,L,T)?$$

**b)** At small length scales, surface tension is often the dominant force. A drop of water dominated by surface tension will pull itself into a sphere to minimize surface area. However, a larger drop, dominated by gravity, will spread out flat (because gravitational forces pull it down).

Imagine a drop of water of radius $$r,$$ surface tension $$\sigma,$$ density $$\rho,$$ and subjected to gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Find the approximate size $$r$$ at which the drop transitions from being surface-tension dominate to gravity dominated.

(This is not a sudden transition, but a gradual one.) Does this length scale seem reasonable for the transition? For example, do drops of water around this size or smaller have a roughly-spherical shape?

In order to evaluate your answer, use \begin{aligned} \rho &= 1000 \;\mathrm{kg \cdot m^{-3}}, \\ g & = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}, \\ \sigma &= 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \;\mathrm{kg \cdot s^{-2}}. \end{aligned}

**c)** Now let's consider waves on the surface of water. Long wavelengths, like large drops, propagate due to the gravitational forces on them. Short wavelengths propagate due to surface tension forces.

For short wavelengths driven by surface tension, the speed of the waves, $$v,$$ is a function of the wavenumber $$k,$$ (defined as $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda},$$ where $$\lambda$$ is the wavelength of the wave), the surface tension $$\sigma,$$ and the density $$\rho.$$ Find an approximate formula for $$v$$ for surface-tension-driven waves.

**d)** For gravity-driven surface waves (in deep water), the wave speed is determined by $$g$$ and $$k.$$ Find an approximate formula for $$v$$ for gravity-driven surface waves.

**e)** Estimate the minimum speed of waves on the surface of water. If, for example, an insect moves across the surface of the water at a speed slower than this, it will not excite surface waves.

label: FMA12
name: Picking the Answer Choice with the Right Dimensions — A bottle filled with air floats in deep space. Its neck…
desc: A bottle filled with air floats in deep space. Its neck has cross-sectional area $$A_n,$$ and the wider body of the bottle has cross-sectional area $$A_b.$$ A massless, frictionless stopper sits in the neck and seals all the air inside. A force $$F$$ is applied downward (into…
statement:
A bottle filled with air floats in deep space. Its neck has cross-sectional area $$A_n,$$ and the wider body of the bottle has cross-sectional area $$A_b.$$ A massless, frictionless stopper sits in the neck and seals all the air inside. A force $$F$$ is applied downward (into the bottle) on the stopper to hold it in place. What is the force the trapped air applies to the bottom surface of the bottle?

The answer choices are (a) $$F\,\dfrac{A_b^2}{A_n},$$ (b) $$\sqrt{\dfrac{A_n^2}{F A_b}},$$ (c) $$F\,\dfrac{A_n}{A_b},$$ (d) $$F\,\dfrac{A_b}{A_n},$$ (e) $$F^2\,\dfrac{A_n^3}{A_b^5}.$$ Recall that a force has dimensions $$=MLT^{-2}$$ and an area has dimensions $$L^2.$$

__(a)__ The answer must be a force. Use dimensions to eliminate every choice that cannot possibly be a force. You need not compute the full dimensions of a messy expression: checking just one dimension (say mass, or time) is often enough to rule a choice out.

__(b)__ Two choices survive the dimension check; both are dimensionally a force, so dimensions alone cannot separate them. Use physical reasoning about pressure to pick the correct one. (The stopper has area $$A_n$$ and is held by force $$F,$$ so the pressure in the neck is $$F/A_n,$$ and this is the pressure throughout the sealed air.)

label: FMA12
name: Scaling a Projectile to Another Planet — A ball is fired at speed $$v$$ and angle $$\phi$$ above the…
desc: A ball is fired at speed $$v$$ and angle $$\phi$$ above the horizontal from the top of a hill that slopes downward at angle $$\theta.$$ Air resistance is neglected and the gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ The relevant dimensions are $$=LT^{-2}$$ and $$=LT^{-1},$$ while…
statement:
A ball is fired at speed $$v$$ and angle $$\phi$$ above the horizontal from the top of a hill that slopes downward at angle $$\theta.$$ Air resistance is neglected and the gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ The relevant dimensions are $$=LT^{-2}$$ and $$=LT^{-1},$$ while $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ are __dimensionless__. Finding an exact landing formula would require solving a quadratic for the intersection of the parabolic trajectory with the sloped ground, but dimensional analysis answers the scaling questions below with almost no work.

__(a)__ The ball lands a straight-line distance $$d$$ from where it was fired, so $$=L.$$ Find a combination of $$v$$ and $$g$$ with the dimensions of a length, and explain why the most general dimensionally-allowed formula is $$d=\dfrac{v^2}{g}\,f(\phi,\theta)$$ for some unknown dimensionless function $$f.$$

__(b)__ The experiment is repeated with everything identical except on a planet with gravitational acceleration $$g/5.$$ How far from the firing point does the ball land now? Explain why you can answer even though $$f$$ is unknown.

__(c)__ Instead of the straight-line distance $$d,$$ let $$s$$ be the length of the curved path the ball travels through the air, and let $$h$$ be the maximum height it reaches. On the $$g/5$$ planet, what are the new values of $$s$$ and $$h$$ in terms of the originals?

__(d)__ Let $$A$$ be the area enclosed under the parabolic arc on the original planet. Find both its value on the $$g/5$$ planet and a formula for how $$A$$ depends on $$v$$ and $$g.$$ Then, staying on the original planet, find how $$A$$ changes if the ball is fired twice as fast.

label: FMA12
name: When Dimensional Analysis Is Not Enough — You throw a rock at speed $$v$$ at angle $$\phi$$ above the…
desc: You throw a rock at speed $$v$$ at angle $$\phi$$ above the horizontal from the top of a building of height $$h.$$ It lands a horizontal distance $$d$$ from the base of the building. An earlier, nearly identical problem (a ball fired from a hill sloping at angle $$\theta$$)…
statement:
You throw a rock at speed $$v$$ at angle $$\phi$$ above the horizontal from the top of a building of height $$h.$$ It lands a horizontal distance $$d$$ from the base of the building. An earlier, nearly identical problem (a ball fired from a hill sloping at angle $$\theta$$) could be solved by pure dimensional analysis: shrinking $$g$$ scaled $$d$$ in a simple way, because the only available length scale was $$v^2/g.$$

From a dimensional-analysis standpoint, what makes the building version fundamentally different, so that dimensions alone cannot tell you how $$d$$ scales with $$g?$$ For reference, the exact answer is $$d=\dfrac{v\cos\phi}{g}\left(v\sin\phi+\sqrt{v^2\sin^2\phi+2gh}\right).$$ Use it to explain why simple proportional scaling fails here.

label: FMA12
name: Building the Speed of Sound from Dimensions — The speed of sound in a gas depends on the gas's pressure $$P$$…
desc: The speed of sound in a gas depends on the gas's pressure $$P$$ and density $$\rho.$$ Even with no knowledge of the physics of sound waves, dimensional analysis can construct the formula. The useful dimensions are: speed $$=LT^{-1};$$ density $$[\rho]=ML^{-3};$$ and pressure…
statement:
The speed of sound in a gas depends on the gas's pressure $$P$$ and density $$\rho.$$ Even with no knowledge of the physics of sound waves, dimensional analysis can construct the formula. The useful dimensions are: speed $$=LT^{-1};$$ density $$[\rho]=ML^{-3};$$ and pressure (force per area) $$=ML^{-1}T^{-2}.$$

__(a)__ Build a quantity from $$P$$ and $$\rho$$ with the dimensions of a speed. (Hint: only $$P$$ carries the time dimension, so use it to fix the time first; then use $$\rho$$ to clear away the leftover mass.) Why can dimensional analysis determine the formula only up to an unknown dimensionless constant $$\alpha?$$

__(b)__ At sea level the speed of sound is about $$330\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ At a high altitude the pressure is reduced by a factor of $$2$$ and the density by a factor of $$1.7.$$ Find the speed of sound there.

__(c)__ A student worries that the mass $$m$$ of an individual gas molecule should also appear in the formula (so that helium and nitrogen would differ). Explain why $$m$$ cannot be inserted into $$c=\alpha\sqrt{P/\rho}$$ without breaking the dimensions.

label: FMA12
name: Why a Wrong-Dimension Formula Can't Be Right — A careless student guesses the (incorrect) formula…
desc: A careless student guesses the (incorrect) formula $$c=\dfrac{P}{\rho}$$ for the speed of sound, where $$P$$ is the pressure and $$\rho$$ is the density, planning to just plug in numbers and attach whatever speed unit seems appropriate at the end. Show that this practice is…
statement:
A careless student guesses the (incorrect) formula $$c=\dfrac{P}{\rho}$$ for the speed of sound, where $$P$$ is the pressure and $$\rho$$ is the density, planning to just plug in numbers and attach whatever speed unit seems appropriate at the end. Show that this practice is self-contradictory by computing $$c$$ two different ways. Use atmospheric pressure $$P=10^5\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$$ and air density $$\rho=1\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}.$$

__(a)__ Working in meters and seconds, plug in and read off $$c$$ in $$\mathrm{m/s}.$$

__(b)__ Convert $$P$$ and $$\rho$$ to units built from kilograms, __centimeters__, and seconds, then plug into the same formula and read off $$c$$ in $$\mathrm{cm/s}.$$

__(c)__ Compare the two answers, recalling that $$1\;\mathrm{m/s}=100\;\mathrm{cm/s}.$$ What does the discrepancy reveal, and how does the correct formula $$c=\sqrt{P/\rho}$$ avoid it?

label: FMA12
name: A Modified Spring Law and Kepler's Third Law — An ordinary spring obeys Hooke's law $$F=-kx,$$ and its…
desc: An ordinary spring obeys Hooke's law $$F=-kx,$$ and its oscillation period is independent of amplitude. Consider instead a modified force law $$F=-\dfrac{k'}{x^2},$$ where a mass $$m$$ oscillates with amplitude $$A.$$ Solving the motion exactly requires difficult calculus, but…
statement:
An ordinary spring obeys Hooke's law $$F=-kx,$$ and its oscillation period is independent of amplitude. Consider instead a modified force law $$F=-\dfrac{k'}{x^2},$$ where a mass $$m$$ oscillates with amplitude $$A.$$ Solving the motion exactly requires difficult calculus, but dimensional analysis gives the amplitude-dependence of the period directly. (Write $$T$$ for the period and $$\mathrm{T}$$ for the time dimension; the amplitude $$A$$ is a length and $$=MLT^{-2}.$$)

__(a)__ Find the dimensions of the modified spring constant $$k'.$$ Note these are __not__ the dimensions of an ordinary spring constant.

__(b)__ Assume the period has the form $$T=D\,k'^{\alpha}m^{\beta}A^{\gamma}$$ for a dimensionless constant $$D.$$ Write one equation for each of the mass, length, and time dimensions, solve for $$\alpha,\beta,\gamma,$$ and state the resulting formula for $$T.$$

__(c)__ If the amplitude is multiplied by $$4,$$ by what factor does the period change? Show this is equivalent to $$T^2\propto A^3,$$ and name the famous law it reproduces for an inverse-square force.

label: FMA12
name: Two Planets of Equal Density (2008 F=ma) — Consider two uniform spherical planets of equal density but…
desc: Consider two uniform spherical planets of equal density but unequal radius. Which of the following quantities is the __same__ for both planets? (2008 F=ma exam.) The choices are: (a) the escape velocity from the surface; (b) the acceleration due to gravity at the surface; (c)…
statement:
Consider two uniform spherical planets of equal density but unequal radius. Which of the following quantities is the __same__ for both planets? (2008 F=ma exam.) The choices are: (a) the escape velocity from the surface; (b) the acceleration due to gravity at the surface; (c) the orbital period of a satellite skimming just above the surface; (d) the orbital period of a satellite at a given fixed distance from the planet's center; (e) none of the above.

Treat each choice with dimensional analysis. The relevant dimensional variables are the density $$\rho,$$ the planet radius $$r,$$ and Newton's constant $$G,$$ whose dimensions follow from $$F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$$ to be $$=L^3M^{-1}T^{-2}.$$ The planet's mass need not be listed separately, since $$M=\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho.$$

__(a)__ Find, up to a dimensionless constant, formulas for the escape velocity $$v$$ and the surface gravity $$g_s.$$ Do they depend on the radius $$r?$$

__(b)__ Find a formula for the orbital period $$\tau$$ of a satellite skimming just above the surface. Does it depend on $$r?$$

__(c)__ For a satellite at a fixed distance $$R$$ from the center, explain why dimensional analysis no longer determines $$\tau$$ uniquely, then use physical reasoning to decide whether it is the same for both planets. State the final answer choice.

label: FMA12
name: Scaling the Pitch of a Tuning Fork — Two tuning forks are made of the same material and have the same shape…
desc: Two tuning forks are made of the same material and have the same shape, but the second is $$1.5$$ times the size of the first in every dimension. The first fork rings at $$440\;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ With little knowledge of the physics of tuning forks, dimensional analysis still…
statement:
Two tuning forks are made of the same material and have the same shape, but the second is $$1.5$$ times the size of the first in every dimension. The first fork rings at $$440\;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ With little knowledge of the physics of tuning forks, dimensional analysis still predicts the second fork's frequency. The relevant variables are the material's Young's modulus $$Y$$ (a stiffness that, like pressure, has dimensions $$=ML^{-1}T^{-2}$$), the density $$\rho$$ with $$[\rho]=ML^{-3},$$ and the fork's length $$l.$$ A frequency has $$=T^{-1}.$$

__(a)__ Construct a formula for $$f$$ in terms of $$Y,\rho,$$ and $$l$$ (up to a dimensionless constant $$\alpha$$).

__(b)__ Use the scaling of your formula to find the frequency of the larger fork.

__(c)__ The combination $$\sqrt{Y/\rho}$$ resembles the speed of sound $$\sqrt{P/\rho}$$ in a gas. Interpret $$\sqrt{Y/\rho}$$ for the solid fork, and give a physical meaning to the relation $$f=\alpha\dfrac1l\sqrt{Y/\rho}$$ (equivalently $$T=\dfrac1\alpha\dfrac{l}{\sqrt{Y/\rho}}$$). A vibrating stretched string behaves the same way:
